It is summed over nitrogen ion charge states and excludes neutral nitrogen; it is not a charge-state-resolved density or a flux-surface average. The locus distinguishes this quantity from [nitrogen density at the plasma boundary](name:nitrogen_density_at_plasma_boundary), which represents the same charge-state-summed nitrogen-ion density at the plasma boundary rather than at the pedestal top.

rows.name: parallel_ion_charge_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient
rows.description: Fick's-law proportionality coefficient relating the density-normalized parallel diffusive thermal energy flux of a specified ion charge state to its local temperature gradient.
rows.documentation: The ion charge-state energy diffusion coefficient $D_{i,z,E,\parallel}$ quantifies gradient-driven diffusive transport of thermal energy carried by ions in one specified charge state $z$ along the magnetic field. It is the parallel component of the direction-agnostic [ion charge-state energy diffusion coefficient](name:ion_charge_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient). The defining relation for the density-normalized parallel diffusive energy flux is: $$ \frac{Q_{i,z,\parallel,\mathrm{diff}}}{n_{i,z}} = -D_{i,z,E,\parallel}\,\nabla_{\parallel} T_{i,z} $$ where $Q_{i,z,\parallel,\mathrm{diff}}$ is the parallel diffusive thermal-energy flux of charge state $z$, $n_{i,z}$ is its number density, $T_{i,z}$ is its temperature, and $\nabla_{\parallel}$ is the derivative along the magnetic-field direction. This coefficient applies to one specified ion charge state and is not summed over charge states. It excludes convective, advective, and $E \times B$ contributions; the broader [parallel ion energy diffusion coefficient](name:parallel_ion_energy_diffusion_coefficient) represents the corresponding transport aggregated over ion species.

rows.name: parallel_neutral_momentum_flux_limiter_coefficient
rows.description: Dimensionless factor scaling the collisionless free-streaming cap on the magnetic-field-parallel component of neutral momentum flux in edge-fluid transport closures.
rows.documentation: This coefficient sets the free-streaming upper bound on the parallel component of neutral-particle [momentum](name:momentum) flux in edge-fluid transport closures. Parallel denotes the local magnetic-field direction, used as a geometric reference without implying that neutral particles follow magnetic field lines. The limiting flux magnitude is defined by $$ \Pi^{0,\max}_{\parallel} = \alpha^0_{\parallel}\Pi^{0,\mathrm{fs}}_{\parallel} $$ where $\alpha^0_{\parallel}$ is this nonnegative limiter coefficient, $\Pi^{0,\mathrm{fs}}_{\parallel}$ is the nonnegative collisionless free-streaming reference magnitude, and $\Pi^{0,\max}_{\parallel}$ is the resulting upper bound. The superscript $0$ denotes neutral particles, and $\parallel$ denotes the magnetic-field-parallel component. The limited neutral momentum flux $\Pi^0_{\parallel}$ satisfies $|\Pi^0_{\parallel}|\leq\Pi^{0,\max}_{\parallel}$; limiting its magnitude does not reverse its direction. The free-streaming normalization and limiting function are specified by the transport closure, not by this coefficient alone. This quantity is the parallel directional component of the [neutral momentum flux-limiter coefficient](name:neutral_momentum_flux_limiter_coefficient), not the momentum flux itself or a momentum diffusivity. It applies to the selected neutral population without explicit internal-state resolution, unlike the [parallel neutral-state momentum flux-limiter coefficient](name:parallel_neutral_state_momentum_flux_limiter_coefficient). No summation or averaging rule for state-resolved coefficients is implied.

rows.name: particle_diffusivity
rows.description: Effective Fickian transport coefficient relating particle flux to particle-number-density gradients, with directional or population-specific components represented by more specific quantities.
rows.documentation: Particle diffusivity is an effective Fickian coefficient describing the diffusive part of particle transport driven by a particle-number-density gradient. It may be resolved by transport direction or by the particle population being transported. For each resolved direction $i$, the diffusive particle flux is defined by $$ \Gamma_{p,i}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{p,i}\,\frac{\partial n_p}{\partial x_i} $$ where $\Gamma_{p,i}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusive particle flux, $D_{p,i}$ is the corresponding diffusivity component, $n_p$ is the particle number density, and $x_i$ is the coordinate along the resolved transport direction. The minus sign defines down-gradient diffusive transport for a positive coefficient. This parent quantity does not specify a particle population, charge-state aggregation, transport direction, or microscopic mechanism. Population- and direction-specific instances include [neutral particle diffusivity](name:neutral_particle_diffusivity) and poloidal particle diffusivity.

rows.name: toroidal_argon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary
rows.description: Toroidal component in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame of the argon-ion bulk-flow velocity at the last closed flux surface.
rows.documentation: This quantity is the local toroidal component of the argon-ion bulk-flow velocity evaluated at the plasma boundary, identified with the last closed flux surface. It is a pointwise boundary value rather than an average over that flux surface. The charge-state-aggregated toroidal velocity is defined by $$ V_{\mathrm{Ar},\phi} = \frac{\sum_z n_{\mathrm{Ar},z} v_{\mathrm{Ar},z,\phi}}{\sum_z n_{\mathrm{Ar},z}} $$ where $V_{\mathrm{Ar},\phi}$ and $v_{\mathrm{Ar},z,\phi}$ are toroidal velocity components in m s$^{-1}$, $n_{\mathrm{Ar},z}$ is the argon-ion number density in m$^{-3}$, and $z$ indexes argon ion charge states. The toroidal component is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The local value is distinct from the toroidal flux-surface-averaged argon velocity at the plasma boundary, which averages the same component over the boundary flux surface. Neutral argon is excluded from the ion bulk-flow aggregation. Sign convention: Positive when the argon-ion bulk velocity projects onto the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

rows.name: toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_pedestal_top
rows.description: Toroidal component of the helium-3 ion fluid velocity at the pedestal top, resolved along the toroidal direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame. It is the density-weighted mean over all helium-3 ion charge states and is signed positive for flow toward increasing φ.
rows.documentation: Toroidal component of the helium-3 ion fluid velocity at the pedestal top is the helium-3 ion bulk-flow component resolved along $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. For species-level helium-3, this intensive quantity is the density-weighted mean over all helium-3 ion charge states at the pedestal top. The charge-state-aggregated toroidal component is defined by $$ v_{\phi,\,^3\mathrm{He}}^{\mathrm{ped}} = \frac{\sum_q n_{^3\mathrm{He}^{q+}}^{\mathrm{ped}}\left(\mathbf{v}_{^3\mathrm{He}^{q+}}^{\mathrm{ped}} \cdot \hat{\phi}\right)}{\sum_q n_{^3\mathrm{He}^{q+}}^{\mathrm{ped}}} $$ where $q$ indexes helium-3 ion charge state, $n_{^3\mathrm{He}^{q+}}^{\mathrm{ped}}$ is the number density of that charge state at the pedestal top, $\mathbf{v}_{^3\mathrm{He}^{q+}}^{\mathrm{ped}}$ is its ion fluid velocity there, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$. This quantity excludes radial and vertical components in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, vector speed, arithmetic averages over charge states, and values at other loci such as the [magnetic axis](name:toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_magnetic_axis). It is defined where the total helium-3 ion density in the averaging denominator is nonzero. Sign convention: Positive when the helium-3 ion fluid velocity is directed toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

rows.name: toroidal_ion_charge_state_momentum_source
rows.description: The toroidal component of the area-normalized momentum source for a specified ion charge state represents directional momentum transfer in an edge plasma.
rows.documentation: The toroidal component of the area-normalized momentum source for a specified ion charge state represents directional momentum transfer in an edge plasma. It is resolved for one ion species and charge state rather than summed over charge states. The toroidal component is defined by $$ S_{\phi,i,q} = \mathbf{S}_{i,q} \cdot \hat{\phi} $$ where $\mathbf{S}_{i,q}$ is the area-normalized momentum source for ion species $i$ in charge state $q$, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal unit vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. This quantity is the toroidal specialization of the charge-state-resolved vector [ion charge state momentum source](name:ion_charge_state_momentum_source). It represents net momentum transfer associated with ionization, recombination, charge exchange, and related collisional processes; unlike [toroidal ion momentum source](name:toroidal_ion_momentum_source), it is not summed over ion charge states. Its corresponding poloidal projection is [poloidal ion charge state momentum source](name:poloidal_ion_charge_state_momentum_source). Sign convention: Positive when the sourced momentum points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

rows.name: toroidal_iron_velocity_at_pedestal_top
rows.description: Density-weighted toroidal bulk-flow velocity of ionized iron at the core-side shoulder of the H-mode edge transport barrier, resolved along increasing toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
rows.documentation: Toroidal iron velocity at the pedestal top is the density-weighted mean bulk-flow velocity of ionized iron ions at the core-side shoulder of the H-mode edge transport barrier. It includes all populated iron charge states from Fe+ through fully stripped iron and excludes neutral iron. For charge states $q=1,\ldots,26$, the velocity is defined by $$ v_\phi^{\mathrm{Fe}} = \frac{\sum_{q=1}^{26} n_q u_{\phi,q}}{\sum_{q=1}^{26} n_q} $$ where $n_q$ is the number density of iron charge state $q$ in m$^{-3}$, $u_{\phi,q}$ is its toroidal bulk-flow component in m s$^{-1}$, and $v_\phi^{\mathrm{Fe}}$ is the resulting density-weighted velocity. This charge-state aggregation is distinct from a charge-state-resolved velocity and is analogous to [toroidal krypton velocity at the pedestal top](name:toroidal_krypton_velocity_at_pedestal_top); its locus differs from [toroidal iron velocity at the internal transport barrier](name:toroidal_iron_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier). Sign convention: Positive when the density-weighted iron-ion flow points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

rows.name: toroidal_momentum_flux_limiter_coefficient
rows.description: Dimensionless coefficient that scales the collisionless free-streaming upper bound on toroidal momentum-flux density in multi-fluid edge plasma transport closures, capping the flux magnitude while leaving its sign direction unchanged.
rows.documentation: In multi-fluid edge plasma transport models, gradient-driven diffusive closures can produce toroidal momentum-flux densities that exceed the physically realizable collisionless free-streaming limit in steep-gradient regions. A toroidal momentum-flux-limiter coefficient $\alpha_{m,\phi}$ is introduced to bound the effective $\hat{\phi}$-projected momentum-flux density, where $m$ denotes momentum and $\phi$ denotes the toroidal projection. The toroidal projection is along $\hat{\phi}$, the tangent to increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{R}, \hat{\phi}, \hat{Z})$ and $\hat{R} \times \hat{\phi} = \hat{Z}$. The bounded toroidal momentum-flux density satisfies the limiter constraint: $$ |\Pi_{\phi}^{\mathrm{lim}}| \le \alpha_{m,\phi}\,\Pi_{\phi}^{\mathrm{FS}} $$ where $\Pi_{\phi}^{\mathrm{lim}}$ is the limited toroidal momentum-flux density, $\Pi_{\phi}^{\mathrm{FS}}$ is the toroidal free-streaming momentum-flux reference scale, and $\alpha_{m,\phi}$ is the toroidal momentum-flux-limiter coefficient. This coefficient is the toroidal directional specialization of [momentum-flux-limiter coefficient](name:momentum_flux_limiter_coefficient), not a particle-, heat-, or energy-flux limiter and not the momentum-flux density itself. It is intrinsically non-negative: it caps the magnitude of the modeled toroidal momentum-flux density and does not carry the positive or negative sign of that flux. Directional siblings include the poloidal, radial, [parallel](name:parallel_momentum_flux_limiter_coefficient), and [diamagnetic](name:diamagnetic_momentum_flux_limiter_coefficient) momentum-flux-limiter coefficients.

rows.name: toroidal_neon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary
rows.description: Toroidal neon velocity at the plasma boundary is the toroidal component of the density-weighted bulk velocity of neon impurity ions at the last closed flux surface, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame. It is the density-weighted mean over all neon ion charge states and is local, not a flux-surface average.
rows.documentation: Toroidal neon velocity at the plasma boundary is the toroidal component of the density-weighted bulk velocity of neon impurity ions at the last closed flux surface. The toroidal component is taken in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. Because no neon ionization state is specified, the elemental neon velocity is the density-weighted mean over all neon ion charge states present at that locus. The component and charge-state aggregation are defined by $$ v_{\phi,\mathrm{Ne}} = \left(\frac{\sum_q n_{\mathrm{Ne}^{q+}}\,\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Ne}^{q+}}}{\sum_q n_{\mathrm{Ne}^{q+}}}\right) \cdot \hat{\phi} $$ where $q$ indexes neon ion charge states, $n_{\mathrm{Ne}^{q+}}$ is the number density of charge state $q$, $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Ne}^{q+}}$ is its bulk velocity, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$. This quantity is a local boundary value and does not imply a flux-surface average, poloidal average, toroidal average, or charge-state sum. The flux-surface-averaged boundary counterpart is toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_neon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary; the same toroidal component at other radial loci includes [toroidal_neon_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_neon_velocity_at_magnetic_axis) and [toroidal_neon_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:toroidal_neon_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier). Sign convention: Positive when the density-weighted neon ion flow is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

rows.name: total_ion_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer
rows.description: Positive e-folding distance for the outward decrease of total ion number density across magnetic flux surfaces in the scrape-off layer.
rows.documentation: This quantity is the positive cross-field decay length of the total ion number density in the scrape-off layer. It is the species- and charge-state-summed specialization of ion decay length over the scrape-off layer. $$ \lambda_{i,\mathrm{tot}} = \left|\frac{1}{n_{i,\mathrm{tot}}}\frac{\partial n_{i,\mathrm{tot}}}{\partial \ell_\perp}\right|^{-1} $$ Here $n_{i,\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total ion number density, summed over the included ion species and charge states, and $\ell_\perp$ is outward distance normal to magnetic flux surfaces, measured in m. The quantity excludes electron and neutral-particle densities and is non-negative by definition.

rows.name: tritium_density_at_pedestal_top
rows.description: Tritium ion number density at the top of the H-mode edge pedestal, summed over all tritium charge states.
rows.documentation: Tritium ion number density at the top of the H-mode edge pedestal is the local concentration of tritium ions at the core-side shoulder of the edge transport barrier. The charge-state-summed density is defined by $$ n_{\mathrm{T}} = \sum_z n_{\mathrm{T}}^{z+} $$ where $n_{\mathrm{T}}$ is the tritium ion number density, $n_{\mathrm{T}}^{z+}$ is the number density of tritium ions with charge state $z$, and $z$ is the positive integer charge state. For tritium, the physically ionized population has one positive charge state, so the sum reduces to the density of singly ionized tritium. The quantity applies only to tritium ions and is evaluated locally at the pedestal top, whose position is defined by the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate of the pedestal](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_pedestal). It is not a chord-, volume-, or species-averaged density, and it excludes neutral tritium and all non-tritium species. This is the tritium-specific component of [density at the pedestal top](name:density_at_pedestal_top), rather than the corresponding total or non-species-resolved density. The same tritium ion density concept evaluated at a different transport-barrier location is [tritium density at the internal transport barrier](name:tritium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier).

rows.name: tritium_density_at_plasma_boundary
rows.description: Number density of tritium ions at the plasma boundary, evaluated as the local, intensive particle count per physical volume on the last closed magnetic flux surface.
rows.documentation: Number density of tritium ions at the plasma boundary is the local, intensive particle count per physical volume for the tritium-ion population evaluated on the last closed magnetic flux surface. The plasma boundary is the limiting closed magnetic flux surface separating confined plasma from the open-field-line scrape-off-layer region. The local tritium-ion number density is the zeroth velocity moment of the tritium-ion distribution function at a boundary point: $$ n_\mathrm{T}(\mathbf{x}_b,t) = \int f_\mathrm{T}(\mathbf{x}_b,\mathbf{v},t)\,d^3v $$ where $n_\mathrm{T}$ is the tritium-ion number density, $\mathbf{x}_b$ is a point on the last closed magnetic flux surface, $t$ is time, $\mathbf{v}$ is tritium-ion velocity, $f_\mathrm{T}$ is the tritium-ion phase-space distribution function, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element. This quantity applies specifically to ionized tritium and excludes neutral tritium, deuterium, protium, electrons, impurity ions, and total ion density. It is a local boundary value, with no averaging over the boundary surface or over a volume; for tritium, the relevant positive ion population is singly ionized tritium, so no aggregation over multiple positive ionization stages is applied. It is the tritium-specific instance of [density at the plasma boundary](name:density_at_plasma_boundary). The related flux-surface-averaged tritium density at the plasma boundary instead represents the average of tritium-ion density over the same last closed magnetic flux surface, while [hydrogen density at the plasma boundary](name:hydrogen_density_at_plasma_boundary) and [deuterium density at the plasma boundary](name:deuterium_density_at_plasma_boundary) refer to different hydrogen-isotope ion populations.

rows.name: tungsten_density_at_separatrix
rows.description: Tungsten-ion number density on the last closed magnetic flux surface, summed over all positive ionization states and distinguished from its flux-surface average.
rows.documentation: Tungsten-ion number density at the plasma boundary represents the local population of positively charged tungsten ions on the separatrix, the last closed magnetic flux surface. The same physical quantity may also be evaluated as a flux-surface average over that boundary surface; the local and averaged forms are distinct. The charge-state-summed local density is defined from the velocity distributions by: $$ n_{\mathrm{W}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{Z=1}^{Z_{\max}} \int f_{\mathrm{W}}^{Z}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v $$ where $n_{\mathrm{W}}$ is the tungsten-ion number density, $\mathbf{x}$ is a position on the separatrix, $Z$ is the positive tungsten ion charge state, $Z_{\max}$ is the highest included charge state, $f_{\mathrm{W}}^{Z}$ is the velocity distribution of that charge state, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element. This quantity applies to tungsten ions evaluated at the plasma boundary and sums over all positive ionization states. It excludes neutral tungsten and does not select an individual charge state. The local form is evaluated at a boundary position, whereas the flux-surface-averaged tungsten density at the plasma boundary averages the same charge-state-summed density over the boundary flux surface. The flux-surface-averaged quantity is therefore an aggregation of this local density over the same separatrix, not a different species or charge-state convention. It is distinct from [volume-averaged tungsten density](name:volume_averaged_tungsten_density), which averages tungsten-ion density over the plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface.

rows.name: vertical_neutral_momentum_flux_limiter_coefficient
rows.description: Dimensionless vertical momentum flux-limiter coefficient that scales the free-streaming upper bound on neutral-particle momentum-flux density in edge-plasma transport closures.
rows.documentation: The vertical neutral momentum flux-limiter coefficient is the vertical component of the neutral-particle specialization of the general momentum flux-limiter coefficient vector, providing the dimensionless limiter factor for neutral momentum transport along the vertical $Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame in multi-fluid edge-plasma models. It bounds the vertical neutral momentum-flux density by the free-streaming limit when the neutral mean free path is large relative to macroscopic gradient scales. The vertical component $\alpha_Z$ is defined as the ratio of the magnitude of the modeled vertical neutral momentum-flux density to its positive free-streaming upper bound: $$ \alpha_Z = \frac{|\Pi_Z|}{\Pi_Z^{\rm free}}, \qquad \Pi_Z^{\rm free} = m_n n_n \left(u_Z^{\rm free}\right)^2 $$ where $\Pi_Z$ is the modeled vertical neutral momentum-flux density component along $\hat{Z}$, $\Pi_Z^{\rm free}$ is the corresponding free-streaming upper bound, $m_n$ is the neutral particle mass, $n_n$ is the neutral number density, and $u_Z^{\rm free}$ is the nonnegative free-streaming reference speed for neutral motion along $\hat{Z}$. The constraint $\alpha_Z \in [0, 1]$ makes the coefficient a magnitude limiter; any sign of the vertical momentum flux is carried by $\Pi_Z$, not by $\alpha_Z$. This quantity is the vertical member of the [neutral momentum flux-limiter coefficient](name:neutral_momentum_flux_limiter_coefficient) vector and is distinct from the [parallel neutral momentum flux-limiter coefficient](name:parallel_neutral_momentum_flux_limiter_coefficient), which is taken along the magnetic-field direction, and the toroidal neutral momentum flux-limiter coefficient, which is taken along $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is a limiter coefficient, not the neutral momentum-flux density itself.

rows.name: calibration_polarization_angle_of_optical_element
rows.description: Calibration polarization angle of an optical element is the signed angle from a reference transverse polarization direction to the element's selected polarization axis, viewed along its line of sight toward the plasma.
rows.documentation: Calibration polarization angle of an optical element is the orientation angle of the polarization-selective axis of that element in the plane perpendicular to its line of sight. It identifies the electric-field component selected by the element relative to a defined transverse reference direction. The signed angle is defined by $$ \alpha_\mathrm{cal} = \operatorname{atan2}\!\left[-\hat{\ell}\cdot\left(\hat{e}_\mathrm{ref}\times\hat{e}_\mathrm{sel}\right),\ \hat{e}_\mathrm{ref}\cdot\hat{e}_\mathrm{sel}\right] $$ where $\hat{\ell}$ is the line-of-sight unit vector directed from the optical element toward the plasma, $\hat{e}_\mathrm{ref}$ is the reference polarization unit vector in the plane normal to $\hat{\ell}$, and $\hat{e}_\mathrm{sel}$ is the selected polarization-axis unit vector in the same transverse plane. This quantity is an axis-alignment calibration parameter, not a measure of polarization ellipticity, polarization purity, or the handedness of a full polarization state. Sign convention: Positive when the selected polarization axis is rotated counter-clockwise from the reference transverse polarization direction as seen looking from the optical element toward the plasma along the line of sight.

rows.name: length_variation_of_interferometer_beam
rows.description: Signed plasma-induced change in the effective optical path accumulated along an interferometer beam relative to its corresponding no-plasma reference path.
rows.documentation: This quantity is the signed plasma-induced change in effective optical path length accumulated along an electromagnetic propagation path represented by an interferometer beam. It describes an optical delay or advance caused by the plasma, rather than the unperturbed geometric path length. The variation is defined as $$ \Delta L = L_{\mathrm{plasma}} - L_{\mathrm{ref}} $$ where $\Delta L$ is the optical path-length variation, $L_{\mathrm{plasma}}$ is the effective optical path along the beam in the presence of plasma, and $L_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the corresponding effective path without plasma. This quantity applies to the net change accumulated along the interferometer beam's complete line of sight. It is a path-integrated optical quantity, not a local path-length density, an unperturbed geometric length, or a separate phase-calibration coefficient. As the variation of [length of an interferometer beam](name:length_of_interferometer_beam), it expresses the plasma-induced departure from the reference path. The associated phase shift provides the optical information used to derive [line-integrated electron number density](name:line_integrated_electron_number_density). Sign convention: Positive when the plasma-affected effective optical path length exceeds the corresponding no-plasma reference path.

rows.name: line_averaged_electron_density
rows.description: Number density of free electrons averaged along a specified plasma chord with equal path-length weighting, excluding electrons bound in atoms, molecules, or ions.
rows.documentation: Number density of electron The line average is defined by $$\bar{f} = \frac{1}{L}\int_0^L f\,dl$$ where $\bar{n}_e$ is the line-averaged electron density, $n_e$ is the local free-electron number density evaluated along the chord, $L$ is the positive length of the specified chord, and $l$ is distance along it. The integration interval and length denominator refer to the same chord segment. The electron population includes thermal and nonthermal free electrons over the full velocity distribution; electrons bound in atoms, molecules, or ions are excluded. The average uses equal path-length weighting, without additional density or volume weighting. Unlike [volume-averaged electron density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density), this quantity averages along a chord rather than over the plasma volume. It equals the local density everywhere on the chord only when that density is uniform. The [line-integrated electron number density](name:line_integrated_electron_number_density) is instead a column abundance; dividing that abundance by its corresponding path length yields this mean when both quantities refer to the same path. The [line-averaged xenon density](name:line_averaged_xenon_density) applies the same chord-mean operation to xenon ions rather than electrons. The [ratio of line-averaged electron density to Greenwald density](name:ratio_of_line_averaged_electron_density_to_greenwald_density) uses this electron chord mean as its numerator and is a separate normalized quantity.

rows.name: parallel_wave_electric_field_real_part
rows.description: Signed in-phase quadrature of the coherent wave electric-field phasor projected along the local equilibrium magnetic field, relative to the chosen wave phase reference.
rows.documentation: This quantity is the signed in-phase quadrature of the wave electric-field phasor parallel to the local equilibrium magnetic field. It describes local wave polarization along a beam or ray path relative to a chosen phase reference. The defining projection and real-part operation are $$ E_{\parallel,\mathrm{R}} = \operatorname{Re}\widetilde E_\parallel = \operatorname{Re}\left(\widetilde{\mathbf E}\cdot\hat{\mathbf b}\right) $$ where $E_{\parallel,\mathrm{R}}$ is this real quadrature, $\widetilde E_\parallel$ is the [parallel wave electric-field phasor](name:parallel_wave_electric_field), $\widetilde{\mathbf E}$ is the full wave electric-field phasor, and $\hat{\mathbf b}$ is the unit vector along the local equilibrium magnetic field. Together with the [imaginary quadrature](name:parallel_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part), denoted $E_{\parallel,\mathrm{I}}$, it reconstructs the parent phasor through $\widetilde E_\parallel=E_{\parallel,\mathrm{R}}+iE_{\parallel,\mathrm{I}}$, where $i$ is the imaginary unit. Its value depends on the phase reference; it is neither the phasor magnitude nor the instantaneous oscillating field. The quantity is local along the propagation path, not a path integral or average, and excludes the equilibrium electric field. Unlike the [left-hand circularly polarized wave electric-field real part](name:left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_real_part), it resolves the field-aligned component rather than a transverse circular polarization component. Sign convention: Positive when the in-phase wave electric-field projection points along the local equilibrium magnetic field at the chosen phase reference.

rows.name: perpendicular_refractive_index
rows.description: Magnitude of the electromagnetic wave vector perpendicular to the local background magnetic field, normalized by the vacuum wave number at the same frequency.
rows.documentation: The perpendicular refractive index is the magnitude of the component of the [refractive-index vector](name:refractive_index) perpendicular to the local background magnetic field. It describes the field-transverse part of electromagnetic phase propagation. Its defining relation is $$ n_\perp = \left|\mathbf{n} - (\mathbf{n}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}})\hat{\mathbf{b}}\right| = \frac{k_\perp}{k_0} $$ where $n_\perp$ is the perpendicular refractive index, $\mathbf{n}$ is the refractive-index vector, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is the unit vector along the local background magnetic field, $k_\perp$ is the [perpendicular wave-vector magnitude](name:perpendicular_wave_vector_magnitude), and $k_0$ is the vacuum wave number at the same wave frequency. Vertical bars denote the Euclidean vector magnitude. This quantity is evaluated locally along a beam or ray path, rather than averaged or integrated along that path, and is not restricted to electron cyclotron emission. It is nonnegative and retains no direction within the perpendicular plane; it is therefore distinct from a signed projection onto a specified transverse axis. For a real phase-gradient vector, $|\mathbf{n}|^2 = n_\parallel^2 + n_\perp^2$, where $n_\parallel$ is the signed [parallel refractive index](name:parallel_refractive_index). The two quantities resolve the parent vector's magnitude relative to the magnetic-field direction.

rows.name: radiative_temperature_at_ece_channel
rows.description: Equivalent blackbody temperature of electron cyclotron emission intensity detected by a frequency-selective ECE channel, representing the radiation brightness temperature.
rows.documentation:
Radiative temperature at an ECE channel is the equivalent blackbody temperature associated with the detected electron cyclotron emission intensity at that channel's selected frequency. It is a brightness-temperature representation of the radiation, not the kinetic temperature of the electron population. For specific intensity represented by a blackbody spectrum, the radiation temperature $T_{\mathrm{rad}}$ is defined by $$ I_
u =  rac{2h
u^3}{c^2}\left[\exp\left( rac{h
u}{T_{\mathrm{rad}}}ight)-1ight]^{-1} $$ where $I_
u$ is the detected specific intensity at frequency $
u$, $h$ is Planck's constant, $c$ is the speed of light, and $T_{\mathrm{rad}}$ is the energy-equivalent blackbody temperature. The quantity applies to one ECE channel and its selected frequency; it is not summed or averaged over channels. It excludes the separate kinetic electron temperature and polarization-resolved radiation quantities. When the emitting plasma is optically thick, $T_{\mathrm{rad}}$ approaches the local electron temperature. The [radiative temperature at the magnetic axis](name:radiative_temperature_at_magnetic_axis) uses the same brightness-temperature definition at a different evaluation locus.

rows.name: refractive_index
rows.description: Dimensionless ratio of an electromagnetic wave’s phase-gradient vector to its vacuum wavenumber, retaining propagation direction and signed components.
rows.documentation: The refractive-index vector describes electromagnetic phase propagation relative to propagation in vacuum. It preserves the direction of the wave phase gradient while expressing its magnitude relative to the vacuum reference. The defining relation is $$ \mathbf{n} = \frac{\mathbf{k}}{k_0}, \qquad k_0 = \frac{\omega}{c} $$ where $\mathbf{n}$ is the refractive-index vector, $\mathbf{k}$ is the wave vector, $k_0$ is the vacuum wavenumber, $\omega$ is the wave angular frequency, and $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum. Directional representations include the projection parallel to the local magnetic field, represented by [parallel_refractive_index](name:parallel_refractive_index), and the magnitude of the perpendicular projection, represented by [perpendicular_refractive_index](name:perpendicular_refractive_index). The same normalized phase-propagation concept applies to propagation through an optical element.

rows.name: total_electron_count
rows.description: Total inventory of free electrons within the plasma, including thermal and fast populations and excluding electrons bound in atoms or molecules.
rows.documentation: The total free-electron count is the number of unbound electrons contained within the plasma volume, aggregated over all electron populations. $$ N_e = \int_V n_e(\mathbf{x})\,dV $$ where $N_e$ is the total free-electron count, $n_e(\mathbf{x})$ is the local [total electron density](name:total_electron_density), $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $dV$ is the differential volume element, and $V$ is the plasma volume. This quantity includes thermal, fast, and other free-electron populations present within $V$ and sums them over the entire plasma volume. It excludes electrons bound in neutral atoms or molecules and is distinct from local or volume-averaged density, which describes electrons per physical volume rather than the integrated inventory. The count is obtained by integrating the complete local electron density; a [line-averaged electron density](name:line_averaged_electron_density) represents a chord average and cannot substitute for this volume integral.

rows.name: vertical_wave_electric_field
rows.description: Complex phasor of an electromagnetic-wave electric field projected onto the vertical Z direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, preserving local amplitude and phase.
rows.documentation: The vertical wave electric field is the complex phasor obtained by projecting the electromagnetic-wave electric-field phasor onto the vertical basis direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. It is the Z-directed component of the [wave electric field](name:wave_electric_field), retaining its local amplitude and phase. The projection is defined by $$ \widetilde{E}_Z(\mathbf{r},\omega)=\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}_{\mathrm{wave}}(\mathbf{r},\omega)\cdot\hat{\mathbf{Z}} $$ where $\widetilde{E}_Z$ is the vertical wave-electric-field phasor, $\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}_{\mathrm{wave}}$ is the complex wave-electric-field vector phasor, $\mathbf{r}$ is position, $\omega$ is angular frequency, and $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the vertical unit vector. This wave contribution is distinct from the static [vertical electric field](name:vertical_electric_field) and from the field-aligned [parallel wave electric field](name:parallel_wave_electric_field). Sign convention: Positive when the electric-field phasor projection is along $+\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$, the direction of increasing vertical coordinate $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

rows.name: vertical_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam
rows.description: Signed vertical component of the electromagnetic wave vector along a beam-tracing beam, giving local spatial phase variation with vertical height.
rows.documentation: The vertical wave-vector component is the signed projection of the local electromagnetic wave vector onto the vertical direction, evaluated locally along a beam-tracing beam. The component is defined by $$ k_Z = \mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{z}} = \frac{\partial S}{\partial Z}. $$ Here $k_Z$ is the vertical wave-vector component, $\mathbf{k}$ is the local [wave vector](name:wave_vector), and $S$ is the wave phase whose spatial gradient is $\mathbf{k}$. The unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ points along the positive toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is the [vertical coordinate of the beam position](name:vertical_coordinate_of_beam_tracing_beam). This quantity applies pointwise along the beam path and is not restricted to the launch point; no path integration or averaging is implied. It retains the spatial phase scale, unlike the [normalized vertical wave-vector component](name:vertical_wave_vector_normalized_of_beam_tracing_beam), which equals $k_Z/|\mathbf{k}|$ for a nonzero wave vector, where $|\mathbf{k}|$ is the wave-vector magnitude. Sign convention: Positive when the wave vector has a component toward increasing vertical coordinate $Z$.

rows.name: current_weighted_average_external_magnetic_flux
rows.description: Current-weighted average external magnetic flux is the component-wise mean of magnetic flux produced by sources outside the plasma, weighted over the plasma current-carrying region by the corresponding current density. It excludes flux generated by the plasma current itself; concrete children specify components such as the poloidal component.
rows.documentation: Current-weighted average external magnetic flux is the component-wise mean of externally generated magnetic flux over the plasma current-carrying region. It represents the part of the magnetic flux linked by the plasma current that is generated by sources outside the plasma, with the plasma self-generated flux excluded. For any component $a$, the current-weighted component average is $$ \overline{\Phi}_{\mathrm{ext},a}^{J} = \frac{\int_{\Omega_a} \Phi_{\mathrm{ext},a}(\mathbf{x})\, j_a(\mathbf{x})\, dA} {\int_{\Omega_a} j_a(\mathbf{x})\, dA} $$ where $a$ labels a magnetic-flux component, $\overline{\Phi}_{\mathrm{ext},a}^{J}$ is the current-weighted average external magnetic-flux component, $\Phi_{\mathrm{ext},a}(\mathbf{x})$ is the externally generated magnetic-flux component at position $\mathbf{x}$, $j_a(\mathbf{x})$ is the corresponding plasma current-density component used as the weight, $\Omega_a$ is the current-carrying plasma cross-section for that component, and $dA$ is its area element. The denominator is the corresponding total plasma current component and must be nonzero. This parent quantity does not specify a particular magnetic-flux component or surface orientation. Concrete component names supply that specialization; for example, [poloidal current-weighted average external magnetic flux](name:poloidal_current_weighted_average_external_magnetic_flux) is the poloidal component. External magnetic flux includes contributions from active conductors and passive induced currents outside the plasma and excludes flux produced by the plasma current. Sign convention: Positive when the current-density-weighted integral of the selected external magnetic-flux component has the same sign as the total plasma current component used for its normalization, with both signs evaluated in the positive orientation of that component.

rows.name: derivative_of_volume_of_flux_surface_with_respect_to_toroidal_flux_coordinate
rows.description: Geometric rate at which the cumulative volume enclosed by a nested magnetic flux surface changes with its dimensionful toroidal-flux coordinate.
rows.documentation: This quantity is the geometric derivative of the cumulative volume enclosed by a nested magnetic flux surface with respect to the dimensionful toroidal-flux coordinate. It describes how rapidly the enclosed region expands as the flux-surface label changes. The defining relation is $$ \frac{dV}{d\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}} $$ where $V$ is the [volume enclosed by a flux surface](name:volume_of_flux_surface) and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the dimensionful toroidal-flux coordinate labeling the nested surfaces. The quantity applies to the three-dimensional region inside each selected nested magnetic flux surface. The volume is cumulative, beginning at the magnetic axis and extending to the specified surface; this is not a local plasma-population quantity and carries no species weighting. It is the derivative with respect to the toroidal-flux coordinate, not the volume itself or the derivative of the enclosed poloidal area. As the derivative of [volume enclosed by a flux surface](name:volume_of_flux_surface), it provides the volume increment associated with a change in toroidal-flux coordinate and serves as a geometric coefficient in flux-surface-averaged transport relations. The derivative of area with respect to the toroidal-flux coordinate is the analogous area derivative, while [the temporal derivative of this volume derivative](name:time_derivative_of_derivative_of_volume_of_flux_surface_with_respect_to_toroidal_flux_coordinate) describes its change in time.

rows.name: external_magnetic_flux
rows.description: External magnetic flux is the signed surface integral of the magnetic field generated by sources outside the plasma current distribution over an oriented surface.
rows.documentation: External magnetic flux is the signed surface integral of the magnetic field generated by sources outside the plasma current distribution over an oriented surface. It is the source-separated member of the [magnetic flux](name:magnetic_flux) family. The defining surface integral is: $$ \Phi_{\mathrm{ext}}(S) = \int_S \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{ext}} \cdot d\mathbf{A} $$ where $\Phi_{\mathrm{ext}}(S)$ is the external magnetic flux associated with the oriented surface $S$, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is the magnetic-field vector produced by sources outside the plasma current distribution, and $d\mathbf{A}$ is the oriented surface-area element. The scope is the external-source contribution integrated over the complete surface specified by a concrete specialization. At this parent level, no poloidal or toroidal projection, spatial locus, or averaging weight is imposed; the quantity is a signed surface aggregate, not a local magnetic-field value, a flux-surface average, or a contribution generated by the plasma current itself. The child [average external magnetic flux](name:average_external_magnetic_flux) is a concrete poloidal specialization with averaging over the plasma cross-section. The related [current-weighted average external magnetic flux](name:current_weighted_average_external_magnetic_flux) uses plasma-current weighting for that aggregation; both remain source-separated instances of external magnetic flux. Sign convention: Positive when the net external magnetic field points along the positive normal of the oriented integration surface in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

rows.name: flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_major_radius
rows.description: Flux-surface average of reciprocal squared major radius, providing a geometric metric coefficient for parallel-gradient and neoclassical transport calculations.
rows.documentation: This quantity is the flux-surface average of the reciprocal square of the major radius on a nested equilibrium magnetic flux surface. It is a positive geometric metric coefficient used in parallel-gradient operators and neoclassical and gyrokinetic transport equations. It is defined by $$ g_{m1}(\psi)=\left\langle \frac{1}{R^2}\right\rangle_{\psi} $$ where $g_{m1}$ denotes this metric coefficient, $R$ is the major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux labeling the surface, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\psi}$ denotes the flux-surface average on that surface. The quantity applies to the entire magnetic flux surface and has no species, field-component, or source-process restriction. Its aggregation convention is a flux-surface average of the local reciprocal-square geometric factor; it is not the reciprocal square of a flux-surface-averaged major radius. It is the flux-surface-averaged form of the pointwise [inverse of square of major radius](name:inverse_of_square_of_major_radius). It differs from the related [flux-surface-averaged inverse of major radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_major_radius), which averages the first reciprocal power of $R$ rather than its reciprocal square.

rows.name: flux_surface_averaged_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude
rows.description: Flux-surface average of the squared magnitude of the total equilibrium magnetic field, providing a geometric coefficient for equilibrium and neoclassical transport relations.
rows.documentation:
This quantity is the surface-averaged squared strength of the total magnetic field on a nested magnetic flux surface. It is a geometric metric coefficient used in equilibrium descriptions and in bounce-averaged and neoclassical transport relations. The flux-surface average is defined by $$ \left\langle B^2 ightangle_\psi =  rac{\displaystyle\oint_{S(\psi)}  rac{B^2}{\lvert
abla\psivert}\,dS}{\displaystyle\oint_{S(\psi)}  rac{1}{\lvert
abla\psivert}\,dS} $$ where $B^2$ is the [square of the magnetic-field magnitude](name:square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude), $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic-flux label of the surface, $S(\psi)$ is the closed magnetic flux surface with that label, $
abla\psi$ is the gradient of the flux label, and $dS$ is the surface-area element. The quantity applies to the total equilibrium magnetic field, including all of its components, and is aggregated over each closed flux surface with the inverse-$\lvert
abla\psivert$ weighting shown above. It is not the pointwise value of $B^2$, the square of a flux-surface-averaged magnetic-field magnitude, or a single magnetic-field component. It is the flux-surface-averaged form of [square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude](name:square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude). It differs from [flux_surface_averaged_magnetic_field_magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_magnetic_field_magnitude), which averages the field magnitude before squaring, and from [flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude), which averages its reciprocal.

rows.name: flux_surface_averaged_toroidal_current_density
rows.description: Flux-surface-averaged toroidal current density is the net conventional toroidal charge flux per area, averaged over a closed magnetic surface with additional inverse-major-radius weighting.
rows.documentation:
Flux-surface-averaged toroidal current density is the signed geometric toroidal component of the net plasma current density, averaged over a closed magnetic flux surface with additional inverse-major-radius weighting. The defining weighted average is $$\langle fangle = \oint f\,dS/|
abla\psi| \,/\, \oint dS/|
abla\psi|$$ where $j_\phi^{\mathrm{FS}}$ is this averaged current density, $j_\phi$ is the local [toroidal current density](name:toroidal_current_density), $R$ is major radius, and $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux labeling the selected surface. Angle brackets denote the flux-surface average, defined by $\langle fangle = \oint f\,dS/|
abla\psi| \,/\, \oint dS/|
abla\psi|$, where $f$ is the averaged quantity, $S$ is the closed magnetic surface, $dS$ is its area element, and $
abla\psi$ is the poloidal-flux gradient. The quantity includes the net contribution from all plasma current-carrying populations and mechanisms over the complete selected surface, including closed surfaces in the core plasma. It is neither a pointwise current density nor the total current through the enclosed plasma cross-section. The additional inverse-major-radius weighting distinguishes it from the ordinary flux-surface average $\langle j_\phiangle$. The underlying [current-density vector](name:current_density) is projected onto the geometric toroidal direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $\phi$ is toroidal angle and $Z$ is vertical height. Unlike [flux-surface-averaged parallel current density](name:flux_surface_averaged_parallel_current_density), this quantity uses the geometric toroidal projection rather than a magnetic-field-aligned projection. Sign convention: Positive when the weighted net conventional current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, counterclockwise when viewed from above.

rows.name: height_of_plasma_filament
rows.description: Full vertical extent of the rectangular cross-section of a discrete plasma current-carrying filament element, measured along the machine’s vertical axis.
rows.documentation: This quantity is the full vertical dimension of the rectangular cross-section associated with one discrete plasma current-carrying filament. It is a geometric extent, not the filament current or its current density. The height $H$ is defined by the difference between the upper and lower vertical coordinates: $$ H = Z_{\mathrm{upper}} - Z_{\mathrm{lower}} $$ where $Z_{\mathrm{upper}}$ and $Z_{\mathrm{lower}}$ are the upper and lower coordinates in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, with $Z$ denoting vertical height and $\hat{Z}$ the vertical basis direction. This quantity applies only to the vertical dimension of the rectangular filament cross-section. The horizontal full width is defined separately by [plasma filament width](name:plasma_filament_width), while the in-plane thickness is defined by thickness of plasma filament.

rows.name: inner_squareness_of_flux_surface
rows.description: Dimensionless Luce shape coefficient quantifying how much the high-field-side (inner) corners of a nested magnetic flux surface deviate from a reference ellipse; positive values indicate a boxier corner, negative values a more diamond-like or indented corner.
rows.documentation: The inner squareness of a flux surface is the dimensionless Luce (2013) shape coefficient that characterizes how much the high-field-side (inboard, smaller major radius) corners of a nested toroidal magnetic flux surface depart from a reference ellipse sharing the same center, horizontal half-width, and [elongation](name:elongation_of_flux_surface). It is the inboard counterpart within the [squareness_of_flux_surface](name:squareness_of_flux_surface) family, complementing the outboard variants [upper_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:upper_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface) and [lower_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:lower_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface). This parent quantity abstracts over the quadrant-resolved coefficients [upper_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:upper_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface) and [lower_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:lower_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface), which independently describe the upper and lower high-field-side corners. The coefficient $\zeta$ enters the parametric flux-surface shape model as an additional harmonic beyond elongation $\kappa$ and triangularity $\delta$, evaluated at the high-field-side corners of the poloidal cross-section in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. A value of zero recovers the reference ellipse precisely; deviations capture corner shaping not expressible through $\kappa$ and $\delta$ alone. The inner squareness is inferred from equilibrium reconstruction by fitting closed flux-surface contours to a multi-parameter shape model. Asymmetry between upper and lower inner quadrants can arise in vertically asymmetric or diverted configurations, motivating the quadrant-resolved child quantities.

rows.name: inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude
rows.description: Reciprocal square of total magnetic-field strength, providing a positive magnetic-geometry factor for equilibrium and flux-surface-averaged transport relations.
rows.documentation: The inverse square of total magnetic-field strength is a local magnetic-geometry factor that increases as the total field weakens and remains positive wherever the field magnitude is nonzero. It is defined as the reciprocal of the [square of magnetic-field magnitude](name:square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude): $$ B^{-2} = \frac{1}{B^2} = \frac{1}{\lvert \mathbf{B} \rvert^2} $$ where $\mathbf{B}$ is the total magnetic-field vector and $B$ is its magnitude. The quantity applies to the full magnetic field in an equilibrium plasma, including all vector components and without restriction to a particle population. At the parent level it is a local quantity with no flux-surface or volume aggregation; it is distinct from the squared field magnitude itself and from the reciprocal square of any selected field component. The [flux-surface-averaged inverse square of magnetic-field magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude) is obtained by applying a flux-surface average to this local factor. The averaging is a separate aggregation operation and does not alter the reciprocal-square transformation.

rows.name: inverse_of_square_of_major_radius
rows.description: Geometric inverse-square-major-radius coefficient for toroidal plasma equilibrium, including flux-surface-averaged forms used in magnetic-geometry relations.
rows.documentation: This quantity represents the reciprocal-square major-radius dependence of a geometric coefficient in toroidal plasma equilibrium. It characterizes the metric scaling associated with the distance from the machine symmetry axis. For the direct inverse-square form, the coefficient is defined by $$ K_R = \frac{1}{R^2} $$ where $K_R$ is the inverse-square-major-radius coefficient and $R$ is the major radius in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. The quantity applies to toroidal equilibrium geometry and is not the major radius itself or its direct square. It denotes the inverse-square geometric factor; any aggregation over a magnetic flux surface is an additional operation rather than part of the unaggregated quantity. The [flux-surface-averaged inverse-square-major-radius coefficient](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_major_radius) is the corresponding instance obtained by averaging this inverse-square factor over a magnetic flux surface. The quantity is therefore the reciprocal-square counterpart of [square_of_major_radius](name:square_of_major_radius), with the inverse relationship supplying the geometric scaling.

rows.name: lower_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary
rows.description: Dimensionless Luce squareness parameter for the lower-inner (below-midplane, high-field-side) plasma boundary in a poloidal cross-section at fixed toroidal angle φ in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, measuring its departure from the reference ellipse set by boundary minor radius, elongation, and triangularity.
rows.documentation: The lower-inner squareness of the plasma boundary is the dimensionless Luce shape coefficient quantifying how much the lower-inboard quadrant of the last-closed flux surface deviates from the reference ellipse determined by the boundary minor radius, elongation, and triangularity. The lower-inboard quadrant is the part of the boundary at smaller major radius and below the reference-ellipse center in a poloidal cross-section. In the Luce higher-order boundary parameterization, the lower-inner boundary contour at fixed toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame is represented over the lower-inboard interval of the poloidal angle $\theta$ by the coefficient $\zeta_{\mathrm{LI}}$: $$ \begin{aligned} R(\theta) &= R_{\mathrm{geo}} + a\cos\!\left[\theta + \arcsin(\delta_{\mathrm{ref}})\sin\theta - \zeta_{\mathrm{LI}}\sin(2\theta)\right],\\ Z(\theta) &= Z_{\mathrm{geo}} + a\kappa_{\mathrm{ref}}\sin\!\left[\theta + \zeta_{\mathrm{LI}}\sin(2\theta)\right] \end{aligned} $$ where $R(\theta)$ and $Z(\theta)$ are the major-radius and vertical coordinates of the boundary point, $R_{\mathrm{geo}}$ and $Z_{\mathrm{geo}}$ are the coordinates of the geometric center of the reference ellipse, $a$ is the boundary minor radius, $\kappa_{\mathrm{ref}}$ and $\delta_{\mathrm{ref}}$ are the elongation and triangularity entering the same reference boundary description, and $\theta=0$ labels the outboard midplane with increasing $\theta$ first moving toward $+Z$. The geometric center of the reference ellipse is not the magnetic-axis position unless those points coincide for the chosen boundary geometry. This quantity is restricted to the lower-inboard quadrant and excludes the upper-inboard quadrant represented by [upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary). It is a quadrant-resolved component of [inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary), distinct from the outer-side squareness components, and complements [elongation_of_plasma_boundary](name:elongation_of_plasma_boundary) and [triangularity_of_plasma_boundary](name:triangularity_of_plasma_boundary) in describing boundary shape beyond the reference ellipse. With the sign shown in the Luce representation, positive $\zeta_{\mathrm{LI}}$ moves the lower-inboard corner toward smaller $R$ and lower $Z$ relative to the reference ellipse, making that corner more rectangular; negative values make it rounder.

rows.name: magnetic_field
rows.description: Local total magnetic-induction vector in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where R is major radius, φ is toroidal angle, and Z is vertical height; it does not select a source contribution, perturbation state, component, magnitude reduction, or evaluation locus.
rows.documentation: Local total magnetic-induction vector is the magnetic flux-density vector at a point, carrying both the local field direction and field strength. It is the unqualified parent quantity before selecting a source contribution, perturbation state, component, scalar reduction, spatial aggregation, or evaluation locus. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the vector resolves into radial, toroidal, and vertical components as $$ \mathbf{B} = B_R\hat{\mathbf{R}} + B_\phi\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} + B_Z\hat{\mathbf{Z}} $$ where $\mathbf{B}$ is this local total magnetic-induction vector; $B_R$ is its radial projection, $B_\phi$ is its [toroidal magnetic-field component](name:toroidal_magnetic_field), and $B_Z$ is its [vertical magnetic-field component](name:vertical_magnetic_field); and $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$, $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$, and $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ are the corresponding basis vectors. The frame is right-handed with $\hat{\mathbf{R}} \times \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} = \hat{\mathbf{Z}}$; $R$ is major radius measured from the symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counterclockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$, and $Z$ is vertical height. The quantity applies wherever a local magnetic induction is defined, including confined plasma and surrounding vacuum regions, and no particle species or population is selected or aggregated. It is pointwise and vector-valued: it is not the [magnetic field magnitude](name:magnetic_field_magnitude), a flux-surface-average magnetic field, or an extremum such as the [maximum magnetic field](name:maximum_magnetic_field). No cylindrical component, source contribution, perturbation state, or named locus is implied by the unqualified name. When a [magnetic vector potential](name:magnetic_vector_potential) $\mathbf{A}$ is used, $\mathbf{B} = \nabla \times \mathbf{A}$; $\mathbf{A}$ is the magnetic vector potential and $\nabla \times$ is the curl operator, and a gage change affects $\mathbf{A}$ without changing $\mathbf{B}$. Source-qualified fields such as the [vacuum magnetic field](name:vacuum_magnetic_field) and [plasma magnetic field](name:plasma_magnetic_field) are vector contributions of the same kind and add vectorially when they belong to the same electromagnetic state; the [toroidal vacuum magnetic field](name:toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field) is the toroidal projection of the vacuum contribution. The [reference magnetic field](name:reference_magnetic_field) is a reference total magnetic-induction vector of the same kind, not a source-specific contribution; the [toroidal magnetic field at the magnetic axis](name:toroidal_magnetic_field_at_magnetic_axis) is the toroidal projection evaluated at the magnetic-axis locus. Sign convention: Positive when the vacuum toroidal magnetic-field component is directed along increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

rows.name: magnetic_field_at_pedestal_top_high_field_side
rows.description: Magnetic field at the high-field-side pedestal top is the local total magnetic-induction vector evaluated at the high-field-side pressure-pedestal top. It retains field strength and direction before any component selection or magnitude reduction.
rows.documentation: Magnetic field at the high-field-side pedestal top is the local total magnetic-induction vector evaluated at the high-field-side pressure-pedestal top. It includes all directional components of the local magnetic field at that locus and preserves both field strength and direction. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ major radius, $\phi$ toroidal angle, and $Z$ vertical height, the vector may be decomposed as $$ \mathbf{B} = B_R \hat{R} + B_\phi \hat{\phi} + B_Z \hat{Z} $$ where $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field at the high-field-side pedestal top, $B_R$, $B_\phi$, and $B_Z$ are its radial, toroidal, and vertical components at the same locus, and $\hat{R}$, $\hat{\phi}$, and $\hat{Z}$ are the corresponding unit basis vectors. The scope is restricted to the high-field-side branch of the pressure-pedestal top, not to arbitrary plasma positions or to the low-field-side pedestal top. The high-field side is the smaller-major-radius side in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where the toroidal magnetic-field magnitude is larger. The quantity is local at that locus; it is not a spatial average or a flux-surface average. This is a vector quantity, not the scalar [magnetic-field magnitude at the high-field-side pedestal top](name:magnetic_field_magnitude_at_pedestal_top_high_field_side), a single component, a projection, an absolute value, or a vacuum-field approximation. The scalar magnetic-field magnitude at the same locus is the Euclidean norm $|\mathbf{B}|$ of this vector and therefore removes directional information while retaining the shared high-field-side pedestal-top evaluation locus. Sign convention: Positive when a signed component of $\mathbf{B}$ points along the positive direction of the basis vector used for that component; in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame these directions are $+\hat{R}$, increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, and $+\hat{Z}$.

rows.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate
rows.description: Normalized toroidal flux coordinate labels magnetic surfaces by the square root of their axis-to-boundary toroidal-flux fraction, spanning zero at the magnetic axis to one at the equilibrium boundary.
rows.documentation: Normalized toroidal flux coordinate The coordinate is defined by $$ \rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} = \rho_{\mathrm{tor}}/\rho_{\mathrm{tor,b}} $$ where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is the normalized toroidal flux coordinate, $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal flux coordinate of the selected surface, and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,b}}$ is the [toroidal flux coordinate at the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_plasma_boundary). Both unnormalized coordinates use the same magnetic-axis origin and flux reference. Equivalently, $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}^2 = (\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}-\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}})/(\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,b}}-\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}})$, where $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by the selected surface, and $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}$ and $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,b}}$ are its magnetic-axis and equilibrium-boundary values. On nested closed magnetic surfaces, the nonnegative coordinate is constant on each surface, zero at the magnetic axis, and one at the last closed flux surface used as the boundary. It is a surface label, not a surface average, volume integral, geometric distance, toroidal angle, or vector component. The boundary normalization must be nonzero; the definition does not itself specify a continuation outside the last closed flux surface. Signed line-of-sight variants attach an additional geometric branch sign, while their absolute value retains this normalization. Locus-specific quantities, such as the [coordinate at a constraint position](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_constraint_position), evaluate this same label on the magnetic surface containing the specified position. The [coordinate at the separatrix](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_separatrix) equals one when the separatrix defines the equilibrium boundary.

rows.name: poloidal_beta
rows.description: Poloidal beta compares volume-averaged total perpendicular plasma pressure with a magnetic-pressure scale set by the net plasma current and reference major radius.
rows.documentation: Poloidal beta is the ratio of volume-averaged total perpendicular plasma pressure to a reference poloidal magnetic-pressure scale. The reference scale is defined by a whole-plasma, current-based normalization rather than by the poloidal field at a particular point. The defining pressure ratio and its current-based normalization are $$\beta = \frac{2\mu_0 \langle p\rangle}{B^2}$$ Here $\beta_{\mathrm{p}}$ is poloidal beta, $p$ is total perpendicular plasma pressure, $V$ is the entire plasma volume, $dV$ is a volume element, and $\langle p\rangle$ is the pressure averaged over that volume. The quantities $R_0$, $I_{\mathrm{p}}$, and $\mu_0$ are the reference major radius, net toroidal plasma current, and vacuum permeability, respectively. The effective reference poloidal field $B_{\mathrm{p,ref}}$ satisfies $B_{\mathrm{p,ref}}^2=\mu_0^2 I_{\mathrm{p}}^2R_0/(2V)$; it is not a local poloidal-field magnitude. The pressure includes contributions from all plasma populations, rather than electrons alone or only thermal particles. This global quantity differs from a point-local or pedestal-top electron beta. The definition requires nonzero net plasma current and a positive reference major radius. Poloidal beta is the poloidal-field-normalized member of the [beta](name:beta) family, whereas [toroidal beta](name:toroidal_beta) uses a reference toroidal magnetic field. For the same pressure average and a combined reference field formed by adding the squared poloidal and toroidal reference fields, $1/\beta=1/\beta_{\mathrm{p}}+1/\beta_{\mathrm{t}}$, where $\beta$ is combined-field beta and $\beta_{\mathrm{t}}$ is toroidal beta.

rows.name: radial_derivative_of_poloidal_magnetic_flux
rows.description: Rate of change of signed poloidal magnetic flux with the dimensionful toroidal-flux radius labeling nested equilibrium flux surfaces.
rows.documentation: The radial derivative of poloidal magnetic flux is the rate at which the signed poloidal magnetic flux changes across nested equilibrium magnetic flux surfaces. It is a metric coefficient relating the poloidal-flux and toroidal-flux coordinate descriptions. The defining relation is $$ \frac{d\psi}{d\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}} $$ where $\psi$ is the [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux), and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the dimensionful toroidal-flux radius that labels the nested surfaces. This quantity is evaluated as a function of the toroidal-flux radius, with one derivative value associated with each nested equilibrium surface. It is not a surface integral or average, and it is distinct from a derivative with respect to the cylindrical major radius, minor radius, or a normalized flux coordinate. Relative to [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux), this quantity describes how the flux label changes in the outward toroidal-flux-radial direction. It has the same independent coordinate as the derivative with respect to toroidal flux coordinate of area of flux surface, but differentiates poloidal magnetic flux rather than enclosed surface area. Sign convention: Positive when the poloidal magnetic flux increases as $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ increases outward from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

rows.name: squareness_of_flux_surface
rows.description: Squareness of a flux surface is the Luce (2013) shape coefficient for each nested closed magnetic flux surface, including the outer closed boundary when present, quantifying signed corner-sector departure from a reference ellipse in the poloidal cross-section. Positive values are box-like; negative values are diamond-like.
rows.documentation: Squareness of a flux surface is the Luce (2013) shape coefficient that quantifies the signed departure of a nested closed magnetic-flux-surface contour from a reference ellipse in the corner sectors of its poloidal cross-section. Positive values describe box-like corner sectors relative to the reference ellipse, and negative values describe diamond-like or inward-pinched corner sectors. The contour is considered in a poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The quantity is defined separately for each member of the one-parameter family of nested closed flux surfaces, including the plasma boundary when it is the outer closed flux surface; it excludes open-field-line regions and material limiter, wall, or divertor surfaces. It is a contour-shape coefficient, not a flux-surface label, not a coordinate of the contour, not a boundary-only quantity, and not an average over neighboring flux surfaces. It captures corner departure from the reference ellipse; [elongation](name:elongation_of_flux_surface) captures the vertical stretching of the contour, and [triangularity](name:triangularity_of_flux_surface) captures the major-radius displacement of the upper and lower extrema. Sector-resolved squareness quantities use the same Luce reference-ellipse convention on named corner sectors: [upper outer squareness](name:upper_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface) on the upper-$Z$, larger-$R$ sector, [upper inner squareness](name:upper_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface) on the upper-$Z$, smaller-$R$ sector, [lower outer squareness](name:lower_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface) on the lower-$Z$, larger-$R$ sector, and [lower inner squareness](name:lower_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface) on the lower-$Z$, smaller-$R$ sector. [Outer squareness](name:outer_squareness_of_flux_surface) restricts the quantity to larger-$R$ corner sectors, [inner squareness](name:inner_squareness_of_flux_surface) restricts it to smaller-$R$ corner sectors, and [squareness of the plasma boundary](name:squareness_of_plasma_boundary) is the boundary specialization of the flux-surface quantity.

rows.name: surface_area_of_flux_surface
rows.description: Surface area of a complete magnetic flux surface, including its full poloidal and toroidal extent rather than the enclosed poloidal cross-section.
rows.documentation: Area of flux surface The area is defined by $$ A = \iint_{\mathcal S} dS $$ where $A$ is the surface area, $\mathcal S$ is the specified flux surface, and $dS$ is the nonnegative geometric surface-area element. This quantity applies to one complete flux surface, not solely to the plasma boundary. It is integrated over the entire surface and is neither a local area element nor a flux-surface average. Unlike the [poloidal-plane cross-sectional area](name:poloidal_plane_cross_sectional_area_of_flux_surface), it measures the surface itself rather than the planar region enclosed by its contour. It also differs from the [enclosed volume](name:volume_of_flux_surface), which measures the full interior bounded by the same surface. A surface formed by points sharing the same magnetic-flux label in a nested-flux-surface configuration. Where $\psi(R, Z) = \mathrm{const}$, $\psi$ is poloidal magnetic flux.

rows.name: toroidal_magnetic_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
rows.description: Toroidal magnetic flux change through a poloidal cross-section caused by the pressure-gradient-driven plasma response relative to a reference field without that response.
rows.documentation: Toroidal magnetic flux due to diamagnetic drift is the signed, surface-integrated magnetic response associated with pressure-gradient-driven plasma diamagnetism. It is the toroidal specialization of the [magnetic-flux contribution due to diamagnetic drift](name:magnetic_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), defined relative to a corresponding reference field without that response. The contribution through an oriented poloidal cross-section is defined by $$ \Phi_{\phi,\mathrm{dia}} = \int_S \left(\mathbf{B}-\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{ref}}\right)\cdot\hat{\phi}\,\mathrm{d}S $$ where $\Phi_{\phi,\mathrm{dia}}$ is the toroidal diamagnetic flux, $S$ is the poloidal integration surface, $\mathbf{B}$ is the equilibrium magnetic field, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the corresponding reference magnetic field with the same external excitation but without the diamagnetic response, and $\mathrm{d}S$ is a positive surface-area element. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, $Z$ is vertical height, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector toward increasing toroidal angle; the surface normal is chosen along $\hat{\phi}$. This is a global flux contribution over the specified cross-section, not a local magnetic-field value or a flux value at a particular magnetic surface. It excludes the reference-field flux and is distinct from both total toroidal magnetic flux and poloidal magnetic flux. The [toroidal current density due to diamagnetic drift](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) instead describes a local electric-current contribution, not this integrated magnetic response. Sign convention: Positive when the diamagnetic magnetic-field change produces net flux in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

rows.name: triangularity_of_flux_surface
rows.description: Signed dimensionless shape parameter measuring the normalized horizontal displacement of a nested magnetic flux surface’s upper or lower vertical extremum.
rows.documentation: Triangularity of a nested magnetic flux surface is the signed shape parameter formed from the horizontal displacement of an upper or lower vertical extremum, normalized by the surface’s horizontal half-width. For a selected upper or lower vertical extremum, triangularity is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame by $$ \delta_s = \frac{R_c - R_s}{a} $$ where $\delta_s$ is the triangularity, $s$ identifies the selected upper or lower vertical extremum, $R_s$ is its radial coordinate, $R_c$ is the radial midpoint of the flux surface’s horizontal extent, and $a$ is the corresponding horizontal half-width. This is a geometric parameter of an individual nested magnetic flux surface in an equilibrium plasma. The unqualified quantity covers either vertical extremum and carries no aggregation over multiple flux surfaces, plasma volume, or the plasma boundary. Triangularity characterizes the radial displacement of a vertical extremum; it is distinct from [elongation of a flux surface](name:elongation_of_flux_surface), which describes the ratio of vertical to horizontal extent, and from [outer squareness of a flux surface](name:outer_squareness_of_flux_surface), which describes corner deformation. The upper and lower branch-specific quantities are [upper triangularity of a flux surface](name:upper_triangularity_of_flux_surface) and [lower triangularity of a flux surface](name:lower_triangularity_of_flux_surface); each is an instance of this parent quantity with $s$ fixed to the corresponding vertical extremum.

rows.name: vertical_coordinate_of_strike_point
rows.description: Vertical coordinate of a selected divertor strike point, giving its signed height relative to the origin in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
rows.documentation: Vertical coordinate of a selected divertor strike point specifies its signed height relative to the coordinate origin in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Here $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height along the toroidal symmetry axis. $$ Z_{\mathrm{s}} = \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{s}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{z}} $$ where $Z_{\mathrm{s}}$ is the strike-point vertical coordinate, $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{s}}$ is the position vector of that point relative to the coordinate origin, and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ is the unit vector along the positive vertical direction. The value applies to one identified strike point. Inner and outer strike points have separate values; no averaging or summation over them is implied. The generic quantity does not select a particular strike-point branch. This coordinate specifies a different geometric location from the [vertical coordinate of an X-point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_x_point). It also differs from the [vertical coordinate of the divertor-target center](name:z_coordinate_of_divertor_target), which locates the target's geometric center rather than the selected strike point. Sign convention: Positive when the displacement from the coordinate origin to the strike point has a positive projection onto the positive vertical direction $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$. The point where a divertor separatrix branch intersects a plasma-facing target. Where $\psi(R_{\mathrm{s}}, Z_{\mathrm{s}}) = \psi_{\mathrm{X}}$, $R_{\mathrm{s}}, Z_{\mathrm{s}}$ is the point on the target surface; $\psi_{\mathrm{X}}$ is poloidal magnetic flux at the primary X-point.

rows.name: volume_of_flux_surface
rows.description: Volume enclosed by a magnetic flux surface, including the entire plasma interior from the magnetic axis rather than only a shell between neighboring surfaces.
