rows.documentation: Volume of flux surface The volume is defined by $$ V = \int_{\Omega} d^3\mathbf{x} $$ where $V$ is the enclosed volume, $\Omega$ is the spatial domain inside the selected magnetic flux surface, $\mathbf{x}$ is spatial position, and $d^3\mathbf{x}$ is the differential volume element. The integration covers the entire interior from the magnetic axis to the selected surface and excludes regions outside it. The result is the total enclosed volume, not the volume of a shell between neighboring surfaces or the volume of material structures. The volume tends to zero as the selected surface contracts to the magnetic axis. It equals the [volume enclosed by the plasma boundary](name:volume_of_plasma_boundary) when the selected surface coincides with that boundary. Differentiating this cumulative volume with respect to the poloidal magnetic flux coordinate gives the [poloidal-flux volume derivative](name:derivative_of_volume_of_flux_surface_with_respect_to_poloidal_magnetic_flux_coordinate); differentiation with respect to the toroidal-flux coordinate gives the [toroidal-flux volume derivative](name:derivative_of_volume_of_flux_surface_with_respect_to_toroidal_flux_coordinate). Enclosed-volume increments provide the geometric integration measure that converts flux-surface-averaged densities into enclosed totals. A surface formed by points sharing the same magnetic-flux label in a nested-flux-surface configuration. Where $\psi(R, Z) = \mathrm{const}$, $\psi$ is poloidal magnetic flux.

rows.name: fast_particle_pressure
rows.description: Fast-particle pressure is the isotropic scalar pressure contribution of the total suprathermal (nonthermal) particle population, combining its field-parallel and transverse stress contributions.
rows.documentation: Fast-particle pressure is the scalar kinetic pressure of the total suprathermal (nonthermal) particle population. It represents the isotropic pressure associated with the field-parallel and transverse stresses; the directional stresses themselves need not be equal. For a gyrotropic pressure tensor, the scalar pressure is one-third of its trace: $$ p_{\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{p_{\parallel,\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x}) + 2p_{\perp,\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x})}{3} $$ where $p_{\mathrm{fast}}$ is fast-particle pressure, $\mathbf{x}$ is spatial position, $p_{\parallel,\mathrm{fast}}$ is the [parallel fast-particle pressure](name:parallel_fast_particle_pressure), and $p_{\perp,\mathrm{fast}}$ is the [perpendicular fast-particle pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_particle_pressure), defined per transverse direction. Both components refer to the same population at the same position; the factor of two accounts for the two transverse directions. The quantity applies locally to the full suprathermal population, across all velocities, pitch angles, and orbit classes. Contributions are summed over fast-particle species and all charge states, not averaged. A flux-surface average is a separate spatial aggregation of these local values; the unqualified quantity does not require that average. Fast-particle pressure excludes [thermal plasma pressure](name:thermal_plasma_pressure). It is distinct from a species-specific or charge-state-specific pressure, either directional component, and pressure restricted to an individual orbit class. Restricting the same pressure contribution to orbit classes gives the [co-passing fast-particle pressure](name:co_passing_fast_particle_pressure), [counter-passing fast-particle pressure](name:counter_passing_fast_particle_pressure), and [trapped fast-particle pressure](name:trapped_fast_particle_pressure). Their contributions sum to the full fast-particle pressure when the classes form an exhaustive, nonoverlapping partition of the population.

rows.name: total_counter_passing_particle_pressure
rows.description: Total pressure of counter-passing particles is the flux-surface average of one-third of their kinetic-stress trace, including thermal, nonthermal, and directed-motion contributions.
rows.documentation: Total pressure of counter-passing particles is the flux-surface-averaged isotropic part of the kinetic stress carried by the thermal and nonthermal populations of a specified species. Counter-passing particles occupy untrapped guiding-center orbits whose orbit-averaged toroidal motion opposes the plasma current. The nonrelativistic kinetic definition is $$ p_{s,\mathrm{cp}} = \left\langle \frac{m_s}{3}\int_{\mathrm{cp}} |\mathbf{v}|^2 f_s(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v \right\rangle_{\mathrm{FS}} $$ where $p_{s,\mathrm{cp}}$ is the total counter-passing pressure of species $s$, $m_s$ is its particle mass, $\mathbf{x}$ is spatial position, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, $f_s$ is the [particle distribution](name:particle_distribution) including its thermal and nonthermal parts, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element. The integration domain $\mathrm{cp}$ selects counter-passing orbits, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\mathrm{FS}}$ denotes a magnetic-flux-surface average weighted by the differential volume between neighboring surfaces. Velocity is not centered on the counter-passing population's mean flow, so directed-motion stress is retained. “Total” denotes the additive thermal and nonthermal contributions within the specified species, not a sum over all plasma species. Contributions from multiple distributions representing that species are superposed. Trapped and co-passing particles are excluded. This quantity is a flux-surface average rather than a local pressure at a point on the surface; it combines all three velocity degrees of freedom without assuming isotropy and is not a single field-parallel or field-perpendicular stress component. The [counter-passing fast-particle pressure](name:counter_passing_fast_particle_pressure) restricts the kinetic moment to suprathermal particles, whereas this quantity also includes the thermal contribution. The [total co-passing particle pressure](name:total_co_passing_particle_pressure) applies the thermal-plus-nonthermal scope to the opposite passing-orbit class.

rows.name: voltage_of_valve
rows.description: Voltage applied to a gas-injection valve to drive its opening, serving as the electrical input to the valve's gas-flow response.
rows.documentation: Voltage of valve The applied voltage is defined by $$ U = \varphi_{\mathrm{drive}} - \varphi_{\mathrm{ref}} $$ where $U$ is the valve drive voltage, $\varphi_{\mathrm{drive}}$ is the electric potential of the driven terminal, and $\varphi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the electric potential of its circuit reference terminal. The valve response relates this applied signal to the derived [gas flow of the valve](name:gas_flow_of_valve). The voltage is the electrical input to that relationship, not the resulting gas throughput or particle injection rate. Sign convention: Positive when the driven terminal is at higher electric potential than its reference terminal.

rows.name: accumulated_deuterated_methane_prefill_count
rows.description: Cumulative pre-breakdown inventory of deuterated methane (CD4), weighted by ten equivalent electrons per molecule rather than reported as a molecular count.
rows.documentation: This quantity is the cumulative amount of deuterated methane introduced during the plasma prefill phase, expressed as an equivalent-electron inventory. It represents neutral CD4 molecules before plasma breakdown, not the post-breakdown gas-injection inventory. The equivalent-electron count is defined by $$ N_{e,\rm eq}^{\rm prefill} = \int_{t_0}^{t_b} \dot{N}_{e,\rm eq}^{\rm CD_4}(t)\,dt = 10N_{\rm CD_4}^{\rm prefill} $$ where $N_{e,\rm eq}^{\rm prefill}$ is the accumulated equivalent-electron inventory, $\dot{N}_{e,\rm eq}^{\rm CD_4}$ is the [deuterated methane source rate](name:deuterated_methane_source_rate), $t_0$ and $t_b$ delimit prefill before breakdown, and $N_{\rm CD_4}^{\rm prefill}$ is the accumulated number of CD4 molecules. The factor ten is the total electron count of one fully ionizable CD4 molecule. The species-resolved quantity contributes to the [accumulated total prefill gas count](name:accumulated_total_prefill_gas_count), which sums equivalent-electron inventories across gas species.

rows.name: accumulated_total_prefill_gas_count
rows.description: Cumulative equivalent-electron inventory of all gas species introduced by injection during the plasma prefill phase, summed over species.
rows.documentation: This quantity is the total gas inventory accumulated during the plasma prefill phase, expressed as an equivalent-electron count and summed over all injected species. It represents the integrated amount introduced before plasma breakdown, rather than an instantaneous injection rate. The accumulated equivalent-electron count is defined by $$ N_{\mathrm{eq}}(t) = \sum_s \int_{t_0}^{\min(t,t_1)} \dot{N}_{s,\mathrm{eq}}(t')\,dt' $$ where $s$ indexes injected gas species, $\dot{N}_{s,\mathrm{eq}}$ is the equivalent-electron injection rate of species $s$, $t_0$ and $t_1$ delimit the prefill phase, and $t$ is the evaluation time. The sum includes all species; a species-specific quantity such as [accumulated hydrogen prefill count](name:accumulated_hydrogen_prefill_count) is a component of this total. The quantity is distinct from the instantaneous injection rate and from inventories restricted to one species, while [accumulated prefill gas count](name:accumulated_prefill_gas_count) denotes the near-equivalent total inventory.

rows.name: argon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
rows.description: Particle number density of argon ions evaluated on the flux surface assigned to an internal transport barrier, summed over all argon ion charge states and excluding neutral argon.
rows.documentation: Particle number density of argon ions evaluated on the flux surface assigned to an internal transport barrier is the local density of the argon-ion population at that flux-surface location. The number density is defined by $$ n = \lim_{\Delta V\to 0}\frac{\Delta N}{\Delta V} $$ where $n$ is number density, $N$ is the number of counted particles, and $V$ is volume. For argon, the count is summed over all ionic charge states and excludes neutral argon. This species-specific quantity is a member of [density at the internal transport barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier), alongside [boron density at the internal transport barrier](name:boron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier). The internal transport barrier is the designated flux-surface location where reduced cross-field turbulent transport permits steep density gradients.

rows.name: argon_density_at_separatrix
rows.description: Charge-state-summed number density of argon ions, excluding neutral argon, evaluated locally on the magnetic separatrix.
rows.documentation: Argon ion density at the separatrix is the local number of charged argon ions per physical volume on the last closed magnetic flux surface. It is the argon-specific component of density at separatrix. The charge-state-summed density is defined by $$ n_{\mathrm{Ar}} = \sum_{q=1}^{18} n_{\mathrm{Ar}^{q+}} $$ where $n_{\mathrm{Ar}}$ is the argon ion number density, $q$ is the argon ion charge-state index, and $n_{\mathrm{Ar}^{q+}}$ is the number density of argon ions in charge state $q$. Neutral argon is excluded. Unlike flux-surface-averaged argon density at the plasma boundary, this quantity denotes the local value at the separatrix.

rows.name: flux_surface_averaged_krypton_density_at_plasma_boundary
rows.description: Charge-state-summed krypton ion number density averaged over the complete separatrix, distinguishing a flux-surface value from the local boundary value.
rows.documentation: The quantity is the charge-state-summed number density of krypton ions, averaged over the complete plasma-boundary separatrix. It represents krypton particle content associated with the last closed magnetic flux surface, rather than a pointwise value; the corresponding local quantity is the [krypton ion number density at the plasma boundary](name:krypton_density_at_plasma_boundary). The flux-surface average is defined by $$ \left\langle n_{\mathrm{Kr}} \right\rangle_{\mathrm{FS},b} = \frac{\displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{S}_b} n_{\mathrm{Kr}}\,\frac{dS}{\lvert\nabla\psi\rvert}} {\displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{S}_b} \frac{dS}{\lvert\nabla\psi\rvert}} $$ where $n_{\mathrm{Kr}}$ is the local krypton ion number density, $\mathcal{S}_b$ is the plasma-boundary separatrix, $dS$ is the surface-area element, and $\psi$ is the magnetic-flux surface label. All krypton ion charge states are included in $n_{\mathrm{Kr}}$; neutral krypton and any single-charge-state density are excluded.

rows.name: ipb98y2_confinement_time
rows.description: IPB98(y,2) empirical-scaling reference for global energy confinement time, providing the denominator for the H98 confinement enhancement factor.
rows.documentation: The IPB98(y,2) energy confinement time is the global energy-confinement timescale predicted by the IPB98(y,2) empirical scaling law. It is an energy-channel performance benchmark rather than a species-resolved or local transport time. The underlying global energy confinement time is defined by $$ \tau_E = \frac{W}{P_{\mathrm{loss}}} $$ where $\tau_E$ is the global energy confinement time, $W$ is the total thermal energy stored in the plasma, and $P_{\mathrm{loss}}$ is the net power leaving the plasma. The quantity documented here is the IPB98(y,2) scaling prediction of this timescale, not the directly evaluated confinement time for a particular plasma state. The value applies to the complete plasma energy content and its global loss balance; it is not a local profile quantity, a particle confinement time, or a confinement time assigned to an individual species. It is a single empirical reference value for the energy channel. The [energy confinement enhancement factor](name:energy_confinement_enhancement_factor) compares the actual global energy confinement time with this reference through $H_{98} = \tau_E / \tau_{E,98}$, where $H_{98}$ is the dimensionless confinement enhancement factor and $\tau_{E,98}$ is this IPB98(y,2) scaling prediction.

rows.name: magnetic_field_at_pedestal_top_low_field_side
rows.description: Magnetic field at the pedestal top low-field side is the local magnetic induction vector evaluated at the low-field-side pressure-pedestal top. It retains radial, toroidal, and vertical field components in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame before component selection or magnitude reduction.
rows.documentation: Magnetic field at the pedestal top low-field side is the local magnetic induction vector evaluated at the low-field-side top of the pressure pedestal. It gives the total field direction and strength at that locus in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, whose basis is $(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$ with $R$ the major-radius coordinate, $\phi$ the toroidal angle, and $Z$ the vertical coordinate. The vector is decomposed as $$ \mathbf{B}_\mathrm{ped,LFS} = B_R\hat{R} + B_\phi\hat{\phi} + B_Z\hat{Z} $$ where $\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{ped,LFS}$ is the magnetic-field vector at the low-field-side pressure-pedestal top, $B_R$ is its radial component, $B_\phi$ is its toroidal component, $B_Z$ is its vertical component, and $(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$ is the right-handed cylindrical basis. The scope is locus-specific: it applies only at the low-field-side pressure-pedestal top, not throughout the pedestal, not at the pedestal foot or magnetic axis, and not as a spatial average over a flux surface or volume. The quantity has no species, charge-state, or particle-population aggregation; it is the electromagnetic field itself at the specified location. Relative to the unrestricted [magnetic field](name:magnetic_field), this quantity adds the pedestal-top low-field-side evaluation locus while retaining the same vector identity. Its child [magnetic-field magnitude at the pedestal top low-field side](name:magnetic_field_magnitude_at_pedestal_top_low_field_side) is the Euclidean norm $|\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{ped,LFS}| = \sqrt{B_R^2+B_\phi^2+B_Z^2}$ and therefore removes direction and component signs; individual component or projection names denote only the corresponding part of this vector. Sign convention: Positive when a component of $\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{ped,LFS}$ is directed along $+\hat{R}$, $+\hat{\phi}$, or $+\hat{Z}$, respectively, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

rows.name: neon_density
rows.description: Number density of neon impurity ions, summed over the included ionization states; line-averaged and volume-averaged forms express the same elemental content.
rows.documentation: Neon density is the number of neon impurity ions per unit volume, summed over all included charged ionization states. It represents elemental neon content rather than the density of one selected charge state; neutral neon atoms are excluded. $$ n_{\mathrm{Ne}} = \sum_{z \in \mathcal{Z}_{\mathrm{Ne}}} n_{\mathrm{Ne}^{z+}} $$ where $n_{\mathrm{Ne}}$ is the charge-state-summed neon ion density, $n_{\mathrm{Ne}^{z+}}$ is the density of neon ions in charge state $z+$, and $\mathcal{Z}_{\mathrm{Ne}}$ is the set of included charged ionization states. This species-specific quantity is a member of density. The same charge-state-summed field may be spatially averaged; [volume_averaged_neon_density](name:volume_averaged_neon_density) represents its volume average, while a charge-state-resolved quantity such as [ion_charge_state_density](name:ion_charge_state_density) selects one ionization state and is not equivalent.

rows.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_pedestal_top
rows.description: Dimensionless toroidal-flux label locating the top of the H-mode edge pedestal on a nested magnetic surface relative to the magnetic axis and last closed flux surface.
rows.documentation: The normalized toroidal flux coordinate evaluated at the pedestal top is the dimensionless magnetic-surface label assigned to the top of the H-mode edge pedestal. It locates that position within the nested closed-flux-surface family, rather than representing a cylindrical distance or a local vector component. For a nested equilibrium, the coordinate is defined by $$ \rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(\mathrm{ped}) = \left[\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathrm{ped}) - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathrm{axis})}{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathrm{LCFS}) - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathrm{axis})}\right]^{1/2} $$ where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(\mathrm{ped})$ is the normalized toroidal flux coordinate at the pedestal top, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by a magnetic surface, $\mathrm{ped}$ denotes the pedestal-top position, $\mathrm{axis}$ denotes the magnetic axis, and $\mathrm{LCFS}$ denotes the last closed flux surface. The value applies specifically at the top of the H-mode edge pedestal, the inner shoulder of the edge transport barrier. Its position is defined by the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate of the pedestal](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_pedestal). This is a single coordinate evaluation: no species, charge-state, or population aggregation applies, and no surface averaging is implied. It is distinct from a cylindrical radial distance and from the unnormalized [toroidal flux coordinate at the pedestal top](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_pedestal_top). This entry is the pedestal-top specialization of the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate), with the same axis-to-boundary normalization. It should not be interpreted as the corresponding [normalized poloidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate), which labels surfaces using poloidal rather than toroidal magnetic flux.

rows.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_separatrix
rows.description: Dimensionless toroidal-flux surface label at the magnetic separatrix, identifying the outermost closed magnetic surface and its outer normalization value.
rows.documentation: This quantity is the normalized toroidal-flux surface label evaluated at the magnetic separatrix, which is the outermost closed magnetic surface. It identifies the flux-coordinate location of separatrix quantities rather than a cylindrical distance or a local vector component. The normalized toroidal-flux coordinate at the separatrix is defined by $$ \left.\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}\right|_{\mathrm{sep}} = \left(\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,sep}}-\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,LCFS}}-\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}\right)^{1/2} $$ where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is the normalized toroidal-flux coordinate, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,sep}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux at the separatrix, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis, and $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,LCFS}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux at the last closed flux surface. The separatrix is the last closed flux surface for this evaluation, so the value is the outer normalization value, equal to one when the separatrix and last-closed-surface loci are identified. This is a point evaluation of a scalar magnetic-surface label for the separatrix locus; it is not a spatial average, volume integral, flux integral, cylindrical radius, or vector component. The [normalized toroidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate) represents the same coordinate on general nested magnetic surfaces, while this quantity fixes its evaluation at the separatrix. The normalized toroidal flux coordinate at the plasma boundary uses the plasma-boundary locus instead. Those loci may coincide when the plasma boundary is defined as the last closed flux surface, but the two quantities retain distinct locus semantics.

rows.name: oxygen_density_at_plasma_boundary
rows.description: Number density of oxygen ions at the plasma boundary, evaluated as the local, intensive particle count per physical volume on the last closed magnetic flux surface and summed over all charged oxygen ionization states.
rows.documentation: Number density of oxygen ions at the plasma boundary is the local, intensive particle count per physical volume for the oxygen-ion population evaluated on the last closed magnetic flux surface. The plasma boundary is the limiting closed magnetic flux surface separating confined plasma from the open-field-line scrape-off-layer region. The local charge-state-summed oxygen ion density at a boundary point is the zeroth velocity moment of the oxygen-ion distribution functions: $$ n_{\mathrm{O}}(\mathbf{x}_b,t)=\sum_{z=1}^{8}\int f_{\mathrm{O}^{z+}}(\mathbf{x}_b,\mathbf{v},t)\,d^3v $$ where $n_{\mathrm{O}}$ is the oxygen-ion number density, $\mathbf{x}_b$ is a point on the last closed magnetic flux surface, $t$ is time, $z$ is the positive oxygen ionization state, $f_{\mathrm{O}^{z+}}$ is the phase-space distribution function for that state, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element. This quantity applies specifically to oxygen ions and sums the populations from singly ionized through fully stripped oxygen. It excludes neutral oxygen and other ion species, and it is a local boundary value with no averaging over the boundary surface or over a volume. It is the oxygen-specific instance of [density at the plasma boundary](name:density_at_plasma_boundary). The flux-surface-averaged oxygen density at the plasma boundary represents the same charge-state-summed oxygen-ion content averaged over the last closed magnetic flux surface rather than evaluated locally.

rows.name: logarithm_of_density
rows.description: Logarithm of a selected plasma density, representing the natural-log transform of that density relative to a specified reference for the same density quantity. It is the base logarithmic density quantity from which coordinate derivatives may be formed.
rows.documentation: Logarithm of density is the natural logarithm of a selected plasma density after normalization by a reference value for the same density quantity. It represents the logarithmic density variable itself, not a spatial derivative or gradient. The defining logarithmic transform is $$ L_n = \ln\!\left(\frac{n}{n_\mathrm{ref}}\right) $$ where $L_n$ is the logarithm of density, $n$ is the selected plasma density, and $n_\mathrm{ref}$ is the reference value used for the same selected density. The scope covers the logarithmic transform for any explicitly selected density population or component; a more specific standard name supplies the particular population, coordinate dependence, or reference convention. It excludes the density $n$ itself, a density ratio before applying the logarithm, and any coordinate derivative or gradient of $L_n$. A derivative specialization such as [logarithmic-density derivative with respect to normalized minor radius](name:derivative_of_logarithm_of_density_with_respect_to_normalized_minor_radius) denotes a derivative of $L_n$, not $L_n$ itself. For any coordinate $x$, the corresponding logarithmic derivative is $dL_n/dx = (1/n)\,dn/dx$ when $n_\mathrm{ref}$ is independent of $x$, where $x$ is the coordinate of differentiation.

rows.name: normalized_effective_particle_energy
rows.description: Normalized effective particle energy is the ratio of a species effective particle-energy coordinate to the positive species reference thermal-energy scale.
rows.documentation: Normalized effective particle energy is the ratio of a species effective particle-energy coordinate to the positive species reference thermal-energy scale. It is a dimensionless velocity-space coordinate for the effective single-particle energy relative to that species reference, not an independent temperature, mass, or charge ratio. The normalization is $$ \bar{\mathcal{E}}_s = \frac{\mathcal{E}^{*}_{\mathrm{eff},s}}{E_{\mathrm{th,ref},s}} $$ where $\bar{\mathcal{E}}_s$ is the normalized effective particle energy, $s$ labels the particle species, $\mathcal{E}^{*}_{\mathrm{eff},s}$ is the effective particle-energy coordinate for that species expressed on a scale compatible with the denominator, and $E_{\mathrm{th,ref},s} > 0$ is the species reference thermal-energy scale. If the reference is specified by a species reference temperature $T_{\mathrm{ref},s}$, the corresponding denominator is $E_{\mathrm{th,ref},s}=k_B T_{\mathrm{ref},s}$; the same reference temperature appears in [ratio_of_particle_temperature_to_reference_particle_temperature](name:ratio_of_particle_temperature_to_particle_reference_temperature). It is distinguished from [effective_particle_energy](name:effective_particle_energy), which denotes the effective-energy coordinate without requiring this particular species thermal normalization. If the effective particle energy contains an additive effective-potential term $U_{\mathrm{eff},s}$, its normalized contribution is $U_{\mathrm{eff},s}/E_{\mathrm{th,ref},s}$; with the same denominator this is normalized_particle_effective_potential. The detailed split of the effective energy into kinetic and potential terms and the choice of potential-energy zero are not fixed by this name.

rows.name: normalized_perturbed_parallel_gyrocenter_heat_flux_bessel_1
rows.description: Normalized first-Bessel-weighted parallel heat-flux moment of a perturbed gyrocenter distribution in a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode.
rows.documentation: This quantity represents the energy-weighted parallel motion carried by the perturbed gyrocenter population. It is evaluated in the field-aligned parallel direction and includes first-order Bessel weighting. The normalized moment is defined by $$ \widehat{q}_{\parallel,J_1}=\frac{1}{\mathcal{N}_q}\int \frac{1}{2}m v_{\parallel}v^2 J_1\,\delta f_g^{(1)}(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v $$ where $\widehat{q}_{\parallel,J_1}$ is the normalized parallel heat-flux moment, $\mathcal{N}_q$ is the normalization factor for the corresponding heat-flux moment, $m$ is the gyrocenter particle mass, $v_{\parallel}$ is the velocity component parallel to the magnetic field, $v$ is the particle-speed magnitude, $J_1$ is the first-order Bessel weighting factor at the prescribed gyrokinetic argument, $\delta f_g^{(1)}(\mathbf{v})$ is the perturbed gyrocenter distribution function, $\mathbf{v}$ is the velocity-space coordinate, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element. The integral applies to the perturbed gyrocenter distribution associated with a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode and aggregates the represented distribution over velocity space. It excludes the equilibrium or unperturbed distribution and is not an unweighted heat-flux moment. The parallel projection distinguishes this quantity from the perpendicular heat-flux moment perpendicular gyrocenter heat perturbed flux normalized of gyrokinetic eigenmode. It belongs to the same first-Bessel-weighted perturbed gyrocenter moment family as [normalized perturbed parallel gyrocenter current density bessel 1](name:normalized_perturbed_parallel_gyrocenter_current_density_bessel_1), but uses the energy-weighted heat-flux kernel rather than the current-density kernel.

rows.name: normalized_perturbed_parallel_magnetic_field_magnitude
rows.description: Normalized perturbed parallel magnetic-field magnitude is the nonnegative amplitude of a magnetic-field perturbation projected along the local equilibrium magnetic-field direction and divided by a reference magnetic-field magnitude. More specific names may add averaging conventions.
rows.documentation: Normalized perturbed parallel magnetic-field magnitude is the normalized amplitude of the component of a magnetic-field perturbation that is parallel to the local equilibrium magnetic field. It is a nonnegative scalar intensity formed from the absolute value of the parallel projection, not from the full perturbation vector magnitude. A representative definition is $$ \widetilde{B}_{\parallel,N} = \frac{\left|\delta\mathbf{B}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}}_0\right|}{B_\mathrm{ref}} $$ where $\widetilde{B}_{\parallel,N}$ is the normalized perturbed parallel magnetic-field magnitude, $\delta\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field perturbation, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}_0$ is the unit vector along the local equilibrium magnetic field, and $B_\mathrm{ref}$ is the reference magnetic-field magnitude used for the normalization. This parent quantity fixes the parallel projection and normalization by a reference magnetic-field magnitude. It does not by itself fix temporal, spatial, spectral, or flux-surface averaging; those aggregation conventions are supplied only by more specific names. This quantity excludes the normalized total perturbation magnitude, perpendicular-to-field perturbation amplitudes, signed parallel perturbations, and unnormalized perturbation amplitudes. The absolute value in the definition makes the parent a magnitude, so reversal of the perturbation sign along the equilibrium field does not change its value. A concrete child such as [time-averaged normalized perturbed parallel magnetic-field magnitude](name:time_averaged_normalized_perturbed_parallel_magnetic_field_magnitude) adds a time-average aggregation to the same parallel-projected normalized magnitude; it is not a change from parallel projection to total-field normalization.

rows.name: parallel_gyrocenter_momentum_flux_normalized_of_gyrokinetic_eigenmode_due_to_e_cross_b_drift
rows.description: Normalized parallel gyrocenter toroidal angular-momentum flux of a gyrokinetic eigenmode due to E×B drift is the rotating-frame spectral contribution from the perturbed electrostatic potential’s E×B drift to the mode’s parallel gyrocenter momentum transport.
rows.documentation: Normalized parallel gyrocenter toroidal angular-momentum flux of a gyrokinetic eigenmode due to $E\times B$ drift is the normalized spectral contribution, evaluated in the rotating frame, of the perturbed electrostatic potential's $E\times B$ drift to the parallel gyrocenter part of toroidal angular-momentum flux. The toroidal component is the $\hat{\phi}$ component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The normalization is defined relative to the reference momentum-flux normalization for the same eigenmode: $$ \widehat{\Pi}_{\parallel,\phi}^{E\times B} = \frac{\Pi_{\parallel,\phi}^{E\times B}}{\Pi_{\mathrm{ref}}} $$ where $\widehat{\Pi}_{\parallel,\phi}^{E\times B}$ is this normalized contribution, $\Pi_{\parallel,\phi}^{E\times B}$ is the corresponding unnormalized parallel gyrocenter toroidal angular-momentum-flux contribution from the perturbed electrostatic-potential $E\times B$ drift in the rotating frame, $\Pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the reference momentum-flux normalization, $E$ is the perturbed electric field associated with the electrostatic potential, $B$ is the magnetic field, the subscript $\parallel$ denotes the part associated with gyrocenter motion parallel to $B$, and the subscript $\phi$ denotes toroidal angular momentum about the symmetry axis. The quantity applies to one specified linear gyrokinetic eigenmode and to the rotating-frame representation of that mode; it is not summed over eigenmodes, wave-number spectrum, or transport channels. Its aggregation convention is a single-channel normalized eigenmode contribution, not a total turbulent momentum flux. It is the electrostatic-potential $E\times B$ channel in the additive decomposition of the normalized parallel gyrocenter toroidal angular-momentum flux. The perturbed parallel vector-potential channel and the [perturbed parallel magnetic-field channel](name:parallel_gyrocenter_momentum_flux_normalized_of_gyrokinetic_eigenmode_due_to_perturbed_parallel_magnetic_field) are separate contributions and are excluded from this quantity. Sign convention: Positive when the $E\times B$-drift contribution transports positive parallel gyrocenter toroidal angular momentum across a magnetic flux surface toward increasing flux label, with positive toroidal angular momentum corresponding to the $+\hat{\phi}$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

rows.name: perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential
rows.description: Gage-dependent perturbation of the vacuum magnetic vector potential generated by external current sources; its curl gives the corresponding induction perturbation excluding plasma-current contributions.
rows.documentation:
The perturbed vacuum magnetic vector potential is a gage-dependent vector field representing the perturbation of the external-source contribution to the [magnetic vector potential](name:magnetic_vector_potential) relative to a specified reference state. It is the complete vector perturbation, not a single directional component. The corresponding perturbed vacuum magnetic induction is defined by: $$ \delta \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}} = 
abla 	imes \delta \mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{vac}} $$ where $\delta \mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the perturbed vacuum magnetic vector potential, $\delta \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the magnetic-induction perturbation produced by external sources, and $
abla 	imes$ is the curl operator. The perturbation remains gage-dependent: replacing $\delta \mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ by $\delta \mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{vac}} + 
abla \chi$, where $\chi$ is a scalar gage function, leaves $\delta \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ unchanged. This quantity includes the aggregate perturbation of the external-source contribution and excludes magnetic-vector-potential contributions generated by plasma currents. It is distinct from the unperturbed [vacuum magnetic vector potential](name:vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential) and from the full magnetic vector potential that includes plasma-current contributions. Its radial projection is represented by the [radial perturbed vacuum magnetic vector potential](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential), while the corresponding unperturbed radial component is the [radial vacuum magnetic vector potential](name:radial_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential). Components are resolved in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. Sign convention: Positive when a resolved component of the vector points along its corresponding positive basis direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

rows.name: radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential
rows.description: Radial component of a first-order perturbed magnetic vector-potential eigenfunction in the vacuum region for a toroidal linear-MHD mode, represented by its real or imaginary coefficient.
rows.documentation: The quantity is the radial projection of a first-order, complex perturbed magnetic vector-potential eigenfunction in the vacuum region. It is the common radial coefficient represented by separate real and imaginary quadratures. $$ \widetilde{A}_{1R} = \widetilde{\mathbf{A}}_1 \cdot \hat{\mathbf{R}} $$ where $\widetilde{A}_{1R}$ is the complex radial vector-potential coefficient, $\widetilde{\mathbf{A}}_1$ is the complex first-order perturbed magnetic vector-potential eigenfunction, and $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ is the unit vector toward increasing major-radius coordinate $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The subscript $1$ denotes the first-order perturbation. The quantity applies to the vacuum-region radial component associated with a toroidal linear-MHD mode. It represents one mode without summing over toroidal modes and includes both quadratures; it is not restricted to either the real or imaginary coefficient alone. It excludes the complete vector potential and its poloidal and toroidal components. The full vector quantity is [perturbed vacuum magnetic vector potential](name:perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential), of which this quantity is the radial projection. Its two quadrature-specific representations are the [real part](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential_real_part) and [imaginary part](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential_imaginary_part) of the same complex radial coefficient. Sign convention: Positive when the radial vector-potential coefficient points toward increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

rows.name: radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential_imaginary_part
rows.description: Imaginary coefficient of the radial component of a complex perturbed magnetic vector-potential eigenfunction for one toroidal linear-MHD mode in the vacuum region.
rows.documentation: This quantity is the imaginary coefficient of the radial component of the complex perturbed magnetic vector-potential eigenfunction for a single toroidal linear-MHD mode in the vacuum region. The radial imaginary coefficient is defined by $$ A_{R,\mathrm{imag}} = \operatorname{Im}\left(\widetilde{\mathbf{A}}_{\mathrm{vac}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{R}}\right) $$ where $A_{R,\mathrm{imag}}$ is this quantity, $\operatorname{Im}$ extracts the imaginary part, $\widetilde{\mathbf{A}}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the complex perturbed magnetic vector-potential eigenfunction in the vacuum region, and $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ is the radial unit vector. The radial direction is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The scope is the vacuum region outside the plasma and one specified toroidal Fourier mode; coefficients from different toroidal modes are not summed. This quantity contains only the out-of-phase imaginary coefficient and excludes the corresponding real part. The [parent radial perturbed vacuum magnetic vector potential](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential) is the full complex radial component before imaginary-part extraction. It is distinct from the [imaginary radial perturbed vacuum magnetic field](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part), because the magnetic-field perturbation is obtained from the curl of the vector potential rather than being the vector-potential component itself. Sign convention: Positive when the imaginary part of the vector-potential coefficient points in the increasing-$R$ radial direction; its phase sign follows the chosen phase reference of the complex eigenfunction.

rows.name: radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential_real_part
rows.description: Real part of the first-order radial magnetic-vector-potential eigenfunction for a single toroidal mode in the vacuum region.
rows.documentation: The quantity is the real radial projection of the first-order perturbed magnetic vector-potential eigenfunction in the vacuum region for one toroidal Fourier mode. The real part is defined relative to the phase reference of that complex eigenfunction. $$ A_{R,\mathrm{vac}}^{\mathrm{Re}} = \operatorname{Re}\!\left(\widetilde{\mathbf{A}}_{\mathrm{vac}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{R}}\right) $$ Here $A_{R,\mathrm{vac}}^{\mathrm{Re}}$ is the requested real radial component, $\widetilde{\mathbf{A}}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the complex first-order perturbed magnetic vector-potential eigenfunction in the vacuum region, $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ is the radial unit vector, and $\operatorname{Re}$ denotes the real-part operation. The radial direction is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The quantity applies outside the plasma and to one toroidal Fourier mode; it is not summed over modes. It excludes the plasma-region perturbation, the imaginary component, and the unreduced complex radial component. The [radial perturbed vacuum magnetic vector potential](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential) is the full complex parent quantity, of which this entry is the real-part component. It is distinct from the [radial perturbed vacuum magnetic field](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field), which is a magnetic-field perturbation rather than a vector potential. Sign convention: Positive when the real radial projection points toward increasing major radius $R$.

rows.name: time_averaged_normalized_perturbed_parallel_magnetic_field_magnitude
rows.description: Time-averaged normalized perturbed parallel magnetic-field magnitude is the time-averaged amplitude of a magnetic-field perturbation projected along the local equilibrium magnetic field and normalized by a reference magnetic-field magnitude. It does not include flux-surface averaging unless a more specific name states that aggregation.
rows.documentation: Time-averaged normalized perturbed parallel magnetic-field magnitude is the time-averaged scalar amplitude of the component of a magnetic-field perturbation parallel to the local equilibrium magnetic field, normalized by a reference magnetic-field magnitude. It characterizes the parallel perturbation amplitude after the sign of the parallel projection has been removed. The quantity is defined by averaging the normalized magnitude of the parallel perturbation over the time interval defining the quantity: $$ \overline{b}_{\parallel,\mathrm{pert}} = \left\langle \frac{\left|\delta \mathbf{B}\cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}}_0\right|}{B_\mathrm{ref}} \right\rangle_t $$ where $\overline{b}_{\parallel,\mathrm{pert}}$ is the time-averaged normalized perturbed parallel magnetic-field magnitude, $\delta \mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field perturbation, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}_0$ is the unit vector in the direction of the local equilibrium magnetic field, $B_\mathrm{ref}$ is the reference magnetic-field magnitude used for normalization, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_t$ denotes averaging over the time interval defining the quantity. The scope is the time-averaged scalar amplitude before any spatial aggregation is added by a more specific qualifier. It applies wherever the magnetic-field perturbation, local equilibrium-field direction, and normalization reference are defined; this parent by itself does not prescribe a flux-surface, volume, line, or ensemble average. This is not the instantaneous normalized perturbation, the signed normalized parallel component, the perpendicular perturbation, or the total magnetic-perturbation magnitude. The absolute value distinguishes it from signed parallel-field perturbations by discarding the sign of the parallel projection. The [flux-surface-averaged time-averaged normalized perturbed parallel magnetic-field magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_time_averaged_normalized_perturbed_parallel_magnetic_field_magnitude) is obtained by applying an additional magnetic-flux-surface average to this already time-averaged quantity; the additional qualifier changes the spatial aggregation, not the presence of time averaging.

rows.name: breakdown_initial_time
rows.description: Timestamp at which plasma breakdown begins and discharge current starts to flow.
rows.documentation: Timestamp at which plasma breakdown begins and discharge current starts to flow.

rows.name: pulse_duration
rows.description: Elapsed duration of the confined-plasma phase in a single discharge, from plasma breakdown until termination of the confined plasma.
rows.documentation: Elapsed duration from plasma breakdown until termination of auxiliary heating in a single discharge.

rows.name: area_of_flux_loop
rows.description: The effective area of a flux loop is the non-negative field-to-flux sensitivity area of the sensor, including the aperture enclosed by each turn, the number of turns, and calibration factors. It converts a spatially averaged magnetic-field component normal to the loop aperture into total linked magnetic flux.
rows.documentation: The effective area of a flux loop is the non-negative field-to-flux sensitivity factor of the sensor. It represents the aperture area enclosed by each turn, the number of turns, and calibration corrections that make the total linked magnetic flux equivalent to a spatially averaged magnetic-field component normal to the loop aperture. The effective area $A_\mathrm{eff}$ is defined by the relation between linked flux and averaged normal field: $$ A_\mathrm{eff} = \frac{\Phi}{\bar{B}_n} $$ where $\Phi$ is the signed magnetic flux threading the loop and $\bar{B}_n$ is the spatial average of the magnetic-field component along the chosen loop normal. For a specified loop normal and terminal polarity, Faraday's law gives $V = -d\Phi/dt = -A_\mathrm{eff}\,d\bar{B}_n/dt$ when $A_\mathrm{eff}$ is constant. Reversing the winding direction or terminal polarity reverses the signed quantities $\Phi$ and $V$, not the non-negative effective area. This quantity is the flux-loop analog of [area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe) for magnetic-field probes. It differs from [area_of_rogowski_coil](name:area_of_rogowski_coil), which describes coupling to enclosed current rather than linked magnetic flux; the corresponding signed circuit response is [voltage_of_flux_loop](name:voltage_of_flux_loop).

rows.name: calibration_reference_magnetic_field_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe
rows.description: Signed poloidal magnetic-field values forming the linear calibration axis used to characterize a poloidal magnetic-field probe’s nonlinear response.
rows.documentation: This quantity is the signed poloidal magnetic field assigned to the linear-response reference axis of a poloidal magnetic-field probe. It represents the field value corresponding to the probe signal under an assumed linear field-to-signal relation, rather than the corrected field on a nonlinear response curve. The linear calibration relation is represented by $$ S_{\mathrm{lin}} = G B_{\mathrm{ref}} $$ where $S_{\mathrm{lin}}$ is the probe signal predicted by the linear-response model, $G$ is the linear field-to-signal coefficient, and $B_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the signed calibration-reference magnetic field represented by this quantity. The quantity applies to the local poloidal magnetic field at the sensing location of the specified poloidal magnetic-field probe. It retains the signed poloidal field rather than a field magnitude, and no summation over probe locations or magnetic-field components is implied. It is an independent calibration-axis quantity, not a plasma-wide or equilibrium-field aggregate. It is distinct from the local operational field represented by [poloidal magnetic field of a magnetic-field probe](name:poloidal_magnetic_field_of_magnetic_field_probe), which is the probe field value itself, and from the equilibrium reference vector [reference magnetic field](name:reference_magnetic_field). The reference values are paired with the nonlinear-response characterization and do not constitute a single fixed gain or an uncertainty/error quantity. The poloidal component is resolved in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. Sign convention: Positive when the signed poloidal field points along the probe's defined positive sensing direction.

rows.name: length_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe
rows.description: Physical extent of a poloidal magnetic-field probe coil measured along its assigned local normal sensing axis, contributing to the coil’s magnetic-flux response.
rows.documentation: The length of a poloidal magnetic-field probe is the physical extent of its sensing coil along the coil’s assigned local normal sensing axis. It describes the coil geometry rather than the length of a signal lead or the distance between mounting points. This quantity applies to one poloidal magnetic-field probe coil as a whole. It is distinct from the [area of the poloidal magnetic-field probe](name:area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe), which describes the area enclosed by one winding turn, and from the [turn count of the poloidal magnetic-field probe](name:turn_count_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe), which describes the number and orientation of complete turns. The coil length, its enclosed per-turn area, and its winding-turn count jointly characterize the probe’s magnetic-flux coupling and effective sensing geometry. The length does not itself specify the coil area, winding count, or magnetic-field orientation.

rows.name: poloidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe
rows.description: Signed poloidal tilt angle of a toroidal magnetic-field probe’s sensitive-axis normal in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, measured clockwise from +R.
rows.documentation: The quantity is the signed orientation angle of the normal defining a toroidal magnetic-field probe’s sensitive axis. It specifies the probe’s tilt in the poloidal cross-section, rather than the spatial angle of the probe center. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, let $n_R$ and $n_Z$ denote the components of the probe’s oriented sensitive-axis normal along the increasing-$R$ and increasing-$Z$ directions. The poloidal angle $\theta_{\rm pol}$ is defined by: $$ \theta_{\rm pol} = \operatorname{atan2}(-n_Z,n_R) $$ where $\operatorname{atan2}$ is the two-argument arctangent that preserves the quadrant of the projected normal. The scope is one toroidal magnetic-field probe and its oriented sensitive-axis normal. This is a geometric sensor-orientation quantity, not the poloidal coordinate of the probe center, the direction of the measured magnetic field, or a plasma flux-surface coordinate; it has no plasma-population or region aggregation and is not summed over probes or coil windings. It is a probe-specific application of the parent [poloidal angle](name:poloidal_angle_of_flux_surface): the parent defines the geometric angular measure, while this quantity applies it to the probe’s oriented normal. The complementary [toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe) describes the toroidal orientation of the same probe normal, whereas [poloidal_angle_of_measurement_position](name:poloidal_angle_of_measurement_position) describes the angular location of a measurement point. Sign convention: Positive when the sensitive-axis normal points from the outward radial direction toward decreasing $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, following the clockwise direction in the poloidal plane.

rows.name: radial_coordinate_of_flux_loop
rows.description: Major-radius coordinate of each geometric point defining a flux-loop position, measured as perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
rows.documentation: The quantity is the non-negative major-radius coordinate $R$ of each geometric point defining a flux-loop position. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $R$ is the distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. For horizontal Cartesian coordinates $X$ and $Y$ in a right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis whose vertical direction coincides with cylindrical $\hat{Z}$, the coordinate is defined by: $$ R = \sqrt{X^2 + Y^2} $$ where $X$ and $Y$ are the point's Cartesian coordinates along $\hat{x}$ and $\hat{y}$, and $R$ is its major-radius coordinate. The quantity applies separately to every geometric point defining one flux-loop position, including a partial loop; it is not a loop-wide average, centroid, or other aggregation of those points. It is a geometric coordinate only and does not represent the loop's other position coordinates, linked magnetic flux, induced voltage, or [effective flux-loop area](name:area_of_flux_loop). This quantity is the flux-loop-specific specialization of the general [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate): it retains the same major-radius definition while identifying the point as part of flux-loop geometry. The complete point position requires its corresponding toroidal and vertical coordinates.

rows.name: radial_coordinate_of_rogowski_coil
rows.description: Radial coordinate of a Rogowski coil position, equal to the major-radius coordinate of the coil's designated geometric point in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
rows.documentation: The radial coordinate of a Rogowski coil position is the major-radius coordinate of the designated geometric point representing the coil position. It is the non-negative perpendicular distance of that point from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. Using any point on the toroidal symmetry axis as reference, the coordinate is defined by the transverse projection of the coil-position vector relative to that axis: $$ R_{\mathrm{coil}} = \left\| (\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{coil}} - \mathbf{o}_{\mathcal{A}}) - \left[(\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{coil}} - \mathbf{o}_{\mathcal{A}}) \cdot \hat{Z}\right]\hat{Z} \right\| $$ where $R_{\mathrm{coil}}$ is the radial coordinate of the Rogowski coil position, $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{coil}}$ is the position vector of the designated geometric point, $\mathbf{o}_{\mathcal{A}}$ is any position vector on the toroidal symmetry axis $\mathcal{A}$, $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector along that axis, and $\|\cdot\|$ denotes the Euclidean norm. This quantity applies to the single designated geometric point used to locate the Rogowski coil. It is not an average, integral, or other aggregation over the winding path, aperture, conductor cross-section, or physical extent of the coil. This coordinate is the radial member of the Rogowski-coil position coordinates and is distinct from the [vertical coordinate of the Rogowski coil](name:vertical_coordinate_of_rogowski_coil) and any toroidal angular coordinate of the same point. It is also distinct from the [area of the Rogowski coil](name:area_of_rogowski_coil), the [current of the Rogowski coil](name:current_of_rogowski_coil), coil orientation, and winding geometry; those quantities do not change the definition of $R_{\mathrm{coil}}$. As a named instance of [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate), it is invariant under changes of toroidal angle at fixed major radius.

rows.name: stray_breakdown_magnetic_field_magnitude
rows.description: Magnitude of the residual magnetic field at the plasma position during initiation, whose incomplete cancelation can inhibit electron-avalanche breakdown.
rows.documentation: This quantity is the total strength of the residual magnetic-field contribution present at the plasma position during plasma initiation. It is derived from the vector quantity [stray breakdown magnetic field](name:stray_breakdown_magnetic_field) by removing directional information. $$ B_{\mathrm{stray}} = \left|\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{stray}}\right| = \sqrt{B_R^2 + B_\phi^2 + B_Z^2} $$ where $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{stray}}$ is the residual magnetic-field vector, and $B_R$, $B_\phi$, and $B_Z$ are its components in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The magnitude includes all spatial components caused by imperfect cancelation of external coil fields. It is distinct from any individual directional component and does not encode field orientation or sign.

rows.name: turns_per_metre_of_rogowski_coil
rows.description: Linear winding density of a Rogowski coil, specifying the number of turns in a single winding layer per unit coil length.
rows.documentation: The turns-per-length quantity specifies the linear winding density of a Rogowski coil. For a multilayer winding, it refers to one winding layer rather than the combined count of all layers. The winding density is defined by $$ n_t = \frac{N_\ell}{\ell} $$ where $n_t$ is the Rogowski-coil turns density, $N_\ell$ is the number of complete winding turns in one layer over the selected winding length, and $\ell$ is that winding length. This quantity applies to the physical winding of the Rogowski coil and is a linear density, not a discrete total turn count. It excludes the effective cross-sectional area, which is a separate geometric quantity described by the [area of the Rogowski coil](name:area_of_rogowski_coil), and it does not represent the signed winding current described by the [current of the Rogowski coil](name:current_of_rogowski_coil). The winding density and effective cross-sectional area together determine the coil's electromagnetic coupling and therefore its current-sensing sensitivity.

rows.name: vertical_coordinate_of_flux_loop
rows.description: Vertical Z coordinate of a position point associated with one flux loop in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
rows.documentation: The quantity is the vertical coordinate $Z$ of a position point associated with one flux loop. It locates that point along the vertical direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Here $Z$ denotes vertical height, $R$ denotes major radius from the symmetry axis, and $\phi$ denotes toroidal angle. The value applies to an individual position point of a single flux loop; it is not a loop-area quantity, magnetic flux, voltage, or an aggregate over turns, points, or multiple loops. No population or plasma-region restriction is implied. Together with the corresponding radial and toroidal position coordinates, this coordinate locates the flux-loop point in space. It is the flux-loop-specific counterpart of the [vertical coordinate of a measurement position](name:vertical_coordinate_of_measurement_position), which applies the same geometric concept to a generic measurement location. Sign convention: Positive when the flux-loop position lies in the +Z direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

rows.name: voltage_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe
rows.description: Terminal voltage induced at the terminals of a toroidal magnetic-field probe coil by time variation of the local toroidal magnetic-field component in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame threading the coil windings.
rows.documentation: Terminal voltage induced at the terminals of a toroidal magnetic-field probe coil is the signed electric potential difference produced by Faraday induction in a coil sensitive to the toroidal magnetic-field component. The toroidal component is $B_\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. For fixed probe geometry, the defining Faraday-law relation is $$ V_\phi(t) = -\frac{d\Lambda_\phi(t)}{dt} $$ where $V_\phi$ is the terminal voltage, $\Lambda_\phi$ is the signed magnetic-flux linkage of the toroidal magnetic-field probe, and $t$ is time. This quantity applies to one toroidal magnetic-field probe coil and to the local region whose magnetic flux threads that coil. It is not an aggregate over multiple probes, and it excludes the integrated or calibrated local toroidal magnetic-field component derived from the raw terminal voltage. For a uniform local-field approximation, $\Lambda_\phi = N_\phi A_\phi B_\phi$, where $N_\phi$ is the signed [turn count of the toroidal magnetic-field probe](name:turn_count_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe) and $A_\phi$ is the effective sensitive area set by the probe geometry, including the [length of the toroidal magnetic-field probe](name:length_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe). Relative to a reference time $t_0$, the corresponding calibrated field change satisfies $B_\phi(t)-B_\phi(t_0) = -(N_\phi A_\phi)^{-1}\int_{t_0}^{t} V_\phi(t')\,dt'$ when the same fixed sensitivity applies. The corresponding terminal-voltage quantity for a probe sensitive to the poloidal magnetic-field component is [voltage of poloidal magnetic-field probe](name:voltage_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe). Sign convention: Positive when the signed magnetic-flux linkage of the toroidal magnetic-field probe is decreasing in time.

rows.name: area_of_passive_loop
rows.description: Area of a passive loop is the non-negative cross-sectional area of conducting material in a passive loop element, taken on a section normal to the local current path. It excludes the aperture enclosed by the loop.
rows.documentation: Area of a passive loop is the non-negative cross-sectional area of the solid conducting material of a passive conducting loop element, evaluated on a surface normal to the local current path. It is a material cross-section of the conductor, not the aperture enclosed by the loop or the area swept out by the loop centerline. The general geometric definition is the area of the conducting region $\mathcal{S}$ in that normal cross-section: $$ A = \int_{\mathcal{S}} dS $$ where $A$ is the passive-loop conductor area, $\mathcal{S}$ is the subset of the section occupied by conducting material, and $dS$ is the scalar surface-area element. For an annular cross-section, this definition gives $A = \pi(r_o^2-r_i^2)$, where $r_i$ and $r_o$ are the [inner](name:inner_radius_of_passive_loop) and [outer](name:outer_radius_of_passive_loop) radii measured from the annulus center to the conducting boundaries. For a non-annular cross-section, $\mathcal{S}$ is the bounded conducting region defined by the conductor geometry; parameters such as thickness, width, or height describe that boundary but are not themselves the area.

rows.name: area_of_poloidal_field_coil
rows.description: Non-negative full geometric area of the conducting cross section of one poloidal-field-coil element in a poloidal plane at fixed toroidal angle φ of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where R is major radius and Z is vertical height.
rows.documentation: Non-negative full geometric area of the conducting cross section of one poloidal-field-coil element is the surface measure of the conductor region enclosed by that element boundary. It is defined in a poloidal plane at fixed toroidal angle $\phi$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. For an arbitrary conductor cross-section, the area is the integral of the differential surface measure over the conductor region $\mathcal{S}$: $$ A = \int_{\mathcal{S}} dS $$ where $A$ is the area of the poloidal-field-coil element, $\mathcal{S}$ is the conductor region in the poloidal plane, and $dS$ is the differential surface measure on that plane. The quantity is per coil element, not a sum over multiple elements or over a complete coil. For a rectangular cross-section aligned with the $R$ and $Z$ directions of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $A = W H$, where $W$ is [width_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:width_of_poloidal_field_coil) and $H$ is [height_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:height_of_poloidal_field_coil); [thickness_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:thickness_of_poloidal_field_coil) is a separate geometric extent and is not the radial width in this relationship. For an annular cross-section, $A = \pi(r_\mathrm{out}^2-r_\mathrm{in}^2)$, where $r_\mathrm{out}$ is [outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil) and $r_\mathrm{in}$ is [inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil). An insulation envelope, winding-pack envelope, or effective conducting area is a distinct quantity unless it is defined by the same boundary as $\mathcal{S}$.

rows.name: effective_turn_count_of_coil_conductor_element
rows.description: Signed effective winding count used to weight the magnetic-field contribution of an individual poloidal-field coil conductor element.
rows.documentation: The effective turn count is the signed winding multiplicity assigned to one poloidal-field coil conductor element for calculating its contribution to the plasma magnetic field. Its magnitude represents the effective number of turns attributed to that element, while its sign represents winding orientation. This quantity applies to an individual conductor element and is not the total turn count of a complete coil or coil system. It is an effective electromagnetic contribution rather than a purely geometric count of visible conductor revolutions, and it excludes the separate winding counts of magnetic-field probe coils. For a fixed element current and geometry, the element’s magnetic-field contribution scales with its effective turn count; reversing the count reverses the corresponding field contribution. The same signed-winding concept is used for a [poloidal magnetic-field probe turn count](name:turn_count_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe) and a [toroidal magnetic-field probe turn count](name:turn_count_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), although this quantity applies specifically to a poloidal-field coil conductor element.

rows.name: fast_neutron_flux_of_toroidal_field_coil
rows.description: Incident crossing rate of fast neutrons per unit area on the inboard-facing surface of a toroidal field coil.
rows.documentation: Incident crossing rate of fast neutrons per unit area on the inboard-facing surface of a toroidal field coil is the surface density of neutrons whose kinetic energy is at or above the fast-neutron threshold and whose trajectories cross that surface into the coil. The inboard-facing surface is the side of the toroidal field coil facing the toroidal symmetry axis. At a point on that surface, the defining angular-flux integral is: $$ \Phi_\mathrm{fast}^{\mathrm{TF,in}}(\mathbf{x}) = \int_{E_\mathrm{fast}}^\infty \int_{4\pi} \varphi_n(\mathbf{x}, E, \hat{\Omega})\, \max\!\left(0, -\hat{\Omega}\!\cdot\!\hat{\mathbf{n}}_\mathrm{TF,in}(\mathbf{x})\right)\, d\Omega\, dE $$ where $\Phi_\mathrm{fast}^{\mathrm{TF,in}}$ is the fast neutron flux of the toroidal field coil at surface point $\mathbf{x}$, $\mathbf{x}$ is a point on the inboard-facing surface, $E$ is neutron kinetic energy, $E_\mathrm{fast}$ is the fast-neutron threshold, $\hat{\Omega}$ is neutron flight direction, $\varphi_n$ is the angular neutron flux, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_\mathrm{TF,in}$ is the unit normal directed outward from the coil material at the inboard-facing surface, and $d\Omega$ is the solid-angle element. The scope is limited to toroidal field coils and to their inboard-facing surfaces; it does not include correction coils, poloidal field coils, the outboard-facing surface, or a whole-coil combination of surfaces. The quantity is normalized by the receiving surface area and is not the area-integrated neutron rate, cumulative neutron fluence, total neutron production rate, or material response caused by the neutron field. The fast-neutron threshold is an essential part of the convention: neutrons below $E_\mathrm{fast}$ are excluded, and a different threshold defines a different fast-neutron flux. The analogous quantity for a correction coil is [fast neutron flux of correction coil](name:fast_neutron_flux_of_correction_coil); it uses the same incident fast-neutron crossing concept but a different coil population.

rows.name: height_of_correction_coil
rows.description: Full non-negative extent of a rectangular correction-coil conductor cross-section measured along the local Frenet–Serret binormal.
rows.documentation: The correction-coil height is the full external-envelope dimension of its rectangular conductor cross-section along the binormal direction of the local Frenet–Serret frame $(\hat{\mathbf t}, \hat{\mathbf n}, \hat{\mathbf b})$. It is distinct from the transverse dimension measured along the local normal direction, defined by the [width of a correction coil](name:width_of_correction_coil). $$ h = b_{\max} - b_{\min} $$ where $h$ is the conductor height and $b_{\max}$ and $b_{\min}$ are the signed binormal coordinates of the opposing outer faces, consistent with the [binormal coordinate of a correction coil](name:binormal_coordinate_of_correction_coil). The quantity is the full extent, not a half-height, centerline offset, or cross-sectional area.

rows.name: normal_coordinate_of_correction_coil
rows.description: Signed coordinate of a correction-coil conductor cross-section outline vertex along the normal axis of the local Frenet-Serret frame, measured from the conductor centerline.
rows.documentation: Signed coordinate of a correction-coil conductor cross-section outline vertex along the normal axis of the local Frenet-Serret frame, measured from the conductor centerline, is the scalar projection of the displacement from the centerline point to that vertex onto the local normal direction. The local frame is the right-handed Frenet-Serret frame $(\hat{\mathbf{t}}, \hat{\mathbf{n}}, \hat{\mathbf{b}})$ attached to the correction-coil conductor centerline, with $\hat{\mathbf{b}} = \hat{\mathbf{t}} \times \hat{\mathbf{n}}$. The coordinate is defined by $$ q_n = \left(\mathbf{x}_v - \mathbf{x}_c(s)\right) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}(s) $$ where $q_n$ is the signed normal coordinate of the outline vertex, $\mathbf{x}_v$ is the position vector of the outline vertex, $\mathbf{x}_c(s)$ is the position vector of the conductor centerline at centerline parameter $s$, $s$ identifies the corresponding location along the conductor centerline, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}(s)$ is the normal basis vector of the local Frenet-Serret frame. The scope is the local cross-sectional boundary of a correction-coil conductor; each value refers to one outline vertex at one centerline location and describes only its normal-axis displacement in the local $(\hat{\mathbf{n}}, \hat{\mathbf{b}})$ cross-section plane. It excludes the binormal coordinate, any coordinate of the conductor centerline itself, and any projection along a magnetic-flux-surface normal. The paired [binormal coordinate of a correction coil](name:binormal_coordinate_of_correction_coil) gives the complementary component of the same outline vertex in the local $(\hat{\mathbf{n}}, \hat{\mathbf{b}})$ cross-section plane. Together, the paired outline coordinates define the boundary whose enclosed [cross-sectional area of the correction coil](name:area_of_correction_coil) is a related geometric property. The [normal coordinate of a toroidal-field coil](name:normal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil) has the same local-coordinate meaning for a different coil class. Sign convention: Positive when the displacement from the correction-coil conductor centerline to the outline vertex has a component in the $+\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ direction of the local Frenet-Serret frame.

rows.name: outer_radius_of_ferritic_element
rows.description: Outer radial boundary of the annular cross-section of a ferritic element in the axisymmetric equivalent geometry, defining the external extent of the annulus centered at a reference point in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
rows.documentation: The outer radius specifies the external boundary of the annular cross-section used to represent a ferritic element in the axisymmetric thick-line equivalent geometry. Ferritic elements are ferromagnetic inserts, and each element is represented by an axisymmetric body whose cross-section is an annulus centered at a reference point $(R_0, Z_0)$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius from the toroidal symmetry axis and $Z$ is vertical height. For an annular cross-section with inner radius $r_\mathrm{in}$ and outer radius $r_\mathrm{out}$, the enclosed area is $$ A = \pi\bigl(r_\mathrm{out}^2 - r_\mathrm{in}^2\bigr) $$ where $A$ is the cross-sectional area and $r_\mathrm{in}$ and $r_\mathrm{out}$ are radial distances from the annulus center. The constraint is $0 \leq r_\mathrm{in} < r_\mathrm{out}$. Together with [inner radius of the ferritic element](name:inner_radius_of_ferritic_element), this quantity defines the annular cross-section; [radius of the ferritic element](name:radial_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid) specifies its radial placement rather than its outer boundary.

rows.name: outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil
rows.description: Nonnegative distance from the annulus center to the outer conducting boundary of a poloidal field coil's annular conductor cross-section.
rows.documentation: The outer [radius](name:radius) is the larger of the two radii bounding the annular conductor cross-section of one poloidal field coil. It extends from the common annulus center to the outer conducting boundary. The outer radius is defined by $$ R_{\mathrm{out}} = \left\|\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{b}}-\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{c}}\right\| $$ where $R_{\mathrm{out}}$ is the outer radius, $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{b}}$ is the position of any point on the outer conducting boundary, $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{c}}$ is the annulus-center position, and $\|\cdot\|$ denotes Euclidean distance within the cross-sectional plane. The [inner radius](name:inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil) bounds the central aperture. Together, the inner radius, outer radius, and center position specify the annulus geometry. For a nondegenerate conducting annulus, $0 \leq R_{\mathrm{in}} < R_{\mathrm{out}}$, where $R_{\mathrm{in}}$ is the inner radius. This quantity describes one annular cross-section, not the coil's distance from the machine symmetry axis. It is distinct from the [circular-segment curvature radius](name:radius_of_poloidal_field_coil), which describes an arc of the coil cross-sectional contour.

rows.name: temperature_of_coil_conductor
rows.description: Thermodynamic temperature of the conductor in an active poloidal-field or central-solenoid coil, used to establish its allowable current limit.
rows.documentation: This quantity is the thermodynamic temperature of the conducting material in an individual active poloidal-field coil, including central-solenoid and shaping-coil conductors. It applies to the conductor of one active coil and represents the coil's thermal state, not the temperature of a coolant, surrounding structure, or plasma. It is not an aggregate temperature over multiple coils and is distinct from electrical properties such as the [resistance of a poloidal-field coil](name:resistance_of_poloidal_field_coil). The temperature serves as the independent variable for the coil's temperature-dependent maximum allowable current. It therefore identifies the operating-limit condition associated with the conductor temperature, but is not itself a current, resistance, or operating-limit value.

rows.name: thickness_of_iron_core_segment
rows.description: Full non-negative toroidal extent of a rectangular iron-core segment between its pair of opposite faces, measured along the toroidal direction φ in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame. It is perpendicular to the segment's radial width along R and vertical height along Z.
rows.documentation: Full non-negative toroidal extent of a rectangular iron-core segment between its pair of opposite faces, measured along the toroidal direction $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius from the machine symmetry axis, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is the vertical height. The thickness is the face-to-face separation of paired points on the two opposite toroidal-facing faces along the local toroidal unit vector: $$ t = \left| (\mathbf{x}_+ - \mathbf{x}_-) \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} \right| $$ where $t$ is the segment thickness in m, $\mathbf{x}_-$ and $\mathbf{x}_+$ are position vectors in m of paired points on the two opposite faces lying on the same line parallel to $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$, and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ is the local toroidal unit vector of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Together with the [width of the iron-core segment](name:width_of_iron_core_segment), the radial extent along $R$, and the [height of the iron-core segment](name:height_of_iron_core_segment), the vertical extent along $Z$, the thickness completes the mutually orthogonal triplet of extents describing the segment as a rectangular block whose cross section lies in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane and is extruded along $\phi$. It excludes any diagonal, chordwise, or arc-length measure across the segment.

rows.name: toroidal_magnetization_of_ferritic_element
rows.description: Toroidal component of the ferritic-element magnetization vector: the signed projection of the effective magnetization assigned to a discrete ferritic element onto the positive toroidal direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame. This is the element-level convention, not a pointwise bulk-material magnetization field.
rows.documentation: Toroidal component of the ferritic-element magnetization vector is the signed projection of the effective magnetization assigned to a discrete ferritic element onto the toroidal basis direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The projection is defined by: $$ M_\phi^{\mathrm{fe}} = \mathbf{M}^{\mathrm{fe}} \cdot \hat{\phi} $$ where $\mathbf{M}^{\mathrm{fe}}$ is the ferritic-element magnetization vector assigned to the element, $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle, and $M_\phi^{\mathrm{fe}}$ is this toroidal component. In this family, ferritic-element magnetization denotes the effective magnetization attributed to the individual ferritic element for its magnetic source strength. It is not the pointwise bulk magnetization field inside the material, and it is distinct from material properties such as magnetic permeability. Together with the [radial component](name:radial_magnetization_of_ferritic_element) and [vertical component](name:vertical_magnetization_of_ferritic_element), it forms the three cylindrical components of the same effective ferritic-element magnetization vector. Sign convention: Positive when $M_\phi^{\mathrm{fe}}$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

rows.name: vertical_coordinate_of_annulus_center
rows.description: Vertical coordinate of the annulus center specifies its signed height from the zero-height plane, parallel to the symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
