rows.documentation: Vertical coordinate of the annulus center is its signed height in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The coordinate is defined by $$ Z = \mathbf{x}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{z}} $$ where $\mathbf{x}$ is the position vector of the annulus center measured from the coordinate origin, and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ is the unit vector parallel to the symmetry axis toward increasing $Z$. The quantity applies to one annular cross-section, not to points along its boundary or to an average over multiple elements. It specifies position rather than the inner radius, outer radius, or vertical extent of the annulus, and applies to both conducting and magnetizable components. It uses the same vertical projection as the [vertical coordinate of an arc-of-circle center](name:vertical_coordinate_of_arc_of_circle_center), with a different geometric locus. Sign convention: Positive when the annulus center lies above the zero-height plane in the direction of increasing $Z$.

rows.name: vertical_force_of_poloidal_field_coil
rows.description: Signed vertical component of the net electromagnetic Lorentz force on one poloidal-field coil, resolved along increasing Z in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
rows.documentation: This quantity is the net electromagnetic Lorentz force on an individual poloidal-field-coil conductor projected onto the vertical axis of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The force component is defined by $$ F_Z = \int_{V_{\mathrm{coil}}} (\mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{Z}}\,\mathrm{d}V $$ where $F_Z$ is the vertical force component, $V_{\mathrm{coil}}$ is the conductor volume, $\mathbf{J}$ is the current-density vector, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector acting on the conductor, $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the vertical unit vector, and $\mathrm{d}V$ is a differential volume element. This is a signed component rather than the force magnitude or resultant. The radial component is represented separately by [radial force of a poloidal-field coil](name:radial_force_of_poloidal_field_coil), while [force of a poloidal-field coil](name:force_of_poloidal_field_coil) represents the coil’s electromagnetic force resultant. Sign convention: Positive when the net force points toward increasing $Z$.

rows.name: width_of_correction_coil
rows.description: Full non-negative extent of a non-axisymmetric correction-coil conductor cross-section measured along its local normal axis; for circular sections it is the diameter, and for annular sections it is the outer diameter.
rows.documentation: Full non-negative extent of a non-axisymmetric correction-coil conductor cross-section measured along its local normal axis is the characteristic transverse size of that cross-section. It is a geometric property of the conductor cross-section, not a signed displacement or orientation. The defining geometric identification is: $$ w = \begin{cases} a_n, & \text{rectangular or square cross-section},\\ D, & \text{circular cross-section},\\ D_{\mathrm{out}}, & \text{annular cross-section}. \end{cases} $$ where $w$ is this width, $a_n$ is the full cross-section extent along the local normal axis, $D$ is the circular cross-section diameter, and $D_{\mathrm{out}}$ is the annular cross-section outer diameter. The scope is one conductor cross-section of one non-axisymmetric correction coil; the quantity is assigned to the whole cross-section. It is not a sum or average over multiple coils, separate conductor segments, or turns, and it is not the conductor path length or the spatial location of the coil. The companion linear size for a rectangular or square section is the [height of a correction-coil conductor cross-section](name:height_of_correction_coil); the [area of a correction-coil conductor cross-section](name:area_of_correction_coil) is the corresponding area, not another linear dimension. For an annular section, the [inner radius of a correction-coil conductor cross-section](name:inner_radius_of_correction_coil) describes the central opening, whereas this width describes the outer diameter. The [width of a toroidal-field-coil conductor cross-section](name:width_of_toroidal_field_coil) is the analogous geometric quantity for a toroidal-field coil rather than a non-axisymmetric correction coil.

rows.name: width_of_toroidal_field_coil
rows.description: Full geometric width of a toroidal-field-coil conductor cross-section, measured as the boundary-to-boundary transverse extent along the normal direction of the local Frenet-Serret frame. It is an unsigned extent, not a centerline location or coil radius.
rows.documentation: Full geometric width of a toroidal-field-coil conductor cross-section, measured along the normal axis of the local right-handed Frenet-Serret frame $(\hat{t}, \hat{n}, \hat{b})$. The tangent $\hat{t}$ follows the conductor centerline, the normal $\hat{n}$ lies in the cross-section plane, and the binormal $\hat{b} = \hat{t} \times \hat{n}$; the corresponding extent along $\hat{b}$ is [height_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:height_of_toroidal_field_coil). The width is the boundary-to-boundary span of the outer conductor boundary $\partial S$ projected onto $\hat{n}$: $$ w = \max_{\mathbf{r} \in \partial S} (\mathbf{r} \cdot \hat{n}) - \min_{\mathbf{r} \in \partial S} (\mathbf{r} \cdot \hat{n}) $$ where $\mathbf{r}$ is the position of a boundary point in the cross-section plane and $\hat{n}$ is the unit normal. Reversing the sense of $\hat{n}$ leaves $w$ unchanged, so it is an unsigned extent. For a rectangular or square section this is the full side length along $\hat{n}$; for a circular section it is the diameter; for an annular section it is the outer diameter, not the bore diameter or wall thickness. It is a geometric extent of the outer cross-section and is distinct from a centerline location or from a coil radius such as radius_of_toroidal_field_coil or [inner_radius_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:inner_radius_of_toroidal_field_coil).

rows.name: alfven_frequency
rows.description: Alfvén frequency at a given radial position for a single toroidal mode number is the complex local shear-Alfvén continuum angular frequency; its real part gives oscillation and its imaginary part gives growth or damping for the stated time dependence.
rows.documentation: Alfvén frequency at a given radial position for a single toroidal mode number is the complex local shear-Alfvén continuum angular frequency for perturbations propagating along the magnetic field on the flux surface at that radial position. Its [real part](name:alfven_frequency_real_part) is the oscillatory component, and its [imaginary part](name:alfven_frequency_imaginary_part) is the temporal growth or damping component. The ideal shear-Alfvén continuum relation defining the underlying continuum frequency is $$ \omega_A = |k_\parallel| v_A $$ where $\omega_A$ is the real continuum angular frequency, $k_\parallel$ is the component of the wave vector parallel to the magnetic field, and $v_A$ is the Alfvén speed, $B/\sqrt{\mu_0\rho_m}$ with $B$ the magnetic-field magnitude, $\mu_0$ the vacuum permeability, and $\rho_m$ the plasma mass density. This quantity denotes the full complex frequency $\Omega_A=\operatorname{Re}(\Omega_A)+i\operatorname{Im}(\Omega_A)$, not either component alone, and it is an angular frequency rather than a cyclic frequency. The radial position is a flux-surface label in explicitly named flux coordinates such as $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ or $(\psi,\theta,\phi)$, not a cylindrical vector component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. At fixed toroidal mode number, $k_\parallel$ is determined by field-line pitch, magnetic geometry, and poloidal harmonic content, with the [safety factor](name:safety_factor) entering common single-harmonic specializations. Sign convention: Positive when $\operatorname{Im}(\Omega_A)$ makes perturbations proportional to $\exp(-i\Omega_A t)$ grow exponentially in time.

rows.name: perturbed_plasma_mass_density_real_part
rows.description: In-phase component of the complex first-order plasma mass-density eigenfunction for one toroidal Fourier harmonic in linear MHD stability theory.
rows.documentation: The quantity is the real, in-phase component of the complex first-order plasma mass-density perturbation eigenfunction associated with one toroidal Fourier harmonic in linear MHD stability theory. The complete complex quantity is perturbed plasma mass density. The real component is defined by $$ \widetilde{\rho}_{n,\mathrm{real}}(\mathbf{x}) = \operatorname{Re}\!\left[\widetilde{\rho}_n(\mathbf{x})\right] $$ where $\widetilde{\rho}_n$ is the complex first-order mass-density eigenfunction, $n$ is the toroidal Fourier mode number, and $\mathbf{x}$ denotes position. The decomposition is relative to the phase convention of the complex eigenfunction. This quantity excludes the imaginary quadrature component and must not be interpreted as the magnitude of the complex perturbation. Its meaning parallels the real component of the corresponding temperature eigenfunction, [perturbed plasma temperature real part](name:perturbed_plasma_temperature_real_part).

rows.name: plasma_temperature
rows.description: Effective temperature of the plasma in a fluid or MHD description, representing the average thermal kinetic energy per degree of freedom of the combined charged particle population.
rows.documentation: The plasma temperature is a fundamental thermodynamic state variable in fluid and single-fluid MHD models, quantifying the mean random kinetic energy of the charged particle population. In a single-fluid description it is linked to thermal pressure via the equation of state $$ p = n k_B T $$ where $p$ is the scalar pressure, $n$ is the total particle number density, and $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant. In multi-species plasmas an effective plasma temperature may be obtained as a density-weighted combination of electron and ion contributions; applications requiring species resolution use explicitly qualified forms such as particle_temperature or [neutral_temperature](name:neutral_internal_state_temperature). This quantity also appears as the equilibrium background in linear MHD stability analysis, where its first-order perturbation is represented by the complex eigenfunction perturbed_plasma_temperature, encoding the amplitude and phase of the temperature fluctuation for a specified toroidal Fourier harmonic. The total isotropic pressure of the plasma, including contributions summed over all species, is captured by plasma_pressure.

rows.name: plasma_velocity
rows.description: Mass-weighted bulk center-of-mass velocity vector of the plasma fluid, whose projections onto the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) coordinate directions provide the radial, toroidal, vertical, and parallel flow components.
rows.documentation: The plasma velocity is the local center-of-mass (barycentric) flow velocity of the bulk plasma, representing the momentum per unit mass carried collectively by all plasma species. It is the primary kinematic quantity in single-fluid and multi-fluid magnetohydrodynamic descriptions of plasma transport, rotation, and momentum confinement. The center-of-mass velocity vector is defined as: $$ \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{cm} = \frac{\sum_s m_s n_s \mathbf{v}_s}{\sum_s m_s n_s} $$ where the sum runs over all contributing plasma species $s$, $m_s$ is the species mass, $n_s$ is the number density, and $\mathbf{v}_s$ is the mean fluid velocity of species $s$. The full velocity vector decomposes into projections along the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame: the [radial component](name:radial_plasma_velocity) along $\hat{R}$, the [toroidal component](name:toroidal_center_of_mass_velocity) along $\hat{\phi}$, the [vertical component](name:vertical_plasma_velocity) along $\hat{Z}$, and the [parallel component](name:parallel_plasma_velocity) along the local magnetic-field unit vector $\hat{b}$. Individual projections are inferred from Doppler spectroscopy, charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, and motional-Stark-effect diagnostics; Mach probes provide parallel-flow access in the scrape-off layer.

rows.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_halo_boundary
rows.description: Poloidal magnetic flux evaluated on the outermost flux surface of the halo-current region during a disruption. This is the wall-side halo boundary of the halo-current domain, not the inner confined-plasma interface.
rows.documentation: Poloidal magnetic flux at the halo boundary is the value of the [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) function on the outermost magnetic flux surface of the halo-current region during a disruption. The halo boundary is the wall-side flux-surface limit of the halo-current domain, not the inner interface between that domain and any confined-plasma core. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius, $\phi$ the toroidal angle, and $Z$ the vertical height, the value on a halo-boundary point $(R_h, Z_h)$ is defined by the flux of the vertical magnetic field through the horizontal disk centered on the toroidal symmetry axis: $$ \psi_h = \psi(R_h, Z_h) = \int_0^{R_h} B_Z(R', Z_h)\,2\pi R'\,dR' $$ where $\psi_h$ is the poloidal magnetic flux at the halo boundary, $\psi(R_h, Z_h)$ is the poloidal magnetic flux function evaluated on that boundary, and $B_Z$ is the vertical component of the magnetic field. This quantity is the poloidal-flux counterpart of the [toroidal magnetic flux at the halo boundary](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_halo_boundary). It is a flux-surface value and does not denote the total magnetic flux through the halo-current volume or the halo current itself. Sign convention: Positive when $B_Z$ on the integration disk points in the $+Z$ direction.

rows.name: poloidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_vector_potential
rows.description: Poloidal component of the first-order perturbed plasma magnetic vector potential, represented as a linear MHD eigenfunction and distinct from its radial and toroidal components.
rows.documentation: The poloidal perturbed plasma magnetic vector potential is the poloidal component of the first-order departure of the plasma magnetic vector potential from its reference state. In linear magnetohydrodynamic eigenfunction descriptions, it carries the poloidal part of the magnetic-vector-potential perturbation without selecting a real or imaginary phase component. The perturbed magnetic field associated with the full vector potential perturbation satisfies $$ \delta \mathbf{B} = \nabla \times \delta \mathbf{A} $$ where $\delta \mathbf{B}$ is the perturbed plasma magnetic field, $\nabla$ is the spatial gradient operator, and $\delta \mathbf{A}$ is the full perturbed plasma magnetic vector potential. The poloidal component is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major-radius coordinate, $\phi$ the toroidal angle, and $Z$ the vertical coordinate. This quantity is restricted to the poloidal component and is not the complete vector potential, its radial component, its toroidal component, or the perturbed magnetic field itself. It is also distinct from the real-valued specialization [poloidal perturbed plasma magnetic vector potential real part](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_vector_potential_real_part), which selects one phase component of the corresponding eigenfunction. The component is a specialization of the full [perturbed plasma magnetic vector potential](name:perturbed_plasma_magnetic_vector_potential); its curl contributes to the associated perturbed magnetic field. A gage transformation can change the vector-potential representation without changing this curl, so the vector-potential component is not uniquely identical to a magnetic-field component. The radial component provides an adjacent component specialization of the same perturbed-vector-potential family.

rows.name: poloidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part
rows.description: Imaginary component of the complex poloidal projection, along the increasing-θ tangent in flux coordinates (ρ, θ, φ), of the first-order magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction in the current-free vacuum region outside the plasma boundary for a specified toroidal Fourier mode.
rows.documentation: Imaginary component of the complex poloidal projection, along the increasing-$\theta$ tangent in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, of the first-order magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction in the current-free vacuum region outside the plasma boundary for a specified toroidal Fourier mode. It is a signed scalar magnetic-field amplitude of the complex vacuum perturbation. The complex poloidal vacuum perturbation amplitude is decomposed into real and imaginary parts by: $$ \delta B_{\theta}^{(V)}(\rho,\theta;n) = \operatorname{Re}\{\delta B_{\theta}^{(V)}(\rho,\theta;n)\} + i\,\operatorname{Im}\{\delta B_{\theta}^{(V)}(\rho,\theta;n)\} $$ where $\delta B_{\theta}^{(V)}$ is the component of $\delta\mathbf{B}^{(V)}$ along the unit poloidal tangent $\hat{e}_{\theta}=(\partial\mathbf{x}/\partial\theta)_{\rho,\phi}/|(\partial\mathbf{x}/\partial\theta)_{\rho,\phi}|$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\rho$ is the selected magnetic-flux-surface label, $\theta$ is the poloidal angle, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, $n$ is the integer toroidal Fourier mode number, $i$ is the imaginary unit, and $\operatorname{Re}$ and $\operatorname{Im}$ denote the real-part and imaginary-part operators. The quantity named here is $\operatorname{Im}\{\delta B_{\theta}^{(V)}\}$, and all magnetic-field amplitudes in the equation have units of tesla. The superscript $V$ denotes the vacuum-region perturbation and excludes perturbations in the plasma region. In that region the first-order perturbation is current-free and solenoidal, satisfying $\nabla\times\delta\mathbf{B}^{(V)}=0$ and $\nabla\cdot\delta\mathbf{B}^{(V)}=0$. This quantity is paired with [poloidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part](name:poloidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part); a common complex rescaling of a linear eigenfunction changes absolute amplitude and phase but not the component identity defined here. Sign convention: Positive when the imaginary part of the poloidal projection is directed along the unit tangent for increasing $\theta$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

rows.name: poloidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part
rows.description: Real part of the single-toroidal-mode poloidal perturbed vacuum magnetic field, equal to the in-phase projection of the complex first-order vacuum magnetic-field perturbation onto the poloidal unit tangent outside the plasma.
rows.documentation: Real part of the single-toroidal-mode poloidal perturbed vacuum magnetic field is the in-phase scalar component of the complex first-order vacuum magnetic-field perturbation projected onto the poloidal unit tangent outside the plasma. The poloidal unit tangent is defined in a specified flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ as the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ at fixed $\rho$ and $\phi$, where $\phi$ is the toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$. This poloidal direction is a local flux-coordinate tangent, not a cylindrical-basis direction. The real poloidal vacuum perturbation amplitude is defined by projecting the complex vacuum perturbation onto the poloidal unit tangent and taking the real part: $$ \delta B_{\theta,\mathrm{real}}^{\mathrm{vac}}(\rho,\theta;n) = \operatorname{Re}\!\left[\delta\mathbf{B}^{\mathrm{vac}}(\rho,\theta;n) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}\right] $$ where $\delta B_{\theta,\mathrm{real}}^{\mathrm{vac}}$ is this real poloidal vacuum perturbation amplitude, $\delta\mathbf{B}^{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the complex first-order [perturbed vacuum magnetic field](name:perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field) amplitude, $n$ is the integer toroidal mode number, and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}$ is the poloidal unit tangent defined above. The vacuum qualifier restricts the quantity to the current-free region exterior to the plasma, where the first-order perturbation satisfies $\nabla\times\delta\mathbf{B}^{\mathrm{vac}}=0$ and $\nabla\cdot\delta\mathbf{B}^{\mathrm{vac}}=0$. For a single toroidal mode, the complex poloidal amplitude is reconstructed as $\delta B_{\theta}^{\mathrm{vac}}=\delta B_{\theta,\mathrm{real}}^{\mathrm{vac}}+i\,\delta B_{\theta,\mathrm{imag}}^{\mathrm{vac}}$ and enters the toroidal dependence through the factor $\exp(i n\phi)$; this quantity is the real part of that mode amplitude, not a poloidal Fourier coefficient. It is distinct from the [imaginary-part counterpart](name:poloidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part), the [radial](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part) and [toroidal](name:toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part) vacuum projections, and the corresponding [plasma-region component](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_real_part). Sign convention: Positive when the in-phase magnetic-field perturbation component points along $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}$, the unit tangent toward increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ at fixed $\rho$ and $\phi$ in the specified flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

rows.name: radial_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_imaginary_part
rows.description: Imaginary part of the radial flux-coordinate component of the complex first-order perturbed magnetic-field eigenfunction in the confined plasma, for a single toroidal Fourier mode in linear MHD stability analysis. It is not the cylindrical major-radius component.
rows.documentation: Imaginary part of the radial perturbed plasma magnetic field is the imaginary component of the complex first-order magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction in the confined plasma. It applies to one toroidal Fourier mode in linear MHD stability analysis and to the radial coordinate component in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$. The complex radial component is decomposed into real and imaginary parts as: $$ \delta B_{\rho}^{(n)}(\rho,\theta) = \delta B_{\rho,\mathrm{re}}^{(n)}(\rho,\theta) + i\,\delta B_{\rho,\mathrm{im}}^{(n)}(\rho,\theta) $$ where $\delta B_{\rho}^{(n)}$ is the radial flux-coordinate component of the complex perturbed magnetic-field eigenfunction for toroidal mode number $n$, $\delta B_{\rho,\mathrm{re}}^{(n)}$ is the corresponding [real part](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_real_part), $\delta B_{\rho,\mathrm{im}}^{(n)}$ is this quantity, $i$ is the imaginary unit, $\rho$ is the radial flux coordinate, and $\theta$ is the poloidal flux coordinate. The scope is the confined-plasma region for the specified toroidal mode; it excludes the perturbed magnetic field in the vacuum region, any sum over toroidal mode numbers, and any real-valued instantaneous perturbation obtained after applying a toroidal and temporal phase factor. The radial direction here is the coordinate direction associated with increasing $\rho$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$; it is distinct from the major-radius $\hat{R}$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. The quantity is a local eigenfunction component, not a flux-surface average, volume integral, or magnitude. Together with the [real part](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_real_part), this quantity forms the complex radial component $\delta B_{\rho}^{(n)}$. Together with the [poloidal](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_imaginary_part) and [toroidal](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_imaginary_part) imaginary components, it forms the imaginary vector part of the perturbed plasma magnetic-field eigenfunction. The overall complex phase of a linear eigenfunction is arbitrary, so a phase rotation mixes the real and imaginary parts while leaving the represented complex eigenfunction unchanged. Sign convention: Positive when the imaginary radial component points toward increasing radial flux coordinate $\rho$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ for the adopted complex eigenfunction phase.

rows.name: radial_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_vector_potential
rows.description: Radial component of the first-order perturbed plasma magnetic vector-potential eigenfunction for a linear MHD mode, retaining its signed projection toward increasing major radius.
rows.documentation: Radial component of the first-order perturbed plasma magnetic vector-potential eigenfunction associated with a linear MHD mode. The radial component is defined by $$ \delta A_R = \delta\mathbf{A} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{R}} $$ where $\delta A_R$ is the radial component, $\delta\mathbf{A}$ is the perturbed plasma magnetic vector potential, and $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ is the unit vector toward increasing major radius in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. This quantity represents one signed component of the plasma perturbation about a reference state; it is not the complete vector, a magnitude, a sum, or an average. The complete vector quantity is the [perturbed plasma magnetic vector potential](name:perturbed_plasma_magnetic_vector_potential), while the [poloidal perturbed plasma magnetic vector potential](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_vector_potential) provides an adjacent directional component. It includes the full radial eigenfunction rather than selecting only its real or imaginary quadrature; the latter is represented by the [radial perturbed plasma magnetic vector potential imaginary part](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_vector_potential_imaginary_part). The associated perturbed magnetic field $\delta\mathbf{B}$ is obtained from the curl relation $\delta\mathbf{B}=\nabla\times\delta\mathbf{A}$, where $\delta\mathbf{B}$ is the perturbed magnetic field and $\nabla\times$ is the spatial curl operator. The vector potential is gage-dependent, whereas its curl determines the corresponding magnetic-field perturbation. Sign convention: Positive when $\delta A_R$ points toward increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

rows.name: radial_perturbed_plasma_velocity
rows.description: Radial component of the complex first-order plasma velocity perturbation eigenfunction for a specified toroidal Fourier mode in linear MHD stability analysis, abstracting over its real and imaginary scalar parts.
rows.documentation: The radial perturbed plasma velocity is the radial projection of the full complex eigenfunction of [perturbed_plasma_velocity](name:perturbed_plasma_velocity), characterizing the component of first-order oscillatory plasma flow directed along the major-radius coordinate $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. This component is central to stability analyzes of interchange, ballooning, and peeling modes, where cross-field plasma displacement drives the instability. The physical time-domain radial perturbation is recovered as: $$ \delta v_r(\mathbf{r}, t) = \mathrm{Re}\!\left[\delta\hat{v}_r(\mathbf{r})\, e^{-i\omega t}\right] $$ where $\omega$ is the complex mode eigenfrequency and $\delta\hat{v}_r(\mathbf{r})$ is the complex scalar radial eigenfunction amplitude. As a complex phasor, it decomposes into the [real part](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_velocity_real_part) $\mathrm{Re}(\delta\hat{v}_r)$, the in-phase fluid-velocity amplitude, and the [imaginary part](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_velocity_imaginary_part) $\mathrm{Im}(\delta\hat{v}_r)$, the quadrature component relative to the chosen eigenmode phase normalization. The radial plasma displacement eigenfunction is related by $\xi_r = \delta\hat{v}_r / (-i\omega)$, linking fluid velocity to flux-surface deformation. This eigenfunction component is evaluated by linear MHD eigenvalue solvers as part of the full toroidal Fourier harmonic decomposition of the perturbed velocity field. It contributes to the per_toroidal_mode_perturbed_energy alongside poloidal and toroidal velocity components, and couples to eigenfunction components such as [perturbed_plasma_pressure_real_part](name:perturbed_plasma_pressure_real_part) through the linearized momentum equation. Sign convention: Positive when the radial fluid motion is directed in the direction of increasing major radius $R$.

rows.name: radial_perturbed_plasma_velocity_real_part
rows.description: In-phase radial fluid-velocity component obtained from the real part of a complex linear-MHD perturbation eigenfunction for a specified toroidal Fourier mode.
rows.documentation: This quantity is the signed, in-phase radial component of the complex first-order plasma-velocity eigenfunction. It is the real-part component of [radial perturbed plasma velocity](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_velocity), not the velocity magnitude or its imaginary quadrature component. $$ v_{r,\mathrm{Re}}(R,Z;n)=\operatorname{Re}\!\left[\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_1(R,Z;n)\cdot\hat{\mathbf{R}}\right] $$ Here $\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_1$ is the complex perturbed plasma-velocity eigenfunction, $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ is the radial unit vector, $R$ is major radius, $Z$ is vertical height, and $n$ is the toroidal Fourier mode number, all expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. The real part depends on the selected eigenmode phase and normalization. Sign convention: Positive when the radial perturbation velocity points toward increasing major radius $R$.

rows.name: toroidal_halo_current
rows.description: Toroidal component of the electric current carried by halo plasma on open magnetic field lines between the last closed flux surface and first wall during a disruption.
rows.documentation: Toroidal halo current is the toroidal component of the electric-current vector carried by halo plasma on open magnetic field lines between the last closed flux surface and the first wall during a disruption. It is the toroidal member of the vector quantity [halo current](name:halo_current). The component is defined by $$ I_{\phi} = \mathbf{I}_{\mathrm{halo}} \cdot \hat{\phi} $$ where $\mathbf{I}_{\mathrm{halo}}$ is the integrated halo-current vector and $\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal unit vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Unlike [poloidal halo current](name:poloidal_halo_current), this component measures current along the direction of increasing toroidal angle and excludes the poloidal component. Sign convention: Positive when the halo current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

rows.name: toroidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_imaginary_part
rows.description: Imaginary part of the complex amplitude of the mode-n toroidal plasma-velocity perturbation in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame. It is the φ component of a single toroidal Fourier harmonic and is not the equilibrium toroidal flow.
rows.documentation: The imaginary part of the complex amplitude of the mode-$n$ toroidal plasma-velocity perturbation is the coefficient of $i$ in the toroidal component of the first-order plasma velocity perturbation for a single toroidal Fourier harmonic. The toroidal component is the projection onto $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is a perturbation eigenfunction component, not the equilibrium toroidal flow. For a harmonic with phase dependence proportional to $e^{i(n\phi-\omega t)}$, the full complex toroidal component combines this quantity with the matched real part [toroidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_real_part](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_real_part): $$ \delta \hat{v}_{\phi,n}(R,Z) = \delta \hat{\mathbf{v}}_n(R,Z)\cdot\hat{\phi} = \operatorname{Re}\!\left[\delta \hat{v}_{\phi,n}(R,Z)\right] + i\,\operatorname{Im}\!\left[\delta \hat{v}_{\phi,n}(R,Z)\right] $$ where $\delta \hat{\mathbf{v}}_n$ is the complex first-order velocity amplitude for toroidal mode number $n$, $\delta \hat{v}_{\phi,n}$ is its toroidal projection, $\omega$ is the mode angular frequency in the phase factor, and $i$ is the imaginary unit. This quantity is defined for one specified toroidal mode number $n$; contributions from other toroidal harmonics are excluded. A global phase rotation of the eigenfunction changes the split between real and imaginary parts, so this component must be interpreted with the matched real part and the chosen eigenfunction phase reference. Sign convention: Positive when the imaginary coefficient of the toroidal velocity perturbation is directed along $\hat{\phi}$, the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

rows.name: volume_averaged_runaway_electron_kinetic_energy_density
rows.description: Mean relativistic kinetic energy per unit volume of the runaway electron population, obtained by averaging the local kinetic energy density over the confined plasma volume.
rows.documentation: The volume-averaged runaway electron kinetic energy density is a global scalar characterizing the mean suprathermal energy stored per unit volume in the runaway electron (RE) population. It is obtained by integrating the local relativistic kinetic energy density over the total confined plasma volume $V$ and dividing by $V$. The underlying local quantity is the relativistic kinetic energy moment of the RE distribution function: $$ u_\mathrm{RE}(\mathbf{r}) = \int f_\mathrm{RE}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{p})\,(\gamma - 1)\,m_e c^2 \, d^3p $$ where $f_\mathrm{RE}$ is the runaway electron phase-space distribution function, $\gamma = (1 + p^2 / m_e^2 c^2)^{1/2}$ is the Lorentz factor, $m_e$ is the electron rest mass, $c$ is the speed of light, and $\mathbf{p}$ is the relativistic momentum. The volume average is then $\langle u_\mathrm{RE} \rangle = V^{-1} \int_V u_\mathrm{RE}\,dV$. This quantity is evaluated from kinetic or reduced-fluid runaway electron models, particularly in disruption current-quench simulations where RE populations can reach energies of several to tens of MeV per particle. Multiplying by the plasma volume $V$ recovers the total stored relativistic energy given by [runaway_electron_kinetic_energy](name:runaway_electron_kinetic_energy). The local non-averaged counterpart is runaway_electron_kinetic_energy_density, and the corresponding global particle number density is [volume_averaged_runaway_electron_density](name:volume_averaged_runaway_electron_density).

rows.name: coolant_absorbed_power_of_calorimetry_component
rows.description: Thermal power removed from a calorimetry component by its coolant, determined from the coolant enthalpy increase between inlet and outlet.
rows.documentation: This quantity is the instantaneous thermal power transferred from one calorimetry component into its coolant. It is specific to the named component and represents coolant-mediated heat extraction rather than a group-wide or plant-wide power total. The enthalpy-balance definition is $$ P_{\mathrm{cool,abs}} = \dot{m}_{c}\left(h_{\mathrm{out}} - h_{\mathrm{in}}\right) $$ where $P_{\mathrm{cool,abs}}$ is the coolant-absorbed thermal power, $\dot{m}_{c}$ is the coolant mass flow rate, and $h_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $h_{\mathrm{out}}$ are the coolant specific enthalpies at the component inlet and outlet states. The enthalpy difference is evaluated from the corresponding coolant thermodynamic states, including the inlet and outlet temperatures. The quantity excludes heat transferred by channels other than the coolant and does not denote accumulated energy. Its time integral from pulse start is the [accumulated coolant-absorbed energy of the calorimetry component](name:accumulated_coolant_absorbed_energy_of_calorimetry_component), while this quantity remains the instantaneous component-level extraction rate. The coolant inlet state is related to the [coolant temperature at inlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_inlet).

rows.name: displacement_of_passive_structure
rows.description: Displacement of a passive structure is the signed linear displacement of a selected point or defined surface target on a passive component relative to a reference configuration, projected along a defined positive direction.
rows.documentation: Displacement of a passive structure is the signed scalar component of the motion of a selected material point, attachment point, or defined reference point on a passive structural component relative to a reference configuration. It is the passive-structure instance of mechanical displacement, not an absolute position, velocity, acceleration, or strain. The signed projected displacement is defined by $$ u(t) = \left[\mathbf{r}(t) - \mathbf{r}_\mathrm{ref}\right] \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_u $$ where $u(t)$ is the scalar displacement, $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is the current position vector of the selected point, $\mathbf{r}_\mathrm{ref}$ is the position vector of the same point in the reference configuration, and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_u$ is the unit vector defining the positive direction of the displacement component. All vectors and the unit direction are expressed in the same right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame, with $\hat{z}$ vertical. The selected point, reference configuration, and positive direction are part of the semantic definition of any instance. An undeformed, surveyed, calibrated, initial, or previous-time configuration may serve as $\mathbf{r}_\mathrm{ref}$ only if that choice is fixed; changing it changes the displacement, and using a previous-time reference defines an incremental displacement over the interval. A single value describes one projected local displacement; deformation or strain requires spatial variation of displacement or a separate deformation measure. Sign convention: Positive when the selected point is displaced from $\mathbf{r}_\mathrm{ref}$ in the direction of $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_u$.

rows.name: temperature_of_sensor
rows.description: Thermodynamic temperature associated with a selected thermocouple sensor attached to a tokamak structural component.
rows.documentation: This quantity is the absolute thermodynamic temperature associated with one selected sensor member, represented by the thermal state at its thermocouple junction. It characterizes the local thermal condition of the attached structural component at the sensor location. For a system in thermodynamic equilibrium, temperature is defined by $$ T = \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial S}\right)_{V,N} $$ where $T$ is thermodynamic temperature, $U$ is internal energy, $S$ is entropy, $V$ is volume, and $N$ is the amount of material or particle number held fixed in the derivative. The quantity applies to the selected sensor member individually and is not a sum, average, or other aggregation over the sensor set. It denotes the sensor or junction thermal state associated with a structural component, not the temperature of a flowing coolant or of an entire plant connection. It is distinct from [coolant temperature at inlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_inlet), which describes fluid entering a cooling system. Object-specific quantities such as [temperature of a coil conductor](name:temperature_of_coil_conductor) and [temperature of a neutron detector](name:temperature_of_neutron_detector) apply the same thermodynamic concept to explicitly named hardware rather than to the generic sensor locus.

rows.name: toroidal_coordinate_of_reciprocating_probe
rows.description: Toroidal angular coordinate of the reciprocating probe’s average measurement position during a plunge, referenced to the facility’s toroidal-angle origin.
rows.documentation: The toroidal coordinate $\bar{\phi}_{\rm probe}$ identifies the azimuthal location of the reciprocating probe’s average position formed from its measurement locations. It is an angular coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \\phi, Z)$ frame. For an averaged position represented in the right-handed Cartesian $(x,y,z)$ basis, with $z$ aligned with $Z$, the coordinate is defined by $$ \\bar{\\phi}_{\\rm probe} = \\operatorname{atan2}(\\bar{y}_{\\rm probe}, \\bar{x}_{\\rm probe}) $$ where $\\bar{x}_{\\rm probe}$ and $\\bar{y}_{\\rm probe}$ are the Cartesian coordinates of the averaged position. This identifies the probe location analogously to the toroidal coordinate at a [beam tracing point](name:toroidal_coordinate_at_beam_tracing_point), but the locus here is the reciprocating probe’s average position. Sign convention: Positive when $\\bar{\\phi}_{\\rm probe}$ increases in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\\phi$.

rows.name: x_first_measurement_direction_unit_vector_of_strain_gauge
rows.description: Signed direction cosine of a sensor’s unit measurement-direction vector along the x axis of the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame.
rows.documentation: This quantity is the x-directed component of a sensor’s oriented measurement-direction vector. It describes orientation rather than the sensor’s spatial attachment location, which is specified separately by the [x coordinate of the sensor attachment point](name:x_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point). The direction cosine is defined by $$ d_x = \hat{\mathbf d} \cdot \hat{\mathbf x} $$ where $\hat{\mathbf d}$ is the sensor’s unit measurement-direction vector and $\hat{\mathbf x}$ is the unit vector along the x axis of the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame. For a normalized direction vector, $-1 \leq d_x \leq 1$; the corresponding y- and z-axis components are represented by the [y direction unit vector of the sensor](name:y_first_measurement_direction_unit_vector_of_strain_gauge) and [z direction unit vector of the sensor](name:z_first_measurement_direction_unit_vector_of_strain_gauge). Sign convention: Positive when the sensor’s measurement direction has a component toward increasing x.

rows.name: x_second_measurement_direction_unit_vector_of_strain_gauge
rows.description: Signed direction cosine of a strain gage’s second measurement direction along the x axis of the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame.
rows.documentation: The quantity is the x projection of the unit vector defining a strain gage’s second measurement direction. It describes orientation, not the gage’s spatial location or its first measurement direction. The direction cosine is defined by: $$ d_{2x} = \hat{\mathbf d}_2 \cdot \hat{\mathbf x} $$ where $\hat{\mathbf d}_2$ is the unit vector along the second measurement direction and $\hat{\mathbf x}$ is the x-axis unit vector in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame. Together with the y direction cosine of the second measurement direction and z direction cosine of the second measurement direction, it specifies that direction. It is distinct from the [x coordinate of the sensor attachment point](name:x_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point), which locates the gage rather than defining its orientation. Sign convention: Positive when the second measurement direction has a component along increasing x in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame.

rows.name: y_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point
rows.description: Signed Cartesian y coordinate of the point where a sensor is mechanically attached to a device component, in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) machine frame with z vertical.
rows.documentation: Signed Cartesian $y$ coordinate of the point where a sensor is mechanically attached to a device component is the $\hat{y}$ component of the attachment-point position. The coordinate is defined in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis, with $\hat{z}$ vertical and $(\hat{x}, \hat{y})$ spanning the horizontal plane. The coordinate is the projection of the attachment-point position vector onto the $\hat{y}$ basis direction: $$ y_\mathrm{attach} = \mathbf{r}_\mathrm{attach} \cdot \hat{y} $$ where $y_\mathrm{attach}$ is this signed coordinate, $\mathbf{r}_\mathrm{attach}$ is the position vector of the sensor attachment point relative to the Cartesian frame origin, and $\hat{y}$ is the positive $y$-direction unit basis vector. This quantity applies to the mechanical point where the sensor is attached to a device component. It is not the sensor sensing point, line-of-sight point, active volume position, sensor centroid, or a separate component reference point; no averaging or aggregation over multiple attachment points is implied. Together with [x_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point](name:x_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point) and [z_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point](name:z_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point), it specifies the Cartesian position of the same attachment point. This quantity is only the $y$ component and does not include the $x$ or $z$ components. Sign convention: Positive when the attachment point is displaced in the $+\hat{y}$ direction of the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis from the frame origin.

rows.name: y_second_measurement_direction_unit_vector_of_strain_gauge
rows.description: Signed y-axis direction cosine of the unit vector along a strain gage’s second measurement direction in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame.
rows.documentation: This quantity is the y-axis direction cosine of the unit vector defining a strain gage’s second measurement direction. For a strain rosette, it describes the orientation of that local sensing axis, not the gage’s spatial location. The component is defined by $$ d_y = \hat{\mathbf{d}}_2 \cdot \hat{\mathbf{y}} $$ where $\hat{\mathbf{d}}_2$ is the unit vector along the second measurement direction and $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is the positive y-axis unit vector of the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame. Its value is one component of the orientation represented by the corresponding x-axis second measurement direction and z-axis second measurement direction. It is distinct from the [y coordinate of the sensor attachment point](name:y_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point), which locates the gage rather than specifying its orientation. Sign convention: Positive when the second measurement direction has a component toward increasing y.

rows.name: z_first_measurement_direction_unit_vector_of_strain_gauge
rows.description: Signed z-axis component of the unit vector along a strain gage's first measurement direction in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame, with z vertical.
rows.documentation: Signed z-axis component of the unit vector along a strain gage's first measurement direction is the scalar direction cosine of that strain-sensitive direction with the vertical basis direction of the right-handed Cartesian frame with basis $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$. It represents the vertical part of the orientation of the gage's first defined measurement direction. The component is defined by the scalar projection of the first measurement-direction unit vector: $$ u_z^{(1)} = \mathbf{u}^{(1)} \cdot \hat{z} $$ where $\mathbf{u}^{(1)}$ is the unit vector along the strain gage's first measurement direction, $\hat{z}$ is the vertical basis vector of the right-handed Cartesian frame with basis $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$, and $u_z^{(1)}$ is the signed z-axis component of that unit vector. The scope is one strain gage and its first defined measurement direction; no averaging, summation, or aggregation over gages or measurement directions is implied. This quantity is a direction component, not a position coordinate, displacement, or strain value, and it is distinct from the corresponding component of the second measurement direction. Together with the x-axis component $u_x^{(1)}$ and y-axis component $u_y^{(1)}$, it specifies the orientation of the first measurement direction; because $\mathbf{u}^{(1)}$ is a unit vector, $(u_x^{(1)})^2 + (u_y^{(1)})^2 + (u_z^{(1)})^2 = 1$. Sign convention: Positive when the first measurement-direction unit vector has a component in the $+\hat{z}$ direction of the right-handed Cartesian frame with basis $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$.

rows.name: z_second_measurement_direction_unit_vector_of_strain_gauge
rows.description: Signed z-axis direction cosine of a strain gage’s second measurement-direction unit vector in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame.
rows.documentation: The second measurement-direction unit vector of a strain gage specifies the orientation of its second sensing axis. Its z-axis direction cosine is the signed projection of that orientation onto the Cartesian z axis. $$ d_{2z} = \hat{\mathbf{d}}_2 \cdot \hat{\mathbf{z}} $$ where $d_{2z}$ is the z-axis direction cosine, $\hat{\mathbf{d}}_2$ is the unit vector along the second measurement direction, and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ is the unit vector of the z axis in the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame. For a unit direction vector, $-1 \leq d_{2z} \leq 1$. The second-direction component complements the z-axis direction cosine of the first measurement direction and is distinct from the [z coordinate of the sensor attachment point](name:z_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point), which specifies location rather than orientation. Sign convention: Positive when the second measurement direction has a component toward increasing $z$.

rows.name: back_surface_neutron_flux
rows.description: Back-surface neutron flux is the scalar energy flux carried by fusion neutrons escaping through the back surface of an applicable component or module. It is aggregated over neutron energies, fusion reaction channels, and reacting populations; it is not a maximum over the surface.
rows.documentation: Back-surface neutron flux is the scalar surface density of power carried by fusion neutrons crossing outward through the back surface of the applicable component or module. It characterizes the local neutron energy load at that rear surface, not a vector flux and not a surface aggregate. The local scalar flux $q_n$ at a point $\boldsymbol{r}$ on the back surface is defined by $$ q_n(\boldsymbol{r}) = \frac{dP_{n,\mathrm{out}}}{dA}(\boldsymbol{r}) $$ where $q_n$ is the back-surface neutron flux, $\boldsymbol{r}$ is a point on the back surface, $P_{n,\mathrm{out}}$ is the power carried by fusion neutrons crossing outward through that surface, and $A$ is area on the back surface. The scope is the back surface only: the surface opposite the front or plasma-facing side of the object under consideration. The quantity is aggregated over neutron energies, fusion reaction channels, and reacting populations unless a more specific standard name states a narrower selection. This quantity excludes neutron source strength in a volume, total neutron power integrated over an area, flux at other surfaces, and any extremum selected over the back surface. A surface aggregate such as [maximum back-surface neutron flux](name:maximum_of_back_surface_neutron_flux) is obtained by taking the maximum value of this quantity over the applicable back surface; the maximum operation is not part of `back_surface_neutron_flux` itself. The area integral of $q_n$ over a chosen part of the back surface gives the neutron power crossing outward through that part, while the local value remains the surface-density quantity defined at each point.

rows.name: first_local_tangential_width_of_neutron_detector
rows.description: Full transverse extent of the rectangular collimating aperture associated with a neutron detector, measured between its edges along the aperture’s first local tangential direction.
rows.documentation: This quantity is the full transverse width of the neutron detector’s collimating aperture along its first local tangential direction. It describes the aperture opening rather than the external detector body, housing, or shielding. The width is defined by $$ w_1 = x_{1,\max} - x_{1,\min} $$ where $w_1$ is the first local tangential aperture width, and $x_{1,\max}$ and $x_{1,\min}$ are the positions of the two aperture edges along the first local tangential axis. This quantity applies only to a rectangular aperture and represents the complete edge-to-edge opening dimension, not a radius or half-width. The other transverse dimension is represented by the second local tangential width of the neutron detector, whereas a circular opening is characterized by the [radius of the neutron detector](name:radius_of_neutron_detector) rather than by rectangular widths.

rows.name: maximum_of_back_surface_neutron_flux
rows.description: Maximum neutron energy flux escaping through the rear surface of a breeding blanket module toward vessel structures.
rows.documentation: This quantity is the greatest local neutron energy flux crossing outward through the rear surface of one breeding blanket module. It measures the escaping neutron load relevant to attenuation toward vessel structures. The maximum is defined from the local back-surface neutron energy flux as $$ q_{n,\max} = \max_{\mathbf{x}\in S_{\mathrm{back}}} q_n(\mathbf{x}) $$ where $q_n(\mathbf{x})$ is the local neutron energy flux at surface position $\mathbf{x}$, and $S_{\mathrm{back}}$ is the rear surface of the module. The quantity applies to fusion neutrons from all included neutron energies, fusion reaction channels, and reacting populations, aggregated into a single local energy-flux value before taking the maximum over the rear surface of one module. It represents neutrons escaping outward from the module and excludes a surface-integrated module power and neutron flux incident on the module's front surface. It is the maximum-over-surface transformation of [back-surface neutron flux](name:back_surface_neutron_flux), which describes the local value without selecting its maximum. It is distinct from [incident neutron power of a breeder blanket module](name:incident_neutron_power_of_breeder_blanket_module), which is the total neutron power arriving at the module, and from [nuclear heating power of a breeder blanket module](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_module), which describes energy deposited by neutron interactions within the module.

rows.name: neutron_flux_at_first_wall
rows.description: Neutron-carried energy flux arriving at the plasma-facing first-wall surface, providing the carrier-specific local contribution to energy delivered from the plasma to first-wall material.
rows.documentation: Neutron energy flux at the plasma-facing first-wall surface is the local rate of neutron-carried energy delivered per unit surface area. It is the neutron-specific contribution to the energy flux associated with plasma loading of the first wall. $$ q_n(\mathbf{x}) = \int_0^\infty E\,\Phi_n(E,\mathbf{x})\,dE $$ where $q_n(\mathbf{x})$ is the local neutron energy flux, $\mathbf{x}$ is a position on the first-wall surface, $E$ is neutron energy, and $\Phi_n(E,\mathbf{x})$ is the differential neutron number flux at that position and energy. This quantity is local on the first-wall surface, integrates over neutron energy, and includes only the neutron carrier. It is not integrated over the surface and does not include photon, charged-particle, or other plasma-wall energy carriers. It describes energy arriving at the surface rather than nuclear energy deposited throughout the wall volume, which is represented by [nuclear power density of breeder blanket layer](name:nuclear_power_density_of_breeder_blanket_layer). The quantity contributes to the total local energy flux represented by [flux_at_first_wall](name:flux_at_first_wall). The representative [neutron_flux_maximum_at_first_wall](name:neutron_flux_maximum_at_first_wall) is obtained by taking the maximum of $q_n(\mathbf{x})$ over the relevant first-wall surface, while this parent quantity remains the local carrier-specific flux.

rows.name: neutron_flux_maximum_at_first_wall
rows.description: Maximum neutron flux at the first wall of a breeding-blanket module is the largest local neutron energy flux on that module first-wall surface, identifying the highest local neutron loading relevant to material damage and blanket lifetime.
rows.documentation: Maximum neutron flux at the first wall of a breeding-blanket module is the largest local neutron energy flux on the module first-wall surface. It represents the peak neutron loading of that surface. The quantity is defined by the surface maximum of the local neutron energy-flux field: $$ q_{n,\mathrm{FW}}^{\max} = \max_{\mathbf{x}\in S_{\mathrm{FW}}^{\mathrm{module}}} q_n(\mathbf{x}) $$ where $q_{n,\mathrm{FW}}^{\max}$ is the maximum neutron flux at the first wall of a breeding-blanket module, $q_n(\mathbf{x})$ is the local neutron energy flux at surface position $\mathbf{x}$, and $S_{\mathrm{FW}}^{\mathrm{module}}$ is the first-wall surface of that breeding-blanket module. The scope is a single breeding-blanket module and only its first-wall surface. The aggregation convention is a spatial maximum over that surface; it is not an area average, a surface integral, or a module total. It excludes neutron flux on the module back surface and on other module surfaces, and it excludes contributions from non-neutron energy carriers. The same local neutron energy-flux field can be evaluated on other surfaces; [maximum of back-surface neutron flux](name:maximum_of_back_surface_neutron_flux) is the corresponding surface maximum on the module back surface. The related [energy-flux maximum at the first wall](name:energy_flux_maximum_at_first_wall) is the maximum of the total local energy-flux field; this neutron maximum is not generally the neutron contribution evaluated at the location of the total maximum, because the positions of the neutron-field maximum and total-field maximum can differ.

rows.name: neutron_response_function_of_neutron_detector
rows.description: Green-function coefficient giving expected neutron-detector counts from one neutron emitted in a specified plasma voxel and energy bin.
rows.documentation: The neutron-detector response function is the expected registered count contribution from a neutron emitted in a specified plasma voxel and neutron-energy bin. It characterizes the detector-specific mapping from neutron emission to detected events. The response enters the forward relation $$ N_d = \sum_v \sum_k G_d(v,E_k)\,S(v,E_k) $$ where $N_d$ is the total expected count for detector $d$, $G_d(v,E_k)$ is this response function, $v$ labels a plasma voxel, $E_k$ labels the $k$th neutron-energy bin, and $S(v,E_k)$ is the neutron yield from voxel $v$ in that bin. The quantity applies to one neutron detector and to the contribution of a specified source voxel and energy bin; its count response is aggregated over the detector events attributable to that source contribution. It is not the neutron emissivity, the geometric acceptance alone, or an energy-dependent efficiency alone. The geometric distinction is given by [solid angle of a neutron detector](name:solid_angle_of_neutron_detector), while [spectral efficiency of a hard X-ray detector](name:spectral_efficiency_of_hard_xray_detector) illustrates an efficiency quantity that does not represent this neutron-specific source-to-count response.

rows.name: total_neutron_rate
rows.description: Total neutron emission rate produced by deuterium–tritium, deuterium–deuterium, and tritium–tritium fusion reactions in the plasma.
rows.documentation: This quantity is the aggregate number of neutrons emitted per unit time by fusion reactions in the plasma. The total rate is the sum of the neutron-emission rates from the included fusion channels: $$ S_n = R_{n,\mathrm{DT}} + R_{n,\mathrm{DD}} + R_{n,\mathrm{TT}} $$ where $S_n$ is the total neutron emission rate, and $R_{n,\mathrm{DT}}$, $R_{n,\mathrm{DD}}$, and $R_{n,\mathrm{TT}}$ are the neutron-emission rates from deuterium–tritium, deuterium–deuterium, and tritium–tritium fusion reactions, respectively. The quantity includes all three stated fusion reaction channels and their combined neutron production; it is not restricted to a single reaction channel, neutron energy group, or local spatial region. It represents an aggregate emission rate rather than a neutron flux per unit area. The [deuterium–tritium neutron flux](name:deuterium_tritium_flux) describes the deuterium–tritium channel contribution, which is included in this total together with the deuterium–deuterium and tritium–tritium contributions.

rows.name: difference_of_neutral_beam_doppler_wavelength_and_reference_wavelength_of_spectral_line
rows.description: Signed displacement of a neutral-beam spectral-line wavelength from its reference value, produced by bulk neutral-beam motion along the viewing line of sight.
rows.documentation: This quantity is the signed difference between the Doppler-displaced wavelength of a neutral-beam spectral line and its unshifted reference wavelength of the spectral line. It represents the bulk neutral-beam velocity projected along the viewing line of sight. The displacement is defined by $$ \Delta\lambda_{\mathrm{D}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{D}} - \lambda_{\mathrm{ref}} \simeq \lambda_{\mathrm{ref}}\frac{v_{\mathrm{los}}}{c} $$ where $\lambda_{\mathrm{D}}$ is the Doppler-displaced wavelength, $\lambda_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the reference wavelength, $v_{\mathrm{los}}$ is the signed bulk velocity component along the line of sight, and $c$ is the speed of light. The approximation applies when the projected velocity is small compared with $c$. The quantity excludes the distinct wavelength displacement produced by the Lorentz shift from the motional Stark electric field; that effect is represented by [difference of fast neutral beam motional Stark wavelength and fast neutral beam reference wavelength of spectral line](name:difference_of_fast_neutral_beam_motional_stark_wavelength_and_fast_neutral_beam_reference_wavelength_of_spectral_line). Sign convention: Positive when the Doppler-displaced wavelength exceeds the reference wavelength, corresponding to a redshift.

rows.name: floating_electrostatic_potential
rows.description: Electrostatic potential of an electrically floating Langmuir-probe collector relative to a chosen electrical reference, at which the net electric current to the collector vanishes.
rows.documentation: This quantity is the electrostatic potential of an electrically floating Langmuir-probe collector, relative to a chosen electrical reference. It is a current-balance-constrained value of [electrostatic potential](name:electrostatic_potential), specifying electrostatic interaction energy per positive test charge at the collector. The defining floating condition is $$ I_{\mathrm{net}}(V_{\mathrm{f}})=0 $$ where $V_{\mathrm{f}}$ is the collector's floating electrostatic potential relative to the chosen reference and $I_{\mathrm{net}}$ is the total electric current entering the collector, including particle collection and any emission contributions. Zero net current does not require the individual electron, ion, or emitted-particle currents to vanish. This quantity applies to an individual plasma-exposed collector, whether fixed or moving. It is not a wall-surface or magnetic-flux-surface average, and it does not denote an externally imposed collector bias. It is distinct from the [plasma electrostatic potential at a Langmuir-probe position](name:electrostatic_potential_at_langmuir_probe_position): a sheath can sustain a potential difference between the plasma and the floating collector. That difference is governed by current balance and depends on the electron temperature, particle distributions, and any emission contributions; no universal fixed offset is implied. The [fluctuating floating electrostatic potential](name:fluctuating_floating_electrostatic_potential) is the standard deviation of fluctuations of this quantity, rather than its signed value. Sign convention: Positive when a positive test charge has greater electrostatic potential energy at the floating collector than at the chosen reference.

rows.name: line_averaged_argon_density
rows.description: Chord-averaged number density of argon ions along a specified plasma path, with contributions from all ionization stages summed together.
rows.documentation: Line-averaged argon ion number density is the argon ion concentration averaged along a specified chord through the plasma, including all ionization stages. The line average is defined by $$ \overline{n}_\mathrm{Ar} = \frac{1}{L} \int_0^L \sum_{q=1}^{18} n_{\mathrm{Ar},q}(\mathbf{r}(l))\,dl $$ where $L$ is the chord length, $l$ is distance along the chord, $\mathbf{r}(l)$ is the position on the chord, and $n_{\mathrm{Ar},q}$ is the local number density of argon ions in charge state $q$. This path average is distinct from the local [argon ion density](name:argon_density) and from the plasma-volume average [volume-averaged argon density](name:volume_averaged_argon_density).

rows.name: line_averaged_boron_density
rows.description: Line-averaged boron density is the total elemental boron number density averaged along a chord through the plasma. It includes neutral boron and all boron ionization states, giving a chord-averaged measure of elemental boron impurity content.
rows.documentation: Line-averaged boron density is the total elemental boron number density averaged along a chord through the plasma. It includes neutral boron and all ionization states of boron, so it represents the chord-averaged elemental boron impurity content rather than a local point value. The line average over a chord of path length $L$ is defined by the path integral of the local charge-state-summed boron density along arc length $l$: $$ \bar{n}_{\mathrm{B},\ell} = \frac{1}{L}\int_0^L \sum_{z=0}^{5} n_\mathrm{B}^{(z)}(l)\, dl $$ where $\bar{n}_{\mathrm{B},\ell}$ is the line-averaged boron density, $n_\mathrm{B}^{(z)}(l)$ is the local boron number density in ionization state $z$ at position $l$ along the chord, $z=0$ denotes neutral boron, $z=5$ denotes fully stripped B$^{5+}$, and $L$ is the total path length used for the average. This quantity is a chord average of the charge-state-summed elemental [boron density](name:boron_density); it is not a charge-state-resolved boron density and does not exclude neutral boron. It differs from [volume-averaged boron density](name:volume_averaged_boron_density), which averages the same elemental density over the confined plasma volume.

rows.name: line_averaged_oxygen_density
rows.description: Line-averaged oxygen density is the line-of-sight mean of the local oxygen number density, summed over all charge states from neutral O0 through fully stripped O8+, along a specified chord through the plasma.
rows.documentation: The line-averaged oxygen density is the line-of-sight mean of the local oxygen number density—summed over all charge states from neutral O$^0$ through fully stripped O$^{8+}$—along a specified chord through the plasma. It represents the oxygen impurity concentration averaged by arclength rather than the value at a single point. For a chord of length $L$, the line-averaged oxygen density is defined by: $$ \bar{n}_\mathrm{O} = \frac{1}{L}\int_0^L n_\mathrm{O}(\ell)\,d\ell $$ where $\bar{n}_\mathrm{O}$ is the line-averaged oxygen density, $L$ is the physical length of the chord segment included in the average, $\ell$ is arclength along that chord, and $n_\mathrm{O}(\ell)$ is the [local oxygen density](name:oxygen_density) at the point labeled by $\ell$. The scope is the species-level oxygen impurity population intersected by the specified chord: the density is charge-state-summed over neutral oxygen and all oxygen ions, and the spatial aggregation is an arclength average along the chord. It excludes charge-state-resolved oxygen densities, the local point value [oxygen density](name:oxygen_density), and the spatial mean over the confined plasma volume. The essential relationship to [oxygen density](name:oxygen_density) is that the local charge-state-summed density is the integrand of the chord average. [Volume-averaged oxygen density](name:volume_averaged_oxygen_density) is the analogous mean formed over a plasma volume, whereas this quantity is formed only along the specified line of sight and is normalized by the chord length.

rows.name: line_averaged_total_ion_temperature
rows.description: Density-weighted effective temperature of the combined thermal ion population, with all species and charge states contributing by number density and averaged along a specified plasma chord.
rows.documentation: The line-averaged total ion temperature is the line average of the local density-weighted effective temperature of the combined thermal ion population, including all included thermal ion species and charge states. It represents random thermal motion and excludes directed bulk-flow energy. The chord average is defined by $$ T_{i,\mathrm{line}} = \frac{\int_{\mathcal{C}} T_{i,\mathrm{tot}}(\ell)\,d\ell}{\int_{\mathcal{C}}d\ell} $$ where $T_{i,\mathrm{line}}$ is the line-averaged quantity, $T_{i,\mathrm{tot}}(\ell)$ is the local [total ion temperature](name:total_ion_temperature), $\ell$ is path length along the chord, and $\mathcal{C}$ is the specified chord. Species and charge states are combined by number density before the line average is taken. Unlike the [volume-averaged total ion temperature](name:volume_averaged_total_ion_temperature), this quantity weights positions by chord length rather than plasma volume.

rows.name: line_averaged_tritium_density
rows.description: Chord-averaged number density of tritium ions, obtained by averaging local tritium ion density along a specified chord.
rows.documentation: Chord-averaged tritium ion density is the path-length mean of the local tritium ion number density along a specified chord. It is derived from the local [tritium_density](name:tritium_density) and represents the chord-integrated fuel content normalized by chord length. $$ \overline{n}_T = \frac{1}{L} \int_0^L n_T(\ell)\,d\ell $$ where $\overline{n}_T$ is the chord-averaged density, $n_T(\ell)$ is the local tritium ion density at path coordinate $\ell$, and $L$ is the chord length. The average includes the specified chord segment and is distinct from the confined-volume mean [volume_averaged_tritium_density](name:volume_averaged_tritium_density) and from the corresponding helium-4 quantity [line_averaged_helium_4_density](name:line_averaged_helium_4_density).

rows.name: neutral_pressure_of_mass_spectrometer_channel
rows.description: Neutral pressure of a mass-spectrometer channel is the calibrated neutral-gas pressure equivalent assigned to a selected mass-to-charge channel. It denotes a channel-resolved neutral contribution and does not require correspondence to a unique neutral species.
rows.documentation: Neutral pressure of a mass-spectrometer channel is the calibrated neutral-gas pressure equivalent assigned to one mass-discriminated channel of a mass spectrometer. The channel denotes a response in mass-to-charge space after ionization, so the quantity is a pressure equivalent for neutrals that can contribute to that channel, not a pressure of the detected ions. This quantity is neutral in scope: it excludes charged-particle plasma pressure, electron pressure, and any pressure contribution not represented as neutral gas before ionization. It is the neutral-specific counterpart of pressure of a mass-spectrometer channel. A channel value need not be the thermodynamic partial pressure of a single species, because fragmentation, isotopologues, charge states of produced ions, and isobaric species can overlap in the same mass-to-charge channel. Summing channel values represents [total neutral pressure](name:total_neutral_pressure) only when the calibrated channels are non-overlapping, span the neutral mixture being represented, and treat cross-sensitivities consistently.

rows.name: oxygen_density
rows.description: Total number density of oxygen atoms and ions across all charge states, from neutral to fully stripped, giving the local oxygen impurity concentration at a point in the plasma.
rows.documentation: The local oxygen number density $n_\mathrm{O}$ quantifies the total concentration of oxygen impurity per unit plasma volume, encompassing neutral atomic oxygen and all ionic charge states up to fully stripped O$^{8+}$. Oxygen is a ubiquitous low-Z impurity in fusion devices, entering through wall outgassing and vessel conditioning; it contributes to radiative power losses and dilutes the hydrogenic fuel inventory. The total oxygen density is defined as the sum over all ionization states: $$ n_\mathrm{O} = \sum_{Z=0}^{8} n_{\mathrm{O}^{Z+}} $$ where $n_{\mathrm{O}^{Z+}}$ is the number density of oxygen in charge state $Z^+$, with $Z$ ranging from 0 (neutral) to 8 (fully stripped). The local density is inferred from passive extreme-ultraviolet spectroscopy, charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, and soft X-ray emission tomography. Spatially averaged forms include [line_averaged_oxygen_density](name:line_averaged_oxygen_density) (chord integral divided by chord length) and [volume_averaged_oxygen_density](name:volume_averaged_oxygen_density) (integral over the plasma volume). The dimensionless oxygen_fraction relates this local density to the electron density as an impurity concentration measure. In well-conditioned fusion plasmas the core oxygen density is a small fraction of the electron density; edge concentrations of $10^{15}$–$10^{17}$ m$^{-3}$ are representative of limiter and divertor configurations.

rows.name: voltage_of_mass_spectrometer
rows.description: Mass-spectrometer detector bias voltage is the signed detector-bias potential difference between the detector electrode or electron-multiplying stage and its bias reference. It is a device-level setting; voltage_of_mass_spectrometer_channel denotes a channel-specific detector bias.
rows.documentation: Mass-spectrometer detector bias voltage is the signed detector-bias potential difference applied between the detector electrode or electron-multiplying stage and its bias reference. It is a device-level electrical setting that affects ion collection efficiency or electron-multiplier gain. The detector-bias potential difference is defined by the detector and reference electric potentials: $$ V_\mathrm{bias} = \Phi_\mathrm{det} - \Phi_\mathrm{ref} $$ where $V_\mathrm{bias}$ is the detector bias voltage of the mass spectrometer, $\Phi_\mathrm{det}$ is the electric potential of the detector electrode or electron-multiplying stage, and $\Phi_\mathrm{ref}$ is the electric potential of its bias reference. This quantity applies to the mass spectrometer as a device-level detector bias common to the instrument or defined independently of channel selection. It excludes channel-specific detector biases, which are represented by [mass-spectrometer channel detector bias voltage](name:voltage_of_mass_spectrometer_channel). This quantity is distinct from [mass-spectrometer channel ion current](name:ion_current_of_mass_spectrometer_channel): the ion current is the electrical current associated with collected ions in a channel, whereas the detector bias voltage is the applied potential difference that can affect collection efficiency or gain. Sign convention: Positive when the detector electrode or electron-multiplying stage is at higher electric potential than its bias reference.

rows.name: accumulated_ammonia_count
rows.description: Cumulative post-breakdown inventory of ammonia molecules introduced into the plasma vessel, expressed as an equivalent-electron count with ten count units assigned to each neutral NH3 molecule.
rows.documentation: The accumulated ammonia count is the cumulative post-breakdown amount of NH3 introduced into the plasma vessel, represented using an equivalent-electron accounting convention. It is the post-breakdown component of the total ammonia count, not a direct count of free plasma electrons. $$ C_{\mathrm{NH_3}}^{\mathrm{acc}} = (Z_\mathrm{N}+3Z_\mathrm{H})N_{\mathrm{NH_3}}^{\mathrm{acc}} = 10N_{\mathrm{NH_3}}^{\mathrm{acc}} $$ Here, $C_{\mathrm{NH_3}}^{\mathrm{acc}}$ is the accumulated equivalent-electron count, $N_{\mathrm{NH_3}}^{\mathrm{acc}}$ is the cumulative number of ammonia molecules introduced after plasma breakdown, and $Z_\mathrm{N}=7$ and $Z_\mathrm{H}=1$ are the atomic numbers of nitrogen and hydrogen. The quantity excludes ammonia introduced during prefill, which is represented by [ammonia prefill count](name:ammonia_prefill_count), and does not represent instantaneous injection rate, retained neutral inventory, ionization state, or actual free-electron content.

rows.name: accumulated_ammonia_deuterated_count
rows.description: Cumulative post-breakdown inventory of neutral deuterated ammonia (ND3), expressed as an equivalent-electron count with ten count units per molecule.
rows.documentation: This quantity is the cumulative number of neutral deuterated ammonia (ND3) molecules introduced after plasma breakdown, converted to an equivalent-electron count. It is the post-breakdown contribution to ammonia_deuterated_count, distinct from the prefill contribution [ammonia_deuterated_prefill_count](name:ammonia_deuterated_prefill_count). The equivalent-electron count is defined by $$ N_{\mathrm{eq,ND_3}}^{\mathrm{post}} = (Z_{\mathrm{N}} + 3Z_{\mathrm{D}})N_{\mathrm{ND_3}}^{\mathrm{post}} = 10N_{\mathrm{ND_3}}^{\mathrm{post}} $$ where $N_{\mathrm{eq,ND_3}}^{\mathrm{post}}$ is the dimensionless equivalent-electron count, $N_{\mathrm{ND_3}}^{\mathrm{post}}$ is the cumulative neutral-molecule count after breakdown, and $Z_{\mathrm{N}}=7$ and $Z_{\mathrm{D}}=1$ are the atomic numbers of nitrogen and deuterium. This is a bookkeeping quantity, not the number of free electrons in the plasma and not an instantaneous injection rate.

rows.name: accumulated_helium_3_prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection
rows.description: Cumulative equivalent-electron inventory of helium-3 atoms introduced by gas injection during plasma prefill before plasma breakdown, with two count units assigned per atom.
rows.documentation: The quantity is the cumulative inventory of helium-3 atoms delivered by gas injection during the plasma prefill phase, expressed as an equivalent-electron count. It covers injection before plasma breakdown and excludes helium-3 introduced after breakdown. The equivalent-electron count is defined by $$ N_{\mathrm{eq}} = Z_{\mathrm{He\text{-}3}} N_{\mathrm{He\text{-}3}} = 2\int_{t_0}^{t_{\mathrm{bd}}} \dot{N}_{\mathrm{He\text{-}3}}(t)\,dt $$ where $N_{\mathrm{eq}}$ is the equivalent-electron count, $Z_{\mathrm{He\text{-}3}}=2$ is the helium-3 atomic number, $N_{\mathrm{He\text{-}3}}$ is the injected helium-3 atom count, $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{He\text{-}3}}$ is the injection rate in s$^{-1}$, and $t_0$ and $t_{\mathrm{bd}}$ are the prefill start and breakdown times in s. This is the pre-breakdown counterpart of [accumulated helium-3 count due to gas injection](name:accumulated_helium_3_count_due_to_gas_injection); [helium-3 source rate due to gas injection](name:helium_3_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection) represents the instantaneous rate rather than the accumulated inventory.

rows.name: accumulated_particle_count_at_pellet_path_due_to_pellet_injection
rows.description: Cumulative number of particles released by ablation from an injected pellet up to a specified position along its trajectory.
rows.documentation: This quantity is the cumulative particle release from pellet ablation as the pellet travels through the plasma. It counts particles removed from the pellet up to the specified trajectory position, rather than particles remaining in the pellet.
