It includes energy deposition from neutron interactions and absorption of primary and secondary gamma radiation within the tile material; deposition outside the tile is outside its scope. It is not the total nuclear energy deposited over a time interval, not a wall-total nuclear heating power, and not a non-nuclear heat load such as charged-particle, surface photon, ohmic, chemical, or coolant heat transfer. It is distinct from [nuclear heating power of a breeder blanket shield](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_shield), which refers to nuclear heating in a different structural component. The nuclear energy deposited in the limiter tile over a time interval is the time integral of this power; this standard name denotes the deposition rate itself, not that time-integrated energy.

rows.name: nuclear_power_density_of_breeder_blanket_layer
rows.description: Local rate of nuclear energy deposition within the material volume of one breeder blanket layer, generated by neutron interactions and associated photon absorption.
rows.documentation: Nuclear power density is the local volumetric heat-generation rate within one defined breeder blanket material layer. It includes energy deposited by neutron interactions and by absorption of primary or secondary photons, rather than surface heat loads or externally applied heating. The volume integral gives the corresponding layer-integrated nuclear heating power: $$ P_{\mathrm{nuc,layer}} = \int_{V_{\mathrm{layer}}} q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{r})\,\mathrm{d}V $$ where $q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local nuclear power density, $P_{\mathrm{nuc,layer}}$ is the integrated nuclear heating power, $\mathbf{r}$ is position, and $V_{\mathrm{layer}}$ is the material volume of the layer. This quantity is the nuclear-deposition component of power density of a breeder blanket layer and integrates to [nuclear heating power of a breeder blanket layer](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer).

rows.name: nuclear_power_density_of_limiter_tile
rows.description: Local volumetric rate of nuclear energy deposition in limiter-tile material from neutron interactions and associated absorption of primary and secondary gamma radiation.
rows.documentation: Nuclear power density of a limiter tile is the local volumetric energy deposition rate within the material of one limiter tile caused by neutron interactions and associated gamma-radiation absorption. It is the nuclear contribution to the broader power density of a limiter tile, not the total local energy source. $$ P_{\mathrm{nuc}} = \int_{V_{\mathrm{tile}}} q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{r})\,\mathrm{d}V $$ where $q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the nuclear power density at position $\mathbf{r}$, $V_{\mathrm{tile}}$ is the material volume of the limiter tile, and $P_{\mathrm{nuc}}$ is the corresponding [nuclear power of a limiter tile](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_limiter_tile). The quantity includes energy deposited volumetrically by neutron scattering and capture and by absorption of primary and secondary gamma radiation. Surface heat loads, externally applied heating, and nonnuclear energy-transfer mechanisms are excluded.

rows.name: radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module
rows.description: Radiated power associated with a single breeder blanket module, abstracting over plasma electromagnetic power incident on the module surface, the reflected portion, and the absorbed portion retained as a module heat load as distinct radiation energy-budget components.
rows.documentation: Radiated power of a breeder blanket module quantifies the rate at which plasma electromagnetic emission, chiefly bremsstrahlung continuum and atomic line radiation, is assigned to the module-level radiation channel. It is the umbrella scalar for the incident photon power crossing onto the module surface and the absorbed photon power retained after surface reflection, represented by [incident_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:incident_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module) and [absorbed_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:absorbed_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module). The radiated-power component for a single module is defined by integrating the corresponding radiative surface energy flux over the module surface: $$ P_{\mathrm{rad},c} = \int_{A_m} \Phi_{\mathrm{rad},c}\, dA,\qquad c \in \{\mathrm{inc},\mathrm{abs}\} $$ where $P_{\mathrm{rad},c}$ is the module-level radiated-power component in watts, $A_m$ is the module plasma-facing surface, $dA$ is a surface element, $\Phi_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{inc}}$ is the incident photon energy flux density onto that surface, and $\Phi_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{abs}}$ is the retained photon energy flux density after reflection. The incident and absorbed components are related by the surface-reflection balance $P_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{abs}} = P_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{inc}} - P_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{ref}}$, equivalently $P_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{abs}} = (1-\mathcal{R})P_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{inc}}$ for an effective reflectance $\mathcal{R}$. The parent quantity is not a sum of incident and absorbed terms; it identifies the module radiation channel, while the component qualifier identifies which surface-budget term is represented. Neutron surface loads, volumetric nuclear energy deposition, auxiliary heating, and thermal radiation emitted by the module itself are outside this radiated-power channel; the absorbed part contributes to thermal_power_of_breeder_blanket_module within [power_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:power_of_breeder_blanket_module).

rows.name: thickness_of_breeder_blanket_layer
rows.description: Non-negative geometric separation between the inner and outer material interfaces of a breeder blanket layer along the specified thickness direction.
rows.documentation: Non-negative geometric separation between the inner and outer material interfaces of a breeder blanket layer is the local through-thickness of that layer along the specified thickness direction. The quantity applies to a single material or functional layer within the blanket, not to the total breeder blanket module build. The layer thickness is defined by the separation of the two bounding interfaces along the thickness coordinate: $$ d_\ell = \left|s_{\ell,\mathrm{out}} - s_{\ell,\mathrm{in}}\right| $$ where $d_\ell$ is the layer thickness in m, and $s_{\ell,\mathrm{in}}$ and $s_{\ell,\mathrm{out}}$ are the signed coordinates in m of the inner and outer layer interfaces along the specified thickness direction. It is not the toroidal width, poloidal height, surface extent, or volume-equivalent thickness of the layer. It is distinct from module-level quantities such as thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module, [lower_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:lower_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module), and [upper_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:upper_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module). For a radially stacked layer, the thickness direction is the cylindrical $\hat{R}$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

rows.name: upper_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module
rows.description: Upper thickness of a breeder blanket module is the non-negative geometric separation through the upper cap, measured normal to its exterior boundary and main-body interface.
rows.documentation: Upper thickness of a breeder blanket module is the geometric thickness of the cap that closes the module at its upper end. The reference surfaces are the upper exterior boundary of the cap and the interface where the upper cap joins the main module body. It is the top-cap poloidal thickness in a poloidal $(R,Z)$ section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is distinct from the overall thickness of a breeder blanket module and the corresponding [lower thickness of a breeder blanket module](name:lower_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module). The upper-cap thickness is the normal projection of the separation between the reference surfaces: $$ t_{\mathrm{upper}} = \left|\left(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ext}} - \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{int}}\right) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}\right| $$ where $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ext}}$ and $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{int}}$ are corresponding points on the upper exterior boundary and cap-to-body interface, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the local unit normal directed through the upper cap in the poloidal section, and $t_{\mathrm{upper}}$ is the upper-cap thickness. The quantity applies to one breeder blanket module and is not summed or averaged over modules. It is a non-negative geometric magnitude; it is not a signed coordinate, vertical height, or displacement and excludes the thicknesses of internal breeder, coolant, or shielding layers.

rows.name: vertical_outline_of_plasma_facing_component
rows.description: The vertical coordinate of each point on a plasma-facing component boundary outline is the signed height in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
rows.documentation: The vertical outline coordinate is the signed height $Z$ of each boundary-contour point belonging to a plasma-facing component. It describes the component boundary in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. For outline point $i$, the coordinate is defined by $$ Z_i = \mathbf{r}_i \cdot \hat{\mathbf{Z}} $$ where $Z_i$ is the vertical coordinate of point $i$, $\mathbf{r}_i$ is that point's position vector relative to the cylindrical coordinate origin, and $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the unit vector in the vertical direction. The quantity applies pointwise to one component boundary outline and is not an average, extremum, centroid coordinate, or integrated geometric measure. A closed outline does not repeat its first point as a closing point. This coordinate has the same geometric meaning as the corresponding outline coordinate for a limiter tile or divertor tile, such as [vertical outline of limiter tile](name:vertical_outline_of_limiter_tile) and [vertical outline of divertor tile](name:vertical_outline_of_divertor_tile), but its locus is the plasma-facing component boundary in general. Sign convention: Positive when $Z_i$ increases in the $+\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

rows.name: vertical_volumetric_force
rows.description: Vertical component of the electromagnetic body-force density vector acting on plasma volumes or conducting wall and structural elements, projected onto increasing vertical height Z in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
rows.documentation: The vertical volumetric force is the $\hat{Z}$-projection of the local electromagnetic body-force density vector acting on plasma volumes or conducting wall and structural elements. It characterizes the local mechanical load per unit volume along the vertical coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, $Z$ is vertical height, and $\hat{Z}$ is the positive vertical basis direction. The component is defined by projecting the local Lorentz force density onto $\hat{Z}$: $$ f_Z = (\mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot \hat{Z} $$ where $f_Z$ is the vertical volumetric force, $\mathbf{J}$ is current density, and $\mathbf{B}$ is magnetic field. The quantity is local to the plasma, conducting wall, or structural material at the point where the force density is defined; no spatial or component aggregation is implied. It is distinct from a coordinate value, a surface traction, a pressure, the magnitude of the force-density vector, and the net vertical force obtained by integrating over a material volume. Together with the [radial volumetric force](name:radial_volumetric_force) and [toroidal volumetric force](name:toroidal_volumetric_force), it forms the component decomposition of the [volumetric force](name:volumetric_force) in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Sign convention: Positive when the force component points in the direction of increasing vertical height $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

rows.name: volumetric_force
rows.description: Electromagnetic Lorentz body-force density vector acting locally on plasma, conducting wall, or structural material, with components resolved in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
rows.documentation: The volumetric force is the local electromagnetic Lorentz force density acting on plasma and current-carrying conducting or structural material. Its projections include the [radial volumetric force](name:radial_volumetric_force), [toroidal volumetric force](name:toroidal_volumetric_force), and [vertical volumetric force](name:vertical_volumetric_force). The electromagnetic force density is defined by $$ \mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{vol}} = \rho_e \mathbf{E} + \mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{B} $$ where $\mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{vol}}$ is the volumetric force vector, $\rho_e$ is charge density, $\mathbf{E}$ is electric field, $\mathbf{J}$ is current density, and $\mathbf{B}$ is magnetic field. The quantity is local and is distinct from the net force obtained by integrating it over a material volume. Sign convention: Positive when a force component points along its corresponding positive basis direction—increasing $R$, increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, or increasing $Z$—in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

rows.name: volumetric_fraction_of_breeder_blanket_layer
rows.description: Volumetric fraction of a breeder blanket layer is the share of a specified constituent material or phase in the layer's bulk volume. It is a dimensionless effective-medium composition parameter for homogenized breeder-blanket layer properties.
rows.documentation: Volumetric fraction of a breeder blanket layer is the part-to-whole volume ratio for one specified constituent material, phase, void region, coolant region, or gas region within a breeder blanket layer. It describes the layer composition used for homogenized material properties over the same geometric region. For constituent $i$, the fraction is defined by: $$ f_i = \frac{V_i}{V_\mathrm{layer}} $$ where $f_i$ is the volumetric fraction, $V_i$ is the volume of constituent $i$ in cubic meters, and $V_\mathrm{layer}$ is the total bulk volume of the same breeder blanket layer in cubic meters over the homogenization region. The numerator and denominator must refer to the same layer region. For an exhaustive non-overlapping partition of that region, $0 \le f_i \le 1$ and $\sum_i f_i = 1$; separately represented voids, coolant, or gas regions are included as their own constituents. This quantity is distinct from mass fraction, atomic fraction, porosity, and selected-solid packing factor, and its layer denominator differs from the whole-blanket volume described by volume of breeder blanket.

rows.name: beryllium_density_at_magnetic_axis
rows.description: Particle number density of the beryllium ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local beryllium-ion count per physical volume there, summed over all beryllium ionization states.
rows.documentation: Particle number density of the beryllium ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local beryllium-ion count per physical volume at that location, summed over all beryllium ionization states. It represents beryllium ions specifically, rather than neutral beryllium, electrons, or other ion species. The defining relation is $$ n_{\mathrm{Be},\mathrm{axis}} = \sum_Z n_{\mathrm{Be}^{Z+},\mathrm{axis}} = \left.\frac{dN_{\mathrm{Be}}}{dV}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}} $$ where $n_{\mathrm{Be},\mathrm{axis}}$ is the total beryllium-ion number density at the magnetic axis, $n_{\mathrm{Be}^{Z+},\mathrm{axis}}$ is the number density of beryllium ions in charge state $Z$, $Z$ is the ionic charge-state number, $N_{\mathrm{Be}}$ is the number of beryllium ions included in the sum, and $V$ is physical volume. The quantity is local to the magnetic axis, the innermost location of nested closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces where the poloidal-flux gradient vanishes. It applies to the complete beryllium-ion population at that location and is summed over all beryllium ionic charge states. It excludes neutral beryllium and is neither a flux-surface or volume integral nor the density of another species. This is the beryllium-specific realization of the population-independent [density at the magnetic axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis). Like [boron density at the magnetic axis](name:boron_density_at_magnetic_axis), it is species-resolved while retaining charge-state aggregation; it differs from [beryllium density at the plasma boundary](name:beryllium_density_at_plasma_boundary) only in its evaluation locus.

rows.name: boron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
rows.description: Number density of boron ions at the radial location of the internal transport barrier, where suppressed cross-field turbulent transport enables steep impurity density gradients to develop.
rows.documentation: Boron density at the internal transport barrier is the local number density of boron ions ($Z = 5$) on the flux surface designated as the internal transport barrier reference location. Unless a charge state is specified separately, this quantity represents the elemental boron ion density summed over all ionization states (B$^{1+}$ through B$^{5+}$), excluding neutral boron atoms. The local particle number density is the zeroth velocity moment of the boron-ion distribution function $f_\mathrm{B}$: $$ n_\mathrm{B}(\rho_\text{ITB}) = \int f_\mathrm{B}(\mathbf{v},\, \rho_\text{ITB})\, d^3v $$ where $\mathbf{v}$ is the particle velocity and $\rho_\text{ITB}$ is the normalized minor radius identifying the ITB flux surface. The ITB is a confined-plasma region where locally reduced cross-field transport coefficients permit steep radial gradients in density and temperature to be sustained; the parent concept is described in [density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier). For the analogous boron density at the innermost confined flux surface, see [boron_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:boron_density_at_magnetic_axis).

rows.name: boron_density_at_magnetic_axis
rows.description: Particle number density of the boron ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local boron-ion count per physical volume, summed over all boron ionic charge states.
rows.documentation: Particle number density of the boron ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local boron-ion count per physical volume at that location. It represents boron ions specifically, rather than electrons, neutrals, or another plasma population, and is summed over all boron ionic charge states. The defining relation is $$ n_{\mathrm{B,axis}} = \left.\frac{dN_{\mathrm{B}}}{dV}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}} $$ where $n_{\mathrm{B,axis}}$ is the boron ion number density at the magnetic axis, $N_{\mathrm{B}}$ is the number of boron ions summed over all ionic charge states, and $V$ is physical volume. The quantity is local to the magnetic axis, the innermost location of nested closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces where the poloidal-flux gradient vanishes. It applies to the complete ionized boron population at that location and excludes neutral boron; it is neither a flux-surface or volume integral nor a density for another species. This is the boron-specific realization of the population-independent [density at the magnetic axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis). It has the same locus and aggregation convention as [beryllium density at the magnetic axis](name:beryllium_density_at_magnetic_axis), but represents boron ions rather than beryllium ions. It differs from [boron density at the internal transport barrier](name:boron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier), which is evaluated at a different plasma location.

rows.name: bulk_neutral_internal_state_velocity
rows.description: Bulk translational velocity vector of neutral particles in one specified internal quantum or energy state, given by the first moment of their velocity distribution.
rows.documentation: The quantity is the bulk translational velocity vector of neutral particles occupying one specified internal state, such as a quantum or energy state. It retains resolution of that state rather than combining distinct neutral internal states. The state-resolved bulk velocity is the first velocity moment of the corresponding distribution: $$ \mathbf{u}_{\alpha}^{\mathrm{bulk}} = \frac{\int \mathbf{v}\,f_{\alpha}(\mathbf{v})\,d^3\mathbf{v}}{\int f_{\alpha}(\mathbf{v})\,d^3\mathbf{v}} $$ where $\mathbf{u}_{\alpha}^{\mathrm{bulk}}$ is the state-resolved bulk neutral velocity, $\alpha$ identifies the internal state, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, and $f_{\alpha}$ is the neutral-particle velocity distribution for that state. This is the direction-agnostic vector parent for component projections of the same bulk neutral population in the same resolved internal state; it is not itself a radial, toroidal, poloidal, or vertical component. Component quantities such as [vertical bulk neutral internal-state velocity](name:vertical_bulk_neutral_internal_state_velocity) are projections of this vector, with the vertical component defined along $\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It excludes thermal speed and velocity spread, which are moments about the bulk velocity rather than this first velocity moment. Sign convention: Positive when a resolved cylindrical component is directed along the corresponding positive unit vector $+\hat{R}$, $+\hat{\phi}$, or $+\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

rows.name: carbon_density_at_magnetic_axis
rows.description: Particle number density of the carbon-ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local carbon-ion count per physical volume, summed over all carbon ion charge states.
rows.documentation: Particle number density of the carbon-ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local carbon-ion count per physical volume at that location, summed over all carbon ion charge states. It represents carbon ions specifically, rather than electrons, other ion species, or neutral carbon. The defining relation is $$ n_{\mathrm{C,axis}} = \left.\frac{dN_{\mathrm{C}}}{dV}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}} $$ where $n_{\mathrm{C,axis}}$ is the carbon-ion number density at the magnetic axis, the subscript $\mathrm{C}$ denotes the carbon-ion population, $N_{\mathrm{C}}$ is the number of carbon ions, $V$ is physical volume, and the subscript axis denotes evaluation at the magnetic axis. The quantity is local to the magnetic axis, the innermost location of nested closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces where the poloidal-flux gradient vanishes. It applies to the complete carbon-ion population at that location and is summed over all carbon ion charge states; it is neither a flux-surface or volume integral nor a neutral-carbon density. This is the carbon-specific realization of the population-independent [density at the magnetic axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis). It differs from [oxygen density at the magnetic axis](name:oxygen_density_at_magnetic_axis) only in the counted ion species, and from [carbon density at the internal transport barrier](name:carbon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) in the evaluation locus.

rows.name: co_passing_fast_current_density
rows.description: Co-passing fast-particle current density is the signed conventional electric-charge flux per unit area carried by fast particles on co-passing, untrapped guiding-center orbits. It is a vector orbit-class contribution and excludes compensating electron and thermal-ion return currents.
rows.documentation: Co-passing fast-particle current density is the signed conventional charge-flux density carried by fast particles on co-passing, untrapped guiding-center orbits. It is the co-passing orbit-class contribution to [current density](name:current_density), not the sum over all fast-particle orbit classes. The kinetic definition is the charge-weighted first velocity moment restricted to the co-passing orbit class: $$ \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{fast,co}}(\mathbf{x},t)=\sum_{s\in\mathrm{fast}} q_s \int_{\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{co}}} \mathbf{v}\, f_s(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v},t)\, d^3v $$ where $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $t$ is time, $s$ indexes included fast-particle species, $q_s$ is the particle charge of species $s$, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, $f_s$ is the velocity-space distribution function, $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element, and $\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{co}}$ is the velocity-space subset whose guiding-center orbit invariants classify the particle as co-passing. Specific scalar components, such as [toroidal co-passing fast current density](name:toroidal_co_passing_fast_current_density), are projections of this vector; the vector quantity itself is not limited to the $\hat{\phi}$ projection in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is distinct from [counter-passing fast current density](name:counter_passing_fast_current_density) and [trapped fast current density](name:trapped_fast_current_density). Compensating electron and thermal-ion return-current contributions are excluded; they belong to other components of the total current density. Sign convention: Positive when the selected scalar projection of the co-passing fast-particle charge flux is aligned with the positive direction defining that projection.

rows.name: co_passing_fast_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions
rows.description: Collisional co-passing torque density for fast ions is the local vector rate of angular-momentum transfer to or from the co-passing fast-ion population caused by Coulomb collisions with background plasma species.
rows.documentation: Collisional co-passing torque density for fast ions is the local source density of angular momentum transferred to or from the co-passing fast-ion population by Coulomb collisions. It retains the full torque-density vector for fast ions on the co-passing orbit branch rather than selecting a particular component. The local defining relation is: $$ \boldsymbol{\tau}_{f,\mathrm{co},\mathrm{coll}} = \left.\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\ell}_{f,\mathrm{co}}}{\partial t}\right|_{\mathrm{coll}} $$ where $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{f,\mathrm{co},\mathrm{coll}}$ is the co-passing fast-ion collisional torque-density vector, $\boldsymbol{\ell}_{f,\mathrm{co}}$ is the co-passing fast-ion angular-momentum density, and $t$ is time; the subscript $\mathrm{coll}$ selects the Coulomb-collisional contribution. This quantity is restricted to the co-passing fast-ion population; it is not the all-orbit [fast-ion torque density due to collisions](name:fast_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions) and is not an aggregate over counter-passing or trapped fast ions. The [toroidal co-passing fast-ion torque density due to collisions](name:toroidal_co_passing_fast_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions) is the toroidal component-resolved instance of this vector quantity, and this quantity is distinct from collisional energy-transfer density. Sign convention: Positive when a resolved vector component points along its positive basis direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

rows.name: co_passing_thermal_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions
rows.description: Local vector rate of angular-momentum transfer to the thermal-ion population per unit volume caused by Coulomb collisions, restricted to co-passing orbit-class contributions and without restricting spatial direction.
rows.documentation: Co-passing thermal-ion torque density due to collisions is the local torque per unit volume transferred to the bulk thermal ion population by Coulomb collisions with contributing charged-particle populations. It is restricted to the co-passing orbit-class contribution of those collisions and is represented by the full torque-density vector, not by a single spatial component. For the selected thermal-ion population, the co-passing collisional torque-density vector is defined from the co-passing contribution to its collision operator by $$ \boldsymbol{\tau}_{i,\mathrm{coll}}^{\mathrm{co}}(\mathbf{r}) = \int d^3v\,\bigl(\mathbf{r} \times m_i\mathbf{v}\bigr)\,C_{i,\mathrm{coll}}^{\mathrm{co}}[f_i](\mathbf{r},\mathbf{v}) $$ where $\mathbf{r}$ is position relative to the torque origin, $m_i$ is the thermal-ion mass, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, $f_i$ is the thermal-ion distribution function, and $C_{i,\mathrm{coll}}^{\mathrm{co}}$ is the Coulomb-collision operator term giving momentum transfer to thermal ions from the co-passing orbit-class contribution. Co-passing denotes passing-orbit contributions whose toroidal motion in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame is in the same sense as the plasma current, distinct from counter-passing and trapped orbit-class contributions. At parent level, the quantity retains the full vector direction for that orbit class; [toroidal co-passing thermal-ion torque density due to collisions](name:toroidal_co_passing_thermal_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions) is the corresponding $\hat{\phi}$-component restriction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It excludes torque deposited in fast-ion populations. Sign convention: Positive when a resolved torque-density component points along the corresponding positive basis vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

rows.name: counter_passing_fast_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions
rows.description: Volumetric counter-passing torque density deposited in the fast-electron population through Coulomb collisions, the local vector rate of angular-momentum transfer per unit volume.
rows.documentation: The counter-passing fast-electron collisional torque density is the net rate at which Coulomb scattering transfers angular momentum per unit volume to the counter-passing suprathermal electron population. It is the orbit-class specialization of [fast-electron torque density due to collisions](name:fast_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions). The vector torque density is defined from the corresponding collisional force density by $$ \boldsymbol{\tau}_{e,f}^{\mathrm{coll}}=\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{f}_{e,f}^{\mathrm{coll}} $$ where $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{e,f}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the torque-density vector, $\mathbf{r}$ is the position vector from the selected torque origin, and $\mathbf{f}_{e,f}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the collisional force density transferred to counter-passing fast electrons. Its toroidal projection is [toroidal counter-passing fast-electron torque density due to collisions](name:toroidal_counter_passing_fast_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions). The quantity excludes thermal-electron and other orbit-class contributions. Sign convention: Positive when a resolved component points along the corresponding positive direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

rows.name: counter_passing_fast_ion_charge_state_power_density_due_to_collisions
rows.description: Flux-surface-averaged rate of Coulomb-collisional kinetic-energy transfer to counter-passing fast particles from ions of one specified species and charge state.
rows.documentation: This quantity is the flux-surface-averaged rate at which Coulomb collisions with ions of one specified species and charge state change the kinetic-energy density of counter-passing fast particles. Counter-passing particles follow untrapped guiding-center trajectories whose parallel transit is opposite to the reference co-passing direction. The defining kinetic-energy moment is $$ P_{\mathrm{counter},bq}^{\mathrm{coll}} = \left\langle \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{counter}}} \frac{1}{2}m_a v^2 C_{a,bq}[f_a,f_{bq}](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v \right\rangle $$ where $P_{\mathrm{counter},bq}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the counter-passing collisional power density for ion partner species $b$ and ionic charge number $q$; $a$ identifies the fast-particle distribution species; $m_a$ is its particle mass; $\mathbf{x}$ is position; $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity; and $v=|\mathbf{v}|$ is speed. The functions $f_a$ and $f_{bq}$ are the fast-particle and ion-partner velocity distributions, respectively. The operator $C_{a,bq}$ gives the collisional time derivative of $f_a$ caused by that ion partner, $\Omega_{\mathrm{counter}}$ selects counter-passing phase space, $d^3v$ is the velocity-space integration measure, and angle brackets denote a magnetic-flux-surface average. The charge-state label identifies the ion collision partner, not a charge-state restriction on the receiving fast particles. This is a single-partner contribution, with no sum over partner species or charge states. It is a collisional source or sink, not stored kinetic-energy density or spatially integrated power. Together with the [co-passing contribution](name:co_passing_fast_ion_charge_state_power_density_due_to_collisions) and the trapped contribution for the same ion partner, it reconstructs the flux-surface average of the [all-orbit fast-particle collisional power density for that ion charge state](name:fast_ion_charge_state_power_density_due_to_collisions). Sign convention: Positive when collisions with the specified ion charge state increase the kinetic-energy density of the counter-passing fast-particle population; negative when they decrease it.

rows.name: counter_passing_power_density
rows.description: Flux-surface-averaged volumetric energy source rate for counter-passing particles, representing energy transfer to or from particles circulating opposite to the plasma-current direction.
rows.documentation: Counter-passing power density is the flux-surface-averaged rate at which energy is transferred to or from the counter-passing orbit population per unit physical volume. It is the orbit-class specialization of power density; counter-passing particles are passing particles that circulate opposite to the plasma-current direction, distinct from [co-passing power density](name:co_passing_power_density) and [trapped power density](name:trapped_power_density). For the underlying local energy balance, volumetric power density is defined by $$ p_{\mathrm{cp}} = \frac{dE_{\mathrm{cp}}}{dt\,dV} $$ where $E_{\mathrm{cp}}$ is the energy transferred to the counter-passing population, $t$ is time, and $V$ is physical volume. The flux-surface average is applied to this local rate while retaining its per-volume meaning. Positive values denote net energy gain by the counter-passing population; negative values denote net energy loss. Wave-particle interactions, collisions, and particle sources contribute when they are included in the counter-passing energy balance.

rows.name: counter_passing_thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions
rows.description: Flux-surface-averaged rate of Coulomb-collisional energy transfer per unit volume from counter-passing nonthermal particles to bulk thermal electrons.
rows.documentation: Counter-passing thermal-electron collisional power density is the signed volumetric rate of kinetic-energy transfer from counter-passing nonthermal particles to bulk thermal electrons, averaged over a magnetic flux surface. Counter-passing particles follow untrapped guiding-center trajectories whose transit is opposite to the reference co-passing direction. The transfer is defined by the thermal-electron kinetic-energy moment of the Coulomb collision operator: $$ P_{e,\mathrm{counter}}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\psi) = \left\langle \sum_a \int \frac{1}{2}m_e v^2 C_{ea}[f_e^{\mathrm{th}},f_{a,\mathrm{counter}}] \, d^3v \right\rangle_\psi $$ where $P_{e,\mathrm{counter}}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the flux-surface-averaged power density transferred to thermal electrons, $\psi$ labels the magnetic flux surface, $a$ indexes the represented nonthermal donor species, $m_e$ is the electron mass, $\mathbf{v}$ is electron velocity, and $v=|\mathbf{v}|$ is electron speed. The distribution $f_e^{\mathrm{th}}$ describes bulk thermal electrons, $f_{a,\mathrm{counter}}$ is the counter-passing part of the nonthermal distribution of species $a$, and $C_{ea}$ gives the collisional time derivative of the thermal-electron distribution caused by that donor population. The integral covers all electron velocities; the angle brackets denote the physical-volume-weighted average over an infinitesimal shell between neighboring flux surfaces. The orbit restriction applies to the nonthermal donors, not to the receiving thermal electrons. The donor contributions are summed over the represented nonthermal species. Energy transferred to ions or fast electrons, contributions from co-passing or trapped donors, and noncollisional heating are excluded. This quantity describes energy gained by thermal electrons rather than energy gained by the counter-passing donors; the corresponding donor energy exchange has the opposite sign. After applying the same flux-surface average to each contribution, adding the [co-passing thermal-electron contribution](name:co_passing_thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions) and the [trapped thermal-electron contribution](name:trapped_thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions) recovers the flux-surface average of [thermal-electron collisional power density](name:thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions), which includes all represented donor orbit classes. Sign convention: Positive when Coulomb collisions with counter-passing nonthermal particles transfer net kinetic energy to bulk thermal electrons.

rows.name: counter_passing_thermal_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions
rows.description: Counter-passing thermal electron torque density due to collisions is the local angular-momentum transfer rate to bulk thermal electrons from Coulomb collisions with counter-passing fast particles.
rows.documentation: Counter-passing thermal electron torque density due to collisions is the local rate per unit volume at which Coulomb scattering transfers angular momentum to the bulk, near-Maxwellian thermal electron population, restricted to collisions with counter-passing fast particles. $$ \boldsymbol{\tau}_{e,\mathrm{th}}^{\mathrm{coll,cp}} = \left.\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\ell}_{e,\mathrm{th}}}{\partial t}\right|_{\mathrm{coll,cp}} $$ Here $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{e,\mathrm{th}}^{\mathrm{coll,cp}}$ is the collisional torque-density vector deposited in thermal electrons, and $\boldsymbol{\ell}_{e,\mathrm{th}}$ is their angular-momentum density. The subscript $\mathrm{cp}$ restricts the transfer to counter-passing fast particles. This quantity is an orbit-resolved contribution to the [thermal electron torque density due to collisions](name:thermal_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions); its [toroidal counter-passing thermal electron torque density due to collisions](name:toroidal_counter_passing_thermal_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions) is the toroidal projection, while the [toroidal thermal electron torque density due to collisions](name:toroidal_thermal_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions) resolves the corresponding axis component without this orbit restriction. Contributions deposited in fast electrons and torque from non-Coulomb processes are excluded. Sign convention: Positive when a resolved component points along the corresponding positive direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame: increasing $R$, increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, or increasing $Z$.

rows.name: counter_passing_thermal_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions
rows.description: Counter-passing thermal-ion torque density due to collisions is the local angular-momentum transfer rate per unit volume delivered to bulk thermal ions by Coulomb collisions.
rows.documentation: Counter-passing thermal-ion torque density due to collisions is the local torque per unit volume transferred to the bulk thermal ion population by Coulomb collisions with contributing charged-particle populations. It is restricted to the counter-passing particle component while retaining the full torque-vector quantity rather than a single axis component. The collisional torque density is related to the collisional force density by $$ \boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{coll}} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{coll}} $$ where $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the torque density transferred to thermal ions, $\mathbf{r}$ is the position vector from the axis about which torque is resolved, and $\mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the force density transferred to thermal ions by collisions. This quantity is the counter-passing contribution to [thermal_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:thermal_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions); collision partners and channels are included in the collisional transfer, while other orbit classes are excluded. Its toroidal component is represented by [toroidal_counter_passing_thermal_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_counter_passing_thermal_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions), while [toroidal_thermal_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_thermal_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions) provides the corresponding toroidal component aggregated over contributing orbit classes. Sign convention: Positive when a resolved torque component points along its corresponding positive basis direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

rows.name: current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity
rows.description: Full current-density vector arising from the divergence of the parallel viscous stress tensor in a magnetized plasma.
rows.documentation: Full current-density vector arising from the divergence of the parallel viscous stress tensor in a magnetized plasma. It is the current-density contribution associated with the parallel part of viscous momentum transport, where parallel refers to the magnetic-field direction in the stress tensor rather than to the direction of the resulting current. The perpendicular force-balance drift produced by the parallel-viscous force density is $$ \mathbf{J}_{\Pi_\parallel} = \frac{(\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Pi}_\parallel) \times \mathbf{B}}{B^2} $$ where $\mathbf{J}_{\Pi_\parallel}$ is this current-density vector, $\boldsymbol{\Pi}_\parallel$ is the parallel viscous stress tensor, $\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Pi}_\parallel$ is the corresponding viscous force density, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, and $B=|\mathbf{B}|$ is the magnetic-field magnitude. Only the full tensor divergence enters this relation; it is not a scalar-viscosity definition. The vector direction is governed by the right-hand rule applied to the parallel-viscous force density and the magnetic field, and the contribution is locally perpendicular to $\mathbf{B}$. This quantity excludes current density due to [perpendicular viscous stress](name:current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity), including its [field-aligned projection](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity), and the separate [heat-viscosity contribution](name:current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity). Directional projections include the [radial](name:radial_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity), [toroidal](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity), and [vertical](name:vertical_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity) components along $\hat{R}$, $\hat{\phi}$, and $\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height, and the [poloidal component](name:poloidal_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity) in the plane spanned by $\hat{R}$ and $\hat{Z}$. Aggregate viscous-current components such as [radial_current_density_due_to_viscosity](name:radial_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity) and toroidal_current_density_due_to_viscosity combine this contribution with perpendicular-viscosity contributions.

rows.name: density_at_magnetic_axis
rows.description: Local particle concentration of a specified plasma population at the magnetic axis, with ion charge states aggregated and compound fuel mixtures treated as defined populations.
rows.documentation: Particle number density at the magnetic axis is the local number of particles of a specified plasma population per physical volume at the innermost location of nested closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces. The quantity is population-specific and does not denote an unrestricted sum over all plasma species. It is defined locally by: $$ n_P(\mathbf{x}_{\rm axis}) = \lim_{\Delta V \to 0} \frac{N_P(\Delta V;\mathbf{x}_{\rm axis})}{\Delta V} $$ where $n_P$ is the particle number density of population $P$, $\mathbf{x}_{\rm axis}$ is the location of the magnetic axis, $N_P(\Delta V;\mathbf{x}_{\rm axis})$ is the number of particles from population $P$ within a physical volume $\Delta V$ centered at that location, and $\Delta V$ is the shrinking volume used to define the local limit. The value is evaluated at the magnetic axis, rather than over a flux surface, plasma region, or volume, so it is not an average. For an ion species, the population count is summed over all positive ionic charge states and excludes neutral atoms; for electrons, it counts electrons directly. When the population is deuterium–tritium, the mixture is treated as one effective fuel population and includes the ionic charge states of both isotopes. These conventions distinguish particle number density from mass density, charge density, and the density of a single resolved charge state. Species-specific instances include [argon density at the magnetic axis](name:argon_density_at_magnetic_axis), [electron density at the magnetic axis](name:electron_density_at_magnetic_axis), and [deuterium–tritium density at the magnetic axis](name:deuterium_tritium_density_at_magnetic_axis). The same population-specific density concept at another geometric locus is represented by [density at the plasma boundary](name:density_at_plasma_boundary) and [density at the internal transport barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier); those quantities differ in their evaluation location.

rows.name: effective_thermal_ion_charge_state_energy_velocity_due_to_convection
rows.description: Effective vector velocity for convective transport of thermal energy by ions in one specified charge state.
rows.documentation: The thermal ion charge-state energy convection velocity is the effective vector advection velocity assigned to convective transport of thermal energy by ions in one specified charge state. It represents the convective channel rather than the full particle velocity or diffusive energy transport. For the selected charge state, it is defined through the convective thermal-energy flux: $$ \mathbf{q}_{E,\mathrm{conv}} = \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{th}}\,\mathbf{v}_{E,\mathrm{conv}} $$ where $\mathbf{q}_{E,\mathrm{conv}}$ is the convective thermal-energy flux, $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{th}}$ is the thermal-energy transport density used in the flux decomposition, and $\mathbf{v}_{E,\mathrm{conv}}$ is the effective convection velocity. No summation over ion charge states is implied. The quantity excludes diffusive and conductive energy transport and need not equal the mass-weighted [center-of-mass velocity](name:center_of_mass_velocity); its radial instance is represented by the [radial effective thermal ion charge-state energy convection velocity](name:radial_ion_charge_state_energy_convection_velocity). Sign convention: Positive when each vector component points along its positive basis direction—increasing $R$, increasing $\phi$, or increasing $Z$—in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

rows.name: electron_diffusion_coefficient
rows.description: Electron particle transport coefficient relating diffusive flux to the opposing number-density gradient without specifying a spatial direction.
rows.documentation: The electron diffusion coefficient characterizes electron particle diffusion through a local Fickian relation between diffusive particle flux and the electron number-density gradient. It does not select a spatial direction or a particular transport mechanism. For a scalar Fickian closure, the defining relation is: $$ \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_e^{\mathrm{diff}} = -D_e\nabla n_e $$ where $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_e^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusive electron particle flux density, $D_e$ is the electron diffusion coefficient, $n_e$ is the electron number density, and $\nabla$ denotes the spatial gradient. The minus sign expresses down-gradient transport for positive diffusivity. This is an electron-specific [particle diffusivity](name:particle_diffusivity), not an electron energy or momentum transport coefficient. It excludes convective contributions to the electron particle flux and is not a sum of directional diffusion coefficients. The [poloidal electron diffusion coefficient](name:poloidal_electron_diffusion_coefficient) is the poloidal-poloidal diagonal specialization within an anisotropic particle-diffusion tensor. The scalar closure above applies when a single coefficient represents the flux-gradient response; the general quantity does not require equal diffusion in all directions or encode off-diagonal tensor couplings.

rows.name: electron_particle_flux_limiter_coefficient
rows.description: Dimensionless multiplier that limits electron particle-flux density relative to its collisionless free-streaming bound without reversing the transport direction.
rows.documentation: The electron particle flux limiter coefficient is a multiplicative factor that scales the collisionless free-streaming upper bound on electron particle-flux density in a particle-transport closure. It limits the permitted magnitude while preserving the direction or sign assigned by the underlying closure. The admissible electron particle-flux magnitude satisfies: $$ \left\lVert\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_e\right\rVert \leq \Gamma_{e,\max} = L_e\Gamma_e^{\mathrm{fs}} $$ where $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_e$ is the electron particle-flux density, the norm denotes its magnitude, $\Gamma_{e,\max}$ is its maximum permitted magnitude, $L_e$ is the electron particle flux limiter coefficient, and $\Gamma_e^{\mathrm{fs}}$ is the nonnegative collisionless free-streaming bound. The subscript $e$ denotes electrons. The coefficient is nonnegative; values below unity impose a stricter cap than the free-streaming bound. This bound does not prescribe a particular interpolation between unconstrained and limited transport. This coefficient applies to the electron density equation, not to electron energy or momentum transport. It is the electron-specific specialization of the [particle flux limiter coefficient](name:particle_flux_limiter_coefficient), within the broader [flux limiter coefficient](name:flux_limiter_coefficient) family. It is distinct from the [ion particle flux limiter coefficient](name:ion_particle_flux_limiter_coefficient), which limits ion particle transport.

rows.name: electron_pressure
rows.description: Electron kinetic pressure is one-third of the trace of the velocity-space stress, covering thermal, suprathermal, and combined populations.
rows.documentation: Electron kinetic pressure is the isotropic scalar measure of momentum flux generated by random electron motion about the population mean velocity. It may describe a suprathermal component, a thermal component, or their combined electron population. The defining pressure is $$ p_e = \frac{m_e}{3}\int \lvert \mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_e\rvert^2 f_e(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v $$ where $p_e$ is the electron kinetic pressure, $m_e$ is the electron mass, $\mathbf{v}$ is an individual electron velocity, $\mathbf{u}_e$ is the mean velocity of the represented electron population, $f_e(\mathbf{v})$ is its velocity distribution, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element. At parent scope, the quantity applies to a selected thermal or suprathermal electron population or to their full aggregate. Aggregation is over the represented electrons in velocity space, not over ion or neutral species; the full aggregate combines disjoint thermal and suprathermal contributions. This quantity is the trace-based scalar reduction of the electron kinetic stress and does not specify a directional pressure-tensor component. An anisotropic electron stress is therefore represented here only through its trace, while ion pressure, neutral pressure, and individual tensor components are excluded. The [fast-electron pressure contribution](name:fast_electron_pressure) is the suprathermal component within this common kinetic-pressure concept. The [total electron pressure](name:total_electron_pressure) is the aggregate over the designated thermal and suprathermal electron populations and equals their sum when those components are disjoint.

rows.name: electron_temperature_at_magnetic_axis
rows.description: Temperature of electrons at the magnetic axis measures their local mean random kinetic energy per particle, excluding coherent electron flow.
rows.documentation: Temperature of electron at magnetic axis The nonrelativistic defining relation is $$ T_{e,\mathrm{axis}} = \frac{2}{3}\left\langle E_{e,\mathrm{random}}\right\rangle_{\mathrm{axis}} $$ where $T_{e,\mathrm{axis}}$ is the electron temperature at the magnetic axis, $E_{e,\mathrm{random}}$ is the electron kinetic energy relative to the local mean electron flow, and the angle brackets denote a particle-number-weighted average over the local electron population. The subscript $\mathrm{axis}$ denotes evaluation at the magnetic axis. This quantity is a local value, not a volume average or a maximum over the plasma. It specializes [temperature at the magnetic axis](name:temperature_at_magnetic_axis) to the electron kinetic temperature, unlike [radiative temperature at the magnetic axis](name:radiative_temperature_at_magnetic_axis), which represents radiation brightness. It forms the numerator of the [ratio of on-axis to volume-averaged electron temperature](name:ratio_of_electron_temperature_at_magnetic_axis_to_volume_averaged_electron_temperature). That ratio expresses central temperature peaking relative to the electron-temperature volume average inside the last closed magnetic flux surface. The closed magnetic-field line about which nested toroidal magnetic flux surfaces are arranged. Where $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{p}}(R_{\mathrm{axis}}, Z_{\mathrm{axis}}) = 0$, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{p}}$ is poloidal magnetic field; $R_{\mathrm{axis}}, Z_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the O-point inside the nested closed flux surfaces.

rows.name: electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions
rows.description: Torque density due to collisional processes is the angular-momentum transfer rate per unit volume imparted to the electron population, encompassing fast and thermal electrons.
rows.documentation: Torque density due to collisional processes is the local rate of angular-momentum transfer to the electron population per unit volume. It is the common parent of the fast- and thermal-electron specializations, which distinguish the electron populations receiving the collisional transfer. Using $\dot{L}_{e,\mathrm{coll}}$ for the collisional angular-momentum transfer rate to electrons and $V$ for volume, the torque density is defined by $$ \tau_{e,\mathrm{coll}} = \frac{\partial \dot{L}_{e,\mathrm{coll}}}{\partial V} $$ The quantity refines [torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:torque_density_due_to_collisions), while [fast_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:fast_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions) and [thermal_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:thermal_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions) provide its population-specific forms. The corresponding ion-family quantity is [ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions); this name does not imply a volume-integrated torque. Sign convention: Positive when collisions transfer angular momentum to electrons in the positive direction defined for the torque component.

rows.name: fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions
rows.description: Signed local rate of Coulomb-collisional energy transfer per unit volume to a specified fast-ion species, summed over all ionic charge states without an orbit-class restriction.
rows.documentation: Fast-ion collisional power density is the signed local rate at which Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy to the nonthermal population of a specified ion species. It is an energy source or sink for the receiving fast ions, not their stored kinetic-energy density or the collisional heating delivered to bulk thermal ions. The defining kinetic-energy moment is $$ P_{i,\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_q \sum_b \int \frac{1}{2}m_i |\mathbf{v}|^2 C_{iq,b}[f_{iq}^{\mathrm{fast}},f_b](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v $$ where $P_{i,\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the fast-ion collisional power density, $i$ identifies the receiving ion species, $q$ labels its ionic charge states, $b$ labels the designated collision partners, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, and $m_i$ is the receiving ion mass. The function $f_{iq}^{\mathrm{fast}}$ is the fast-ion velocity distribution for charge state $q$, $f_b$ is the collision-partner distribution, and $C_{iq,b}$ is the Coulomb collision operator giving the collisional time derivative of the receiving distribution due to that partner. The receiving population is summed over all ionic charge states and includes all guiding-center orbit classes. Contributions from multiple distributions representing the fast-ion population are additive. The partner sum includes only the designated exchanges and reduces to one contribution when a single distribution species supplies the collision partner. This quantity is spatially local; neither a magnetic-flux-surface average nor a volume integral is implied. The [co-passing](name:co_passing_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions) and [counter-passing](name:counter_passing_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions) variants restrict the contributing particle distribution, whereas the [trapped fast-ion variant](name:trapped_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions) restricts the receiving population to trapped fast ions. The related [fast-ion charge-state collisional power density](name:fast_ion_charge_state_power_density_due_to_collisions) resolves an ion collision-partner charge state; that partner resolution is distinct from summing the receiving species over charge states here. This quantity supplies a fast-population contribution to [ion collisional power density](name:ion_power_density_due_to_collisions). Summing the fast-ion contributions over the included ion species and adding the corresponding thermal-ion contributions gives the aggregate ion collisional power density. Sign convention: Positive when Coulomb collisions increase the kinetic-energy density of the receiving fast-ion population.

rows.name: fast_particle_torque_due_to_j_cross_b_force
rows.description: Fast-particle torque due to the j×B force is the volume-integrated torque vector acting on the fast-particle population through the magnetic Lorentz force density generated by its current density and the magnetic field.
rows.documentation: Fast-particle torque due to the $j \times B$ force is the volume-integrated torque vector acting on the fast-particle population through the magnetic part of the Lorentz force density associated with the fast-particle current density and the magnetic field. It represents angular-momentum transfer to that fast-particle population, not to thermal particles or material structures. The torque vector over a volume $V$ is defined by the moment of the $j \times B$ force density: $$ \boldsymbol{\tau}_{f,j\times B} = \int_V \mathbf{r} \times \left(\mathbf{j}_f \times \mathbf{B}\right)\, dV $$ where $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{f,j\times B}$ is the fast-particle torque due to the $j \times B$ force, $\mathbf{r}$ is the position vector from the chosen torque origin to the volume element, $\mathbf{j}_f$ is the fast-particle current density, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field, and $dV$ is the volume element. This vector parent is distinguished from component-specific projections; [toroidal fast-particle torque due to the $j \times B$ force](name:toroidal_fast_particle_torque_due_to_j_cross_b_force) is the toroidal component of the same fast-particle torque. It excludes torque channels not represented by the fast-particle current-cross-magnetic-field force density. Sign convention: Positive when a reported component of $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{f,j\times B}$ is aligned with the positive direction of its stated projection axis, with vector cross products evaluated by the right-hand rule; in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the toroidal component is positive along $+\hat{\phi}$ toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, counterclockwise when viewed from the $+\hat{Z}$ side.

rows.name: helium_4_density_at_magnetic_axis
rows.description: Particle number density of the helium-4 ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local helium-4 ion count per physical volume at that location, summed over all helium-4 ionic charge states.
rows.documentation: Particle number density of the helium-4 ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local helium-4 ion count per physical volume at that location, summed over all helium-4 ionic charge states. It represents helium-4 ions specifically, rather than neutral helium, electrons, other isotopes, or another plasma population. The defining relation is $$ n_{{}^{4}\mathrm{He},\mathrm{axis}} = \left.\frac{dN_{{}^{4}\mathrm{He},\mathrm{ion}}}{dV}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}} $$ where $n_{{}^{4}\mathrm{He},\mathrm{axis}}$ is the helium-4 ion number density at the magnetic axis, $N_{{}^{4}\mathrm{He},\mathrm{ion}}$ is the number of helium-4 ions summed over all ionic charge states, and $V$ is physical volume. The superscript $4$ identifies the helium isotope with four nucleons. The quantity is local to the magnetic axis, the innermost location of nested closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces where the poloidal-flux gradient vanishes. It applies to the complete helium-4 ion population at that location and is summed over all helium-4 ionic charge states; it is neither a flux-surface or volume integral nor a density of neutral helium or another isotope. This is the helium-4-specific realization of the population-independent [density at the magnetic axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis), whose population is left unspecified at the parent level. It is distinguished from [helium-3 density at the magnetic axis](name:helium_3_density_at_magnetic_axis), which counts helium-3 ions rather than helium-4 ions.

rows.name: hydrogen_density
rows.description: Local number density of hydrogen (protium) ions in the plasma, giving the count of H+ particles per unit volume at a specified spatial position.
rows.documentation: The hydrogen density quantifies the local concentration of protium ions ($^1$H$^+$, the lightest hydrogen isotope with mass number $A = 1$) at a point in the plasma. It is distinct from the neutral atomic hydrogen density and from the number densities of heavier hydrogenic isotopes such as deuterium ($^2$H) and tritium ($^3$H). The number density $n_H$ at position $\mathbf{r}$ is defined as $$ n_H(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{dN_H}{dV} $$ where $N_H$ is the number of hydrogen ions within the infinitesimal volume element $dV$ centered at $\mathbf{r}$. Spatially averaged forms provide experimentally accessible measures of the same quantity: [line_averaged_hydrogen_density](name:line_averaged_hydrogen_density) gives the path-length-normalized ion count along a spectroscopic or interferometric chord, while [volume_averaged_hydrogen_density](name:volume_averaged_hydrogen_density) integrates the ion content over the full plasma volume. The isotopic composition of the hydrogenic fuel is tracked by [ratio_of_hydrogen_density_to_total_hydrogenic_density](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_hydrogen_density_to_volume_averaged_total_hydrogenic_density), which expresses $n_H$ relative to the combined protium, deuterium, and tritium ion density. The aggregate over all three hydrogen isotopes is given by hydrogenic_density, and the full multi-species ion sum by [total_ion_density](name:total_ion_number_density).

rows.name: implicit_electron_particle_source_rate
rows.description: Implicit electron particle source rate is the coefficient multiplying electron number density to give the implicitly treated contribution to free-electron production or removal.
rows.documentation: Implicit electron particle source rate is the signed coefficient of the density-proportional contribution to a decomposed electron particle source. Its designation identifies the contribution assigned to implicit treatment in the electron density transport equation, not a separate physical production mechanism. The source decomposition is defined by $$ S_e = S_e^{\mathrm{exp}} + S_e^{\mathrm{imp}} n_e $$ where $S_e$ is the [electron volumetric source rate](name:electron_volumetric_source_rate) being decomposed, $S_e^{\mathrm{exp}}$ is its additive explicit contribution, $S_e^{\mathrm{imp}}$ is the implicit electron particle source coefficient defined here, and $n_e$ is the free-electron number density. This coefficient applies to the electron population and the particular source contribution being decomposed; it does not imply aggregation over all source mechanisms. It excludes the additive explicit contribution. The coefficient itself is neither a volumetric source nor a volume-integrated production rate: its product with electron number density supplies the implicit volumetric contribution. The analogous [implicit ion particle source rate](name:implicit_ion_particle_source_rate) multiplies ion density instead. Sign convention: Positive when the implicit contribution produces free electrons, and negative when it removes them.

rows.name: implicit_ion_momentum_source_rate
rows.description: Rate coefficient multiplying the primary ion momentum quantity to represent its implicit source or sink contribution in transport equations.
rows.documentation: This quantity is the coefficient for the implicit contribution to an ion momentum source term. It represents proportional momentum addition or removal associated with the primary ion momentum quantity, without selecting a particular directional component. The implicit source contribution is defined by $$ S_{M,i}^{\mathrm{imp}} = C_{M,i}^{\mathrm{imp}} M_i $$ where $S_{M,i}^{\mathrm{imp}}$ is the implicit ion momentum source contribution, $C_{M,i}^{\mathrm{imp}}$ is this rate coefficient, and $M_i$ is the primary ion momentum quantity to which the coefficient is applied. The quantity applies to ion momentum and is independent of the component or direction selected by a specialization. It describes the coefficient itself, not the resulting momentum source and not the primary momentum quantity. A positive coefficient represents proportional momentum sourcing, whereas a negative coefficient represents proportional momentum removal. It is the implicit, proportional component of the broader [ion momentum source rate](name:ion_momentum_source_rate). The [toroidal implicit ion momentum source rate](name:toroidal_implicit_ion_momentum_source_rate) is a directional specialization in which the same coefficient concept is applied to the toroidal ion momentum quantity.

rows.name: ion_charge_state_diffusivity
rows.description: Ion charge-state diffusivity is the effective Fickian particle diffusivity for ions in a specified ionization state, without specifying a spatial projection.
rows.documentation:
Ion charge-state diffusivity is the effective Fickian particle diffusivity for ions in a specified ionization state, without specifying a spatial projection. It is the scalar transport coefficient that relates the diffusive particle flux component of that charge state to the negative directional gradient of its number density. For a chosen projection direction $\hat{\mathbf{e}}$, the defining Fickian relation is: $$ \Gamma^{\mathrm{diff}}_{s,e} = -D_s\,
abla_e n_s $$ where $\Gamma^{\mathrm{diff}}_{s,e}$ is the projected diffusive particle flux density of charge state $s$, $D_s$ is this diffusivity, $n_s$ is the number density of charge state $s$, and $
abla_e n_s = \hat{\mathbf{e}}\cdot
abla n_s$ is the directional derivative of that number density. A positive flux component is directed along $+\hat{\mathbf{e}}$; the minus sign makes a positive diffusivity drive diffusive flux opposite to the projected density gradient. This quantity is charge-state-resolved: it applies to a single ionization state rather than to the density-weighted mean over all charge states represented by ion diffusivity. It is the same physical coefficient as [ion charge-state diffusion coefficient](name:ion_charge_state_diffusion_coefficient) when that name is used for the same Fickian closure. Directionally specified counterparts include [radial ion charge-state diffusivity](name:radial_ion_charge_state_diffusivity) and [parallel ion charge-state diffusivity](name:parallel_ion_charge_state_diffusivity); convective or pinch transport, particle sources and sinks, and energy or momentum transport coefficients are separate quantities.

rows.name: ion_charge_state_momentum_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
rows.description: Ion charge-state momentum flux due to diamagnetic drift is the signed transfer of a selected linear-momentum component per surface area for one ion charge state, attributed to pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic transport.
rows.documentation: Ion charge-state momentum flux due to diamagnetic drift is the signed flux density of a selected component of linear [momentum](name:momentum) for one specified charge state of an ion species, attributed to pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic transport. The transported momentum component and the surface-crossing direction are distinct specifications; neither a toroidal momentum projection nor a flux-surface-normal crossing direction is imposed. For the selected momentum component and oriented surface, the flux is defined by $$ \Gamma_{a,s}^{\mathrm{dia}} = \hat{\mathbf e}_a \cdot \boldsymbol{\Pi}_s^{\mathrm{dia}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf n} $$ where $\Gamma_{a,s}^{\mathrm{dia}}$ is this momentum flux, $s$ labels the specified ion species and charge state, $a$ labels the selected momentum component, $\hat{\mathbf e}_a$ is its direction unit vector, $\hat{\mathbf n}$ is the oriented surface-normal unit vector, and $\boldsymbol{\Pi}_s^{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the diamagnetic contribution to that state's momentum-flux tensor, with its first index denoting transported momentum and its second index denoting crossing direction. This quantity is the charge-state-resolved specialization of [momentum flux due to diamagnetic drift](name:momentum_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift). It contains no sum over ion species or charge states, unlike the charge-state-aggregated [ion momentum flux due to diamagnetic drift](name:ion_momentum_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift). It excludes contributions from non-diamagnetic transport mechanisms and is not the total momentum flux. Sign convention: Positive when positive momentum in the selected component is transported along the oriented surface normal.

rows.name: ion_charge_state_particle_flux
rows.description: Ion charge-state particle flux is the signed net flow of thermal and nonthermal ions of one species and charge state through an oriented surface per unit area and time.
rows.documentation: Ion charge-state particle flux is the net number flow of ions of one specified species and ionization charge state through an oriented surface per unit area and time. It includes thermal and nonthermal ions without selecting a fixed geometric or magnetic-field direction. For a local oriented surface, the defining particle-number moment is: $$ \Gamma_{s,q} = \int (\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}})\,f_{s,q}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v},t)\,d^3v $$ where $\Gamma_{s,q}$ is the particle flux for ion species $s$ and ionic charge number $q$, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the chosen surface-normal unit vector, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, and $f_{s,q}$ is the particle-number distribution in position and velocity for that species and charge state. The symbols $\mathbf{x}$ and $t$ denote position and time, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element; the integral includes all velocities. Thermal and nonthermal contributions are added within the specified charge state, but different charge states are not summed. The quantity counts particles rather than their charge or energy. It is a net flux density, not a surface-integrated crossing rate or a one-way incident flux. No spatial averaging is intrinsic to the general definition; the flux-surface-normal specialization additionally uses a surface average. Summing over all ionic charge states of the same species, with the same orientation and averaging convention, gives the [ion particle flux](name:ion_particle_flux). The [parallel component](name:parallel_ion_charge_state_particle_flux) selects the local magnetic-field direction as the surface normal, whereas the [poloidal component](name:poloidal_ion_charge_state_particle_flux) selects the local poloidal direction. Sign convention: Positive when net ion transport follows the chosen surface-normal direction.

rows.name: ion_charge_state_temperature
rows.description: Temperature of ions in a specified charge state measures their random translational kinetic energy after bulk flow is removed, rather than their ionization or excitation energy.
rows.documentation: Temperature of ions in a specified charge state is an energy-equivalent measure of their random translational motion relative to that population's bulk flow. It characterizes the selected ion population, not its internal electronic energy. For an individual charge state, the defining kinetic relation is $$ T_s = \frac{2}{3}\left\langle E_{\mathrm{rand}}\right\rangle_s $$ where $T_s$ is the energy-equivalent temperature, $s$ identifies the ion species and charge state, $E_{\mathrm{rand}}$ is a particle's translational kinetic energy relative to that population's bulk flow, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_s$ denotes a number-weighted average over particles in that state. The quantity is charge-state-resolved, rather than averaged over all charge states or ion species. When the selected population is a defined charge-state bundle, its temperature is the density-weighted mean over the included charge states, not their sum. The species-level temperature is instead the density-weighted mean over all its charge states. Bulk-flow kinetic energy, ionization energy, and excitation energy are excluded. For a thermal population, this temperature supplies the random kinetic energy per particle entering the [thermal ion charge-state pressure](name:thermal_ion_charge_state_pressure). Unlike [plasma temperature](name:plasma_temperature), it does not combine the electron and ion populations into a single effective thermal state.

rows.name: ion_charge_state_velocity
rows.description: Mean bulk-flow velocity vector of ions belonging to one specified ionization charge state, obtained from the first velocity moment of that charge-state population.
rows.documentation: The ion charge-state velocity is the mean translational velocity of ions in a specified ionization charge state. It describes the charge-state-resolved bulk flow and is distinct from the charge-state-averaged [ion velocity](name:ion_velocity). Let $f_Z(\mathbf{v})$ be the velocity distribution function for ions in charge state $Z$, and let $n_Z$ be their number density. The velocity is defined by $$ \mathbf{u}_Z = \frac{1}{n_Z}\int \mathbf{v}\,f_Z(\mathbf{v})\,d^3\mathbf{v}, \qquad n_Z = \int f_Z(\mathbf{v})\,d^3\mathbf{v} $$ where $\mathbf{u}_Z$ is the charge-state bulk velocity and $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity. The vector may be resolved into directional projections, including the [radial ion charge-state velocity](name:radial_ion_charge_state_velocity), without summing or averaging over other ionization states. Sign convention: Positive components point along the corresponding positive directions of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ basis.

rows.name: ion_energy_diffusivity
rows.description: Effective coefficient linking an ion population's density-normalized diffusive heat flux to its temperature gradient, without prescribing a transport direction.
rows.documentation: Ion energy diffusivity characterizes gradient-driven transport of thermal energy carried by an ion population. It specifies the effective proportionality between density-normalized diffusive heat flux and the corresponding temperature gradient, without selecting a transport direction or implying isotropic transport. For a chosen physical transport direction, the defining Fickian closure is: $$ \frac{Q_{i,\mathrm{diff}}}{n_i} = -k_{\mathrm{B}}D_{i,W}\frac{\partial T_i}{\partial \ell} $$ where $Q_{i,\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusive thermal-energy flux component along that direction, $n_i$ is the ion population's number density, $D_{i,W}$ is its effective energy diffusivity, $T_i$ is its thermodynamic temperature, $\ell$ is physical distance along the selected direction, and $k_{\mathrm{B}}$ is Boltzmann's constant. The subscript $i$ denotes the ion population, and $W$ labels the energy channel. The minus sign makes positive diffusivity correspond to down-gradient transport. The population may comprise one ion species or collectively all ion species. Number density and diffusive heat flux are summed over all included ionic charge states and species, while temperature is their density-weighted mean. When the constituents share a common temperature, the effective diffusivity is their density-weighted mean diffusivity; otherwise it is defined by the combined flux–gradient closure rather than an unqualified average of constituent coefficients. This coefficient excludes convective and advective energy transport and is distinct from particle diffusivity. Electron and neutral heat transport are outside its scope. The [ion charge-state energy diffusion coefficient](name:ion_charge_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient) instead describes transport associated with one specified ionic charge state. The [parallel ion energy diffusivity](name:parallel_ion_energy_diffusivity) specializes this definition to field-aligned transport for the collective ion population, whereas the [poloidal ion energy diffusivity](name:poloidal_ion_energy_diffusivity) specializes it to poloidal transport for a specified ion species.

rows.name: ion_energy_flux_limiter_coefficient
rows.description: Multiplicative factor setting the maximum permitted ion energy flux relative to a collisionless free-streaming reference while preserving the direction assigned by the transport closure.
rows.documentation: The ion energy flux limiter coefficient scales the collisionless free-streaming upper bound on energy flux density carried by a specified ion population. It limits the permitted flux magnitude without choosing or reversing its direction. The limiting relation is: $$ \left|\mathbf{Q}_i\right| \leq f_i Q_{i,\mathrm{fs}} $$ where $\mathbf{Q}_i$ is the limited ion energy flux density, $f_i$ is the ion energy flux limiter coefficient, and $Q_{i,\mathrm{fs}}$ is the nonnegative collisionless free-streaming reference magnitude for the same ion population. The subscript $i$ identifies that population. The coefficient is nonnegative; the free-streaming reference and the transition between unlimited and limited flux are specified by the transport closure. This is the ion-population specialization of the [energy flux limiter coefficient](name:energy_flux_limiter_coefficient), with no particular spatial direction or plasma region prescribed.
