It applies to species-resolved or aggregated ion energy closures, rather than necessarily denoting a total over all ions. The [total ion energy flux limiter coefficient](name:total_ion_energy_flux_limiter_coefficient) specializes this definition to energy summed over all ion species; the limiter coefficient itself is not a sum of species coefficients. The [ion-state energy flux limiter coefficient](name:ion_state_energy_flux_limiter_coefficient) restricts the closure to a specified ion charge state. This coefficient limits energy transport, not particle or momentum transport. It is neither an energy diffusion coefficient nor the fraction of the free-streaming reference actually carried by the flux.

rows.name: iron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
rows.description: Particle number density of iron ions evaluated on the flux surface assigned to an internal transport barrier, summed over all iron ion charge states and excluding neutral iron.
rows.documentation: Particle number density of iron ions evaluated on the flux surface assigned to an internal transport barrier is the local density of the iron-ion population at that flux-surface location. It is the iron-specific member of the [density at the internal transport barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier) family. Iron has atomic number $Z=26$. The number density is defined by $$ n_{\mathrm{Fe}} = \lim_{\Delta V\to 0}\frac{\Delta N_{\mathrm{Fe}}}{\Delta V} $$ where $n_{\mathrm{Fe}}$ is the iron-ion number density, $N_{\mathrm{Fe}}$ is the number of counted iron ions, and $V$ is volume. The count is summed over all iron ionic charge states and excludes neutral iron. The internal transport barrier is the designated flux-surface location where reduced cross-field turbulent transport can sustain steep impurity-density gradients, as for [carbon density at the internal transport barrier](name:carbon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier).

rows.name: krypton_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
rows.description: Particle number density of krypton ions evaluated on the flux surface assigned to an internal transport barrier, summed over krypton charge states and excluding neutral krypton.
rows.documentation: Particle number density of krypton ions evaluated on the flux surface assigned to an internal transport barrier is the local density of the krypton-ion population at that flux-surface location. The [density at the internal transport barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier) is the parent quantity for this krypton-specific population. The number density is defined by $$ n = \lim_{\Delta V\to 0}\frac{\Delta N}{\Delta V} $$ where $n$ is number density, $N$ is the number of particles, and $V$ is volume. The quantity sums all ionized krypton charge states and excludes neutral krypton atoms. It is therefore an elemental ion density, analogous to the ion density at the internal transport barrier, rather than a density for one specified charge state. The internal transport barrier is the designated flux-surface location where locally reduced cross-field turbulent transport permits steep impurity-density gradients.

rows.name: lithium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
rows.description: Local number density of lithium ions at the internal transport barrier reference radius, where reduced cross-field transport can produce steep impurity density gradients.
rows.documentation: Lithium density at an internal transport barrier is the local number density of lithium ions on the flux surface selected as the barrier reference location. Unless a charge state is specified separately, it represents the elemental lithium ion concentration summed over all ionization states, consistent with the broader [density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier) family. The quantity is the sum of charge-state-resolved contributions evaluated at the ITB reference coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{ITB}$: $$ n_\mathrm{Li}(\rho_\mathrm{ITB}) = \sum_{k=1}^{3} n_{\mathrm{Li}^{k+}}(\rho_\mathrm{ITB}) $$ where $k$ indexes the lithium ionization states (Li$^{1+}$, Li$^{2+}$, Li$^{3+}$) and $\rho_\mathrm{ITB}$ is the normalized radial coordinate of the barrier. Lithium (atomic number $Z = 3$) enters fusion plasmas through pellet injection, evaporation from lithium-coated plasma-facing components, or deliberate wall conditioning. As a low-Z impurity it contributes less radiative cooling than high-Z species, but significant concentrations at the ITB can dilute the fuel ion population. The local value at the barrier is inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or from inversion of line-integrated visible or soft-X-ray emission measurements. The corresponding toroidal flow of lithium ions at the same barrier location is given by [toroidal_lithium_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:toroidal_lithium_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier), and the lithium density adjacent to plasma-facing components is separately described by [lithium_density_at_limiter](name:lithium_density_at_limiter).

rows.name: magnetic_shear_at_internal_transport_barrier
rows.description: Magnetic shear at an internal transport barrier is the normalized logarithmic derivative of the safety factor with respect to the outward normalized toroidal-flux radial coordinate at the internal-transport-barrier flux surface.
rows.documentation: Magnetic shear at an internal transport barrier is the local magnetic shear evaluated on the flux surface identified as the internal-transport-barrier location. It characterizes the radial variation of field-line pitch through the safety factor at that locus. The defining relation is $$ s_{\mathrm{ITB}} = \left.\frac{\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}}{q}\frac{d q}{d\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}}\right|_{\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}=\rho_{\mathrm{tor,ITB}}} $$ where $s_{\mathrm{ITB}}$ is the magnetic shear at the internal transport barrier, $q$ is the [safety factor](name:safety_factor), $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the normalized toroidal flux radius used as an outward flux-surface radial coordinate, and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,ITB}}$ is the value of that coordinate at the internal-transport-barrier location. The scope is the local value at the internal-transport-barrier flux surface in a magnetically confined plasma. It is not an average over the barrier width, not the position or width of the barrier, and not the magnetic shear at the pedestal top or another named flux-surface locus. Its aggregation convention is a single flux-surface evaluation with no averaging over neighboring flux surfaces. This quantity is a locus-specific specialization of [magnetic shear at a flux surface](name:magnetic_shear_at_flux_surface): it uses the same normalized logarithmic safety-factor derivative, with the flux-surface label fixed to the internal-transport-barrier location. The derivative is local in $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$, so the quantity represents the local radial slope of $q$ rather than an integral measure across the barrier. Sign convention: Positive when the safety-factor gradient with respect to increasing outward $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ has the same sign as the safety factor at the internal transport barrier.

rows.name: momentum
rows.description: Linear momentum associated with plasma motion, covering concrete quantities that either represent momentum content in a plasma volume or momentum transported through an oriented surface. The specific child name defines whether the quantity is an extensive momentum or a momentum-flux component.
rows.documentation: Momentum is the mass-weighted linear-velocity content associated with plasma matter, together with the corresponding transport of that content when the quantity is defined across an oriented surface. As a parent quantity, it denotes the common linear-momentum concept shared by concrete momentum-content and momentum-transport quantities, not a single fully specified observable. This parent must not be interpreted as imposing one governing equation on all children: [plasma momentum](name:plasma_momentum) is an integrated momentum content, whereas [radial momentum](name:radial_momentum) is a component of momentum transport in the $\hat{R}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. A concrete child supplies the necessary scope, such as included species, volume integration, component direction, and oriented-surface convention. Sign convention: Positive when a specified component is directed along the positive basis vector or oriented-surface direction named by the concrete child quantity.

rows.name: neutral_diffusion_coefficient
rows.description: Effective particle diffusivity relating an internal-state-summed neutral population's diffusive flux to its opposing number-density gradient, without selecting a spatial direction.
rows.documentation: The neutral diffusion coefficient characterizes particle transport driven by the local number-density gradient of an aggregate neutral population. It does not select a spatial direction, a particular neutral species, or a spatial region. For a Fickian closure along a chosen physical direction: $$ \Gamma^{0,\mathrm{diff}}_{s} = -D_0\,\hat{\mathbf{s}}\cdot\nabla n_0 $$ where $\Gamma^{0,\mathrm{diff}}_{s}$ is the diffusive neutral particle flux density along the unit direction vector $\hat{\mathbf{s}}$, $D_0$ is the neutral diffusion coefficient for that closure, and $n_0$ is the neutral number density. The operator $\nabla$ denotes the spatial gradient, and the superscript or subscript $0$ identifies neutrals. The minus sign expresses down-gradient transport for nonnegative diffusivity; choosing a direction for this relation does not impose isotropy. The number density and particle flux are summed over the internal states belonging to the specified neutral population, excluding charged particles. The effective coefficient is defined by the aggregate flux-gradient relation, not by summing internal-state coefficients. In contrast, the [neutral-state diffusion coefficient](name:neutral_state_diffusion_coefficient) applies to one specified internal state. This quantity excludes convective particle flux and is distinct from neutral energy or momentum diffusivity. Directional specializations, such as the [radial neutral diffusion coefficient](name:radial_neutral_diffusion_coefficient), apply the same particle flux-gradient relation to a specified direction.

rows.name: neutral_internal_state_energy_flux_limiter_coefficient
rows.description: Dimensionless closure parameter that limits the admissible energy-flux density carried by neutral particles in a specified internal state.
rows.documentation: This coefficient specifies the strength of the limiter applied to energy transport by neutral particles occupying one selected internal state. It is a closure parameter rather than an energy flux or an energy density. The limiter imposes the bound $$ \lvert \mathbf{q}_E \rvert \leq \alpha_E q_{E,\max} $$ where $\alpha_E$ is this flux-limiter coefficient, $\mathbf{q}_E$ is the energy-flux-density vector carried by the selected neutral internal state, and $q_{E,\max}$ is the prescribed maximum admissible magnitude for that energy flux. The coefficient applies to the energy channel of neutral transport for the specified internal state. It does not sum over neutral internal states or neutral species, does not represent the energy flux itself, and has no edge-region restriction in its definition. It is distinct from the corresponding momentum limiter, such as the [neutral internal-state momentum flux-limiter coefficient](name:neutral_internal_state_momentum_flux_limiter_coefficient_over_edge_region), which constrains momentum rather than energy transport. The coefficient scales the admissible energy-flux bound in the closure: increasing $\alpha_E$ permits a larger maximum energy flux relative to $q_{E,\max}$, while the coefficient itself remains a dimensionless scalar.

rows.name: neutral_internal_state_momentum_velocity_due_to_convection
rows.description: Velocity characterizing convective momentum transport by neutral particles in a resolved internal quantum state, forming the bulk-flow coefficient in the neutral internal-state momentum flux equation.
rows.documentation: The neutral internal-state momentum convection velocity is the fluid velocity at which momentum is transported by bulk convective flow in a neutral particle population that is resolved by internal quantum state (such as a vibrational, rotational, or electronic level). It enters the neutral momentum transport equation as the convective coefficient of the state-resolved momentum flux: $$ \Pi_{\rm conv,s} = m_n n_s v_{\rm conv,s} $$ where $m_n$ is the neutral particle mass, $n_s$ is the number density of internal state $s$, and $v_{\rm conv,s}$ is this convection velocity for state $s$. This is the neutral-species-specific form of the internal-state momentum convection velocity, enabling state-resolved neutral momentum transport to be tracked separately from ionic or electron channels. Its effective counterpart, [effective_neutral_internal_state_momentum_velocity_due_to_convection](name:effective_neutral_internal_state_momentum_velocity_due_to_convection), incorporates transport contributions beyond simple bulk advection that enter the convective momentum channel. For comparison, neutral_internal_state_velocity_due_to_convection describes the corresponding convective velocity for particle (number) transport rather than momentum transport.

rows.name: neutral_internal_state_temperature
rows.description: Temperature of neutral particles in one specified internal state sets the energy scale of their random translational motion after subtracting that population's mean flow.
rows.documentation: Temperature of neutral particles in a specified internal state characterizes their random translational kinetic energy relative to the bulk motion of that state-resolved population. The internal-state label selects a quantum or excitation state; it does not make this an internal-excitation temperature. A cold or hot neutral temperature is that of the named component alone; without the component it covers the whole neutral population of the selected species. Using temperature in its energy-equivalent form, the defining second-moment relation is $$ T_{0,a} = \frac{m_0}{3n_{0,a}}\int |\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_{0,a}|^2 f_{0,a}(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v $$ where $T_{0,a}$ is the state-resolved neutral temperature, $m_0$ is the neutral-particle mass, $n_{0,a}$ is the number density of that population, $f_{0,a}$ is its velocity distribution normalized to that number density, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, and $\mathbf{u}_{0,a}$ is its [bulk translational velocity](name:bulk_neutral_internal_state_velocity). The subscript $0$ identifies neutral particles, $a$ labels the specified internal state, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element. This quantity applies locally to one neutral species in one internal state, without summing or averaging over internal states, species, or spatial regions. It excludes directed bulk kinetic energy and the energy stored in internal excitation. It is the state-resolved counterpart of [neutral temperature](name:neutral_temperature), retaining an internal-state restriction that the species-level quantity does not.

rows.name: neutral_species_atomic_mass
rows.description: Neutral-species atomic mass is the neutral-atom reference mass per atom of a selected elemental or isotopic constituent, including its bound electrons.
rows.documentation: Neutral-species atomic mass is the reference mass assigned to one atom of a selected elemental or isotopic constituent of a neutral species. It specifies atomic composition using the neutral reference atom, including its bound electrons. The atomic mass is related to the corresponding relative atomic mass by $$ m = A_{\mathrm r}\,m_{\mathrm u} $$ where $m$ is the constituent's reference atomic mass, $A_{\mathrm r}$ is its relative atomic mass, and $m_{\mathrm u}$ is the atomic mass constant, defined as one twelfth of the rest mass of a free neutral carbon-12 atom in its ground state. The value applies per constituent atom, whether the neutral species is atomic or molecular; it is not the total molecular mass or the mass of the neutral population. It is a physical mass, not the integer nucleon count called the mass number, a mass density, or a mass flow rate. The number of constituent atoms per particle is specified separately by [atomic count](name:atomic_count). This quantity specializes [atomic mass](name:atomic_mass) to constituents of neutral species. Unlike [neutral-beam atomic mass](name:neutral_beam_atomic_mass), its scope is not restricted to atoms in an injected beam.

rows.name: nitrogen_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
rows.description: Number density of nitrogen ions evaluated at the radial position of the internal transport barrier, where locally reduced cross-field turbulent transport sustains steep impurity density gradients within the confined plasma.
rows.documentation: Nitrogen (atomic number $Z = 7$) is a medium-Z impurity that is seeded into fusion plasmas for radiative power exhaust control and divertor heat-load mitigation. This quantity gives the local number of nitrogen particles per unit volume at the radial reference position of an internal transport barrier (ITB) — a narrow region within the confined plasma where cross-field turbulent transport is locally suppressed, enabling steep radial gradients to develop and persist. Unless a charge-state-resolved quantity is specified separately, it represents the nitrogen ion density summed over all ionization states, consistent with the parent [density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier). In hot plasma core conditions above approximately 1 keV, nitrogen is found predominantly in high ionization states ($N^{5+}$–$N^{7+}$). Within an ITB, neoclassical impurity transport — including temperature-screening and centrifugal effects on the impurity density profile — can drive strong inward or outward peaking of $n_\mathrm{N}$ at the barrier radius, with direct consequences for the local $Z_\mathrm{eff}$ and radiated power balance. Nitrogen density in the plasma core is measured by charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, which resolves individual charge states whose sum yields the total impurity density; transport analysis then extracts the value at the ITB reference location from the fitted profile. Compare with [neon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:neon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) for a noble-gas impurity of similar use, and with [nitrogen_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:nitrogen_density_at_plasma_boundary) for the corresponding boundary value of the same species.

rows.name: oxygen_density_at_magnetic_axis
rows.description: Particle number density of the oxygen ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local oxygen-ion count per physical volume at that location, summed over all oxygen ionic charge states.
rows.documentation: Particle number density of the oxygen ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local oxygen-ion count per physical volume at that location, summed over all oxygen ionic charge states. It represents oxygen ions specifically, rather than electrons, neutral oxygen, or another plasma population. The defining relation is $$ n_{\mathrm{O,axis}} = \left.\sum_q \frac{dN_{\mathrm{O},q}}{dV}\right|_{\mathrm{axis}} $$ where $n_{\mathrm{O,axis}}$ is the oxygen-ion number density at the magnetic axis, $q$ is an oxygen ionic charge state, $N_{\mathrm{O},q}$ is the number of oxygen ions in charge state $q$, and $V$ is physical volume. The quantity is local to the magnetic axis, the innermost location of nested closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces where the poloidal-flux gradient vanishes. It applies to the oxygen ion population and is summed over all oxygen ionic charge states; neutral oxygen is excluded. It is a local density, not a flux-surface or volume integral. This is the oxygen-specific realization of the population-independent [density at the magnetic axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis). It differs from [neon density at the magnetic axis](name:neon_density_at_magnetic_axis), which applies the same local, charge-state-summed convention to neon ions.

rows.name: parallel_conductivity
rows.description: Local electrical response coefficient relating the electric field along the magnetic field to the conductive current density it drives in plasma.
rows.documentation: Parallel conductivity is the local parallel-parallel component of the plasma electrical-conductivity response, with both projections taken along the local magnetic-field direction. It relates the electric-field component along that direction to the conductive current-density component along the same direction. The tensor projection and same-direction conductive response are defined by $$ \sigma_\parallel = \hat{\mathbf b}\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\hat{\mathbf b},\qquad j_\parallel^{\mathrm{cond}} = \sigma_\parallel E_\parallel $$ where $\sigma_\parallel$ is parallel conductivity, $\hat{\mathbf b}$ is the unit vector along the local magnetic field, and $\boldsymbol{\sigma}$ is the local [plasma electrical conductivity](name:plasma_electrical_conductivity) tensor for the response being described. $E_\parallel$ is the [parallel electric field](name:parallel_electric_field), and $j_\parallel^{\mathrm{cond}}$ is the conductive current-density component due to the same-direction parallel response; for the total response, it is the [parallel ohmic current density]. This is a local coefficient for plasma at the location where the response is defined, not a spatial average or integral. For the total plasma response, it represents the combined electrical response of the charged constituents rather than a species-resolved coefficient. When attributed to a particular source, it denotes that source's conductivity contribution and corresponding driven parallel conductive-current response, not the total conductivity. Only the parallel-parallel coefficient is included. Off-diagonal tensor terms, which can also contribute to parallel current when the electric field has transverse components, are distinct from this coefficient; separately driven currents such as bootstrap current are also excluded. Unlike [poloidal conductivity](name:poloidal_conductivity), which selects the poloidal tangent to a magnetic flux surface, or [toroidal conductivity](name:toroidal_conductivity), which selects the cylindrical $\hat{\phi}$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, this projection follows the local magnetic-field direction. Parallel conductivity is a directional component of [plasma electrical conductivity](name:plasma_electrical_conductivity). Its value is governed primarily by electron temperature and Coulomb collisions; for the total bulk-plasma response, it equals Spitzer conductivity in the classical collisional limit.

rows.name: parallel_counter_passing_fast_particle_pressure
rows.description: Parallel pressure is the kinetic-stress component along the magnetic field, including directed motion, carried by suprathermal particles on untrapped orbits whose orbit-averaged toroidal motion opposes the plasma current. Flux-surface averaging aggregates this same component without changing its orbit-class or parallel-component scope.
rows.documentation: Parallel counter-passing fast-particle pressure is the component of kinetic stress along the local magnetic-field direction, carried by suprathermal particles on counter-passing orbits. Counter-passing particles are untrapped and have orbit-averaged toroidal motion opposite to the plasma-current direction; the uncentered moment includes directed parallel motion. The local component is the second velocity moment of the counter-passing suprathermal distribution: $$ p_{parallel,mathrm{cp,fast}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_s \sum_c m_s \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{cp},s,c}(\mathbf{x})} v_\parallel^2 f_{s,c}^{\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v $$ where $p_{\parallel,\mathrm{cp,fast}}$ is this pressure, $s$ labels a fast-particle species, $c$ labels its charge state, $m_s$ is the mass of species $s$, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, $v_\parallel=\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{b}$ is the velocity component parallel to $\mathbf{b}$, $\mathbf{b}$ is the unit vector along the local magnetic field, $f_{s,c}^{\mathrm{fast}}$ is the phase-space number distribution of fast particles of species $s$ and charge state $c$, $\Omega_{\mathrm{cp},s,c}(\mathbf{x})$ is the velocity-space subset at $\mathbf{x}$ associated with their counter-passing orbits, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element. The subscripts $\mathrm{cp}$ and $\mathrm{fast}$ denote counter-passing and suprathermal particles, respectively. The quantity applies to the suprathermal population and is summed additively over fast-particle species and all charge states. It excludes thermal particles, trapped particles, co-passing particles, and stress perpendicular to the magnetic field. The local component and its flux-surface average have the same population and orbit-class scope; the average aggregates the local component over a magnetic surface. This is the counter-passing contribution to [parallel fast-particle pressure](name:parallel_fast_particle_pressure), which includes parallel stress from other fast-particle orbit classes. Together with the [perpendicular counter-passing fast-particle pressure](name:perpendicular_counter_passing_fast_particle_pressure), it determines the [counter-passing fast-particle pressure](name:counter_passing_fast_particle_pressure), the one-third trace of the kinetic stress for the same population: $p_{\mathrm{cp,fast}}=(p_{\parallel,\mathrm{cp,fast}}+2p_{\perp,\mathrm{cp,fast}})/3$, where $p_{\mathrm{cp,fast}}$ is the counter-passing fast-particle pressure and $p_{\perp,\mathrm{cp,fast}}$ is the perpendicular counter-passing fast-particle pressure.

rows.name: parallel_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity
rows.description: Parallel current density due to parallel viscosity is the signed magnetic-field-aligned projection of the electric current contribution associated with parallel viscous stress.
rows.documentation: Parallel current density due to parallel viscosity is the signed local projection of the current contribution associated with the divergence of parallel viscous stress onto the magnetic-field direction. The two uses of parallel distinguish the current projection from the viscous-stress mechanism. For a nonzero magnetic field, the defining projection is: $$ j_\parallel^{(\mathrm{pv})} = \mathbf{j}^{(\mathrm{pv})}\cdot\frac{\mathbf{B}}{|\mathbf{B}|} $$ where $j_\parallel^{(\mathrm{pv})}$ is the parallel current-density contribution, $\mathbf{j}^{(\mathrm{pv})}$ is the full [current-density vector due to parallel viscosity](name:current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity), $\mathbf{B}$ is the local magnetic-field vector, and $|\mathbf{B}|$ is its magnitude. The superscript $\mathrm{pv}$ identifies the parallel-viscosity contribution. In the magnetized edge plasma, this is a local, mechanism-resolved contribution to [current density](name:current_density), not the total parallel current density or a flux-surface average. It excludes the perpendicular-viscosity contribution, whose field-aligned projection is [parallel current density due to perpendicular viscosity](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity). Parallel viscosity does not require its full current-density contribution to be field aligned. The [radial current density due to parallel viscosity](name:radial_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity) is a different projection of the same parent vector. Sign convention: Positive when the parallel-viscosity current-density contribution has a component in the direction of the local magnetic field.

rows.name: parallel_effective_neutral_internal_state_momentum_velocity_due_to_convection
rows.description: Parallel effective neutral internal-state momentum velocity due to convection is the signed, field-aligned component of the effective convection velocity representing transport of momentum carried by neutrals in a resolved internal state. The parallel direction is along the local magnetic field.
rows.documentation: Parallel effective neutral internal-state momentum velocity due to convection is the scalar component, along the local magnetic-field direction, of an effective convection velocity for transport of momentum carried by a neutral population in one resolved internal state. It is a transport velocity for momentum, not the neutral bulk-flow velocity itself. The scalar projection is defined by $$ v_{\parallel,\mathrm{eff}} = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{eff}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}} $$ where $v_{\parallel,\mathrm{eff}}$ is this parallel effective neutral internal-state momentum velocity due to convection, $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the corresponding [neutral_internal_state_momentum_velocity_due_to_convection](name:neutral_internal_state_momentum_velocity_due_to_convection), and $\hat{\mathbf{b}} = \mathbf{B}/\lvert\mathbf{B}\rvert$ is the unit vector in the direction of the local magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$. The scope is a single resolved neutral internal state, so no summation or averaging over internal states is implied. This quantity is the field-aligned component only; it excludes perpendicular components, particle-density convection velocities, energy convection velocities, diffusivities, and source terms. In a convective momentum-transport closure, it is the effective velocity factor associated with the transported neutral internal-state momentum. Sign convention: Positive when the projection of the effective convection velocity is in the direction of the local magnetic field.

rows.name: parallel_ion_charge_state_energy_diffusivity
rows.description: Parallel ion charge-state energy diffusivity is the field-aligned Fickian diffusivity for thermal-energy transport of a specified ion charge state, defined so the parallel diffusive energy flux is proportional to and opposite the field-aligned gradient of that state's thermal-energy density.
rows.documentation:
Parallel ion charge-state energy diffusivity is the effective transport coefficient for local diffusive smoothing of the thermal-energy density of one specified ionization stage along the magnetic-field direction. It represents the field-aligned Fickian part of that stage's thermal-energy transport, distinct from convective transport and explicit energy sources, and is the parallel component of ion charge-state energy diffusivity. The defining field-aligned closure is $$ q_{E,z,\parallel} = -\chi_{E,z,\parallel}
abla_\parallel w_z $$ where $q_{E,z,\parallel}=\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{q}_{E,z}$ is the parallel component of the diffusive thermal-energy flux density of ionization stage $z$, $\mathbf{b}$ is the unit vector along the magnetic field, $\chi_{E,z,\parallel}$ is the parallel ion charge-state energy diffusivity, $w_z$ is the thermal-energy density of that ionization stage, and $
abla_\parallel w_z=\mathbf{b}\cdot
abla w_z$ is the field-aligned spatial gradient of that density. The minus sign specifies down-gradient transport along the magnetic field. This quantity applies to one specified ion charge state and is not summed over ion species or charge states, unlike [ion energy diffusivity](name:ion_energy_diffusivity). It is a coefficient multiplying the thermal-energy-density gradient, not a temperature-gradient heat-transport coefficient unless the relevant density and heat-capacity factors are explicitly included in the coefficient.

rows.name: parallel_ion_momentum_flux
rows.description: Parallel ion momentum flux is the rate per unit area at which the magnetic-field-aligned momentum of an ion species crosses an oriented surface.
rows.documentation: Parallel ion momentum flux is the transport rate per unit area of the magnetic-field-aligned component of ion [momentum](name:momentum) across an oriented surface. The parallel label selects the transported momentum component, while the surface normal specifies the direction across which transport is evaluated. The defining projection is: $$ \Gamma_{i,\parallel} = \hat{\mathbf b}\cdot\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_i = \hat{\mathbf b}\cdot\boldsymbol{\Pi}_i\cdot\hat{\mathbf n} $$ where $\Gamma_{i,\parallel}$ is this parallel momentum flux, $i$ identifies the ion species, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_i$ is its momentum-flux vector through the oriented surface, $\boldsymbol{\Pi}_i$ is its momentum-flux tensor, and $\hat{\mathbf n}$ is the chosen surface-normal unit vector. The magnetic-field unit vector is $\hat{\mathbf b}=\mathbf B/|\mathbf B|$, where $\mathbf B$ is the local magnetic field. For the specified ion species, the flux is summed over all ionic charge states, combining the corresponding [parallel ion charge-state momentum flux](name:parallel_ion_charge_state_momentum_flux) contributions. It includes convective transport, pressure, and viscous or turbulent stresses, rather than only diffusive transport; electron and neutral contributions are excluded. The surface need not be a magnetic flux surface, and its normal need not be parallel to the magnetic field. Summing the species contributions gives the parallel component of the total [ion momentum flux](name:ion_momentum_flux), which aggregates over all ion species and ionic charge states. Sign convention: Positive when the net momentum transported through the surface in its chosen normal direction has a component co-directed with the local magnetic field.

rows.name: parallel_total_ion_energy_convection_velocity
rows.description: Effective field-aligned velocity multiplying the energy density summed over all ion species to give their combined parallel convective energy flux.
rows.documentation: Field-parallel total-ion energy convection velocity is the effective transport coefficient relating the combined ion population's parallel convective energy flux to its transported energy density in the edge plasma. It is the field-parallel projection of the [total-ion energy convection velocity](name:total_ion_energy_convection_velocity). The defining relation is: $$ Q_{i,\parallel}^{\mathrm{conv}} = \mathcal{W}_i\,v_{i,W,\parallel} $$ where $Q_{i,\parallel}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the combined ion convective energy flux density along the local magnetic field, $\mathcal{W}_i$ is the combined transported ion energy density, and $v_{i,W,\parallel}$ is this effective convection velocity. The subscript $i$ denotes the combined ion population, $W$ identifies the energy transport channel, and $\parallel$ denotes projection along the local magnetic field. The energy density and convective flux are each summed over all ion species and ionic charge states included in the total-ion energy equation; electron and neutral contributions are excluded. The effective velocity is not a sum of constituent velocities and need not equal the bulk ion flow velocity. Gradient-driven diffusive energy flux is excluded from the defining convective flux. Unlike the [parallel ion energy convection velocity](name:parallel_ion_energy_convection_velocity) for an individual ion population, this coefficient closes the summed ion energy equation. Sign convention: Positive when the convective transport is co-directed with the local magnetic field.

rows.name: particle_density
rows.description: Particle number density is the concentration of a selected species, including thermal and nonthermal particles and all orbit classes unless a narrower population is specified.
rows.documentation: Particle number density is the local concentration of particles belonging to a selected species or population. For the full species distribution, it includes both thermal and nonthermal particles and all orbit classes. The local density is the zeroth velocity-space moment of the distribution function: $$ n_s(\mathbf{x}) = \int f_s(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v $$ where $s$ labels the selected species, $n_s$ is its local particle number density, $\mathbf{x}$ is physical position, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, $f_s$ is its particle-number distribution in position and velocity space, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element. The quantity refers to one selected species, not a sum over different species. For a species specified without charge-state resolution, its number density is summed over all charge states; a charge-state-resolved population retains only the selected state's contribution. The local value does not imply flux-surface averaging; a flux-surface-averaged form averages this same local moment over a magnetic flux surface. The [fast-particle density](name:fast_particle_density) is the same moment restricted to suprathermal particles and excludes the thermal population. It contributes to, but is distinct from, the full species density. Distinct nonthermal populations of the same species contribute additively to that full density.

rows.name: particle_torque_due_to_j_cross_b_force
rows.description: Particle torque due to j cross B force is the volume-integrated Lorentz-force torque exerted on a represented particle distribution by its electric current density interacting with the magnetic field. It is the particle-distribution-resolved parent quantity; species- or population-specific names refine it without implying a toroidal-only projection.
rows.documentation: Particle torque due to j-cross-B force is the volume-integrated torque exerted on a represented particle distribution by the Lorentz force density generated from that distribution's electric current density and the magnetic field. The physical torque is an axial-vector quantity before any species, population, or coordinate-component qualifier is applied. The defining volume integral is $$ \boldsymbol{\tau}_p = \int_V \mathbf{r} \times \left(\mathbf{j}_p \times \mathbf{B}\right)\, dV $$ where $\boldsymbol{\tau}_p$ is the particle-distribution-resolved torque, $\mathbf{r}$ is the position vector from the torque origin to the volume element, $\mathbf{j}_p$ is the electric current density carried by the represented particle distribution, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field, and $V$ is the integration volume. This parent does not specify fast, thermal, impurity, neutral, or other particle populations and does not by itself select any coordinate-component projection. Population-specific instances, such as [fast-particle torque due to j-cross-B force](name:fast_particle_torque_due_to_j_cross_b_force), inherit this definition; component-specific quantities are projections of $\boldsymbol{\tau}_p$ rather than redefinitions of the torque source. It excludes torque contributions not arising from the Lorentz force density $\mathbf{j}_p \times \mathbf{B}$ and excludes sums over unrelated plasma sources unless the represented particle distribution is explicitly the aggregation being described. Sign convention: Positive when a scalar component of $\boldsymbol{\tau}_p$ is aligned with the positive direction of the explicitly named projection axis; for a toroidal projection in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, this is the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

rows.name: particle_velocity_due_to_convection
rows.description: Effective advection velocity characterizing non-diffusive transport in the plasma particle channel by bulk convection, without selecting a species or internal state.
rows.documentation: Particle convective velocity is the effective vector velocity associated with non-diffusive transport of plasma particles by bulk convection. It describes motion of the transported particle quantity rather than diffusive spreading or the particle flux itself. For the particle transport channel, the convective particle flux is defined by $$ \mathbf{\Gamma}^{\mathrm{conv}}_p = n_p\,\mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{conv}}_p $$ where $\mathbf{\Gamma}^{\mathrm{conv}}_p$ is the convective particle flux, $n_p$ is the local particle number density, and $\mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{conv}}_p$ is the particle convective velocity. The subscript $p$ identifies the particle transport channel, and the superscript $\mathrm{conv}$ identifies its non-diffusive convective contribution. This is the full vector, channel-level quantity with no selected radial, poloidal, toroidal, or field-parallel component. It applies generically to plasma-particle transport without selecting a particular species, charge state, or internal state; no additional species-level aggregation is implied by the generic channel name. It excludes diffusive transport and must not be interpreted as the single-particle kinematic velocity of an individual particle. The quantity is the particle-channel specialization of [velocity due to convection](name:velocity_due_to_convection). The corresponding [energy velocity due to convection](name:energy_velocity_due_to_convection) uses the same effective-velocity construction for convective energy transport, while [neutral state convection velocity](name:neutral_state_convection_velocity) is a narrower quantity restricted to a specified neutral internal state. The vector components are expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. Sign convention: Positive when a vector component points along the corresponding positive basis direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

rows.name: perpendicular_co_passing_fast_particle_pressure
rows.description: Flux-surface-averaged transverse kinetic stress of nonthermal particles on untrapped orbits whose orbit-averaged toroidal motion follows the plasma current.
rows.documentation: The perpendicular co-passing fast-particle pressure is the flux-surface-averaged field-perpendicular component of the kinetic stress of a represented nonthermal particle species. Co-passing particles occupy untrapped guiding-center orbits with orbit-averaged toroidal motion in the plasma-current direction. The component is defined by the transverse second moment of the co-passing fast-particle distribution: $$ p_{s,\perp,\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{co}}(\psi)=\left\langle\int_{\mathcal{C}_s(\mathbf{x})}\frac{m_s v_\perp^2}{2}\,f_{s,\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v\right\rangle_\psi $$ where $p_{s,\perp,\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{co}}$ is the perpendicular co-passing fast-particle pressure, $s$ labels the represented species, $\psi$ labels a magnetic flux surface, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\mathcal{C}_s(\mathbf{x})$ is the velocity-space subset belonging to co-passing orbits at that position, $m_s$ is the particle mass, $f_{s,\mathrm{fast}}$ is the fast-particle distribution function, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element. The squared transverse speed is $v_\perp^2=|\mathbf{v}-(\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{b})\hat{b}|^2$, where $\hat{b}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the unit vector along the local magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$. The factor of one-half gives the mean stress in the two field-perpendicular directions. The brackets denote a normalized magnetic-flux-surface average with weight proportional to $dS/|\nabla\psi|$, where $dS$ is the surface-area element and $\nabla\psi$ is the spatial gradient of the flux label. Thus the quantity is a surface average, not a local stress at one point. Only the co-passing nonthermal population contributes; thermal, trapped, and counter-passing particles are excluded. Multiple fast-particle populations of the represented species contribute additively, not through a density-weighted mean; no all-species or all-charge-state total is implied. Particle velocities are used without subtracting the mean flow, so perpendicular directed-motion stress is retained. Together with the [parallel co-passing fast-particle pressure](name:parallel_co_passing_fast_particle_pressure), this component determines the [co-passing fast-particle pressure](name:co_passing_fast_particle_pressure) through $p_{s,\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{co}}=(p_{s,\parallel,\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{co}}+2p_{s,\perp,\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{co}})/3$, where $p_{s,\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{co}}$ is one-third of the kinetic-stress trace and $p_{s,\parallel,\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{co}}$ is the corresponding field-parallel component, with the same population restriction and flux-surface averaging.

rows.name: perpendicular_trapped_fast_particle_pressure
rows.description: Perpendicular trapped fast-particle pressure is the field-perpendicular kinetic-pressure component carried by suprathermal particles on magnetically trapped orbits.
rows.documentation: Perpendicular trapped fast-particle pressure is the gyrotropic kinetic-pressure component perpendicular to the local magnetic field, carried by suprathermal particles on magnetically trapped orbits. Trapped particles reverse their field-parallel motion at magnetic mirror points. This is the stress per transverse degree of freedom, not the sum of both transverse stresses or the scalar trace pressure. The local perpendicular pressure is defined by the trapped-population second velocity moment: $$ p_{s,\perp,\mathrm{tr}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_c \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{tr},s,c}(\mathbf{x})} \frac{m_s v_\perp^2}{2} f_{s,c}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v $$ Here, $p_{s,\perp,\mathrm{tr}}$ is the perpendicular trapped fast-particle pressure; $s$ labels the particle species, and $c$ labels its charge state; $m_s$ is the mass of species $s$; $\mathbf{x}$ is position; $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity; $v_\perp$ is the magnitude of the velocity component perpendicular to the local magnetic field; $f_{s,c}$ is the suprathermal distribution for species $s$ and charge state $c$; $\Omega_{\mathrm{tr},s,c}(\mathbf{x})$ is the trapped region of velocity space at that position; and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element. The factor of one half gives the mean over the two perpendicular velocity directions. Contributions are summed over all charge states of species $s$; distinct species are not summed in this species-specific quantity. The local moment may vary over a magnetic flux surface; its flux-surface average is the average of that same moment over the surface. The population is restricted to suprathermal trapped particles and excludes thermal, co-passing, and counter-passing particles. Perpendicular refers to the magnetic-field direction, not the normal to a flux surface. This is the trapped-orbit contribution to [perpendicular fast-particle pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_particle_pressure), excluding the [perpendicular co-passing fast-particle pressure](name:perpendicular_co_passing_fast_particle_pressure) and [perpendicular counter-passing fast-particle pressure](name:perpendicular_counter_passing_fast_particle_pressure). For the same trapped population, the [trapped fast-particle pressure](name:trapped_fast_particle_pressure) is the scalar pressure related to the [parallel trapped fast-particle pressure](name:parallel_trapped_fast_particle_pressure) by $p_{s,\mathrm{tr}}=(p_{s,\parallel,\mathrm{tr}}+2p_{s,\perp,\mathrm{tr}})/3$, where $p_{s,\parallel,\mathrm{tr}}$ is the parallel component and $p_{s,\perp,\mathrm{tr}}$ is this perpendicular component.

rows.name: poloidal_electron_particle_flux
rows.description: Poloidal electron particle flux is the signed net electron crossing rate per unit area perpendicular to the local poloidal direction around a plasma cross-section.
rows.documentation: Poloidal electron particle flux is the signed net electron number flow per unit area normal to the local poloidal direction. It describes particle transport around a plasma cross-section, rather than transport along the toroidal direction or necessarily along the magnetic field. The defining velocity moment is $$ \Gamma_{e,\mathrm{p}} = \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_e \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{p}} = \int (\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{p}}) f_e(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v $$ where $\Gamma_{e,\mathrm{p}}$ is the poloidal electron particle flux, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_e$ is the electron number-flux vector, $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{p}}$ is the positive local poloidal unit tangent, $\mathbf{v}$ is electron velocity, $f_e$ is the local electron velocity distribution normalized to electron number density, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element. The poloidal tangent lies in a constant-toroidal-angle cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. Its positive orientation must be specified by the poloidal-direction convention. The integral includes the full electron velocity distribution, with opposite crossings contributing opposite signs. In the plasma edge, this remains a local flux density: neither surface integration nor flux-surface averaging is implied. This component specializes [electron particle flux](name:electron_particle_flux) to an oriented surface whose normal is the poloidal unit tangent. It is a number flux, not an electric-charge flux; unlike [poloidal electron energy flux](name:poloidal_electron_energy_flux), it has no energy weighting. Sign convention: Positive when the net electron number flow follows the specified positive local poloidal tangent, independently of the negative electron charge.

rows.name: poloidal_flux_limiter_coefficient
rows.description: Poloidal flux limiter coefficient is a multiplicative factor that scales the collisionless free-streaming upper bound on poloidal momentum-flux density while preserving the direction or sign assigned to that component by the transport closure.
rows.documentation: Poloidal flux limiter coefficient is a multiplicative factor that scales the collisionless free-streaming upper bound on poloidal momentum-flux density in a transport closure. It limits the permitted magnitude while preserving the sign assigned to the poloidal momentum-flux component by the unconstrained closure. For an unconstrained poloidal momentum-flux density $\Pi_{\mathrm{pol}}^{\mathrm{cl}}$, a direction-preserving limited flux can be expressed as: $$ \Pi_{\mathrm{pol}}^{\mathrm{lim}} = \operatorname{sgn}\!\left(\Pi_{\mathrm{pol}}^{\mathrm{cl}}\right)\min\!\left(\left|\Pi_{\mathrm{pol}}^{\mathrm{cl}}\right|, L_{\mathrm{pol}} \Pi_{\mathrm{pol}}^{\mathrm{fs}}\right) $$ where $\Pi_{\mathrm{pol}}^{\mathrm{lim}}$ is the limited poloidal momentum-flux density, $\Pi_{\mathrm{pol}}^{\mathrm{cl}}$ is the unconstrained closure value, $\Pi_{\mathrm{pol}}^{\mathrm{fs}}$ is the non-negative collisionless free-streaming bound for the same poloidal component, and $L_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the poloidal flux limiter coefficient. This quantity is the poloidal component of the [momentum-flux limiter coefficient](name:momentum_flux_limiter_coefficient) and a component-specific child of the [flux limiter coefficient](name:flux_limiter_coefficient). It is distinct from the [radial flux limiter coefficient](name:radial_flux_limiter_coefficient) and [toroidal flux limiter coefficient](name:toroidal_flux_limiter_coefficient), and it does not by itself specify a particle species, charge state, neutral internal state, or spatial region. Because $L_{\mathrm{pol}}$ multiplies the non-negative bound $\Pi_{\mathrm{pol}}^{\mathrm{fs}}$, it is a non-negative magnitude-scaling coefficient; the signed direction of the limited flux is carried by $\Pi_{\mathrm{pol}}^{\mathrm{cl}}$ and $\Pi_{\mathrm{pol}}^{\mathrm{lim}}$, not by the coefficient.

rows.name: poloidal_ion_charge_state_momentum_convection_velocity
rows.description: Effective velocity coefficient relating the non-diffusive convective flux of poloidal momentum to the poloidal momentum density of ions of one species in a specified charge state.
rows.documentation: This coefficient governs advective, non-diffusive transport of poloidal [momentum](name:momentum) carried by ions of one specified species and charge state. It specializes the [ion charge-state momentum convection velocity](name:ion_charge_state_momentum_convection_velocity) to the poloidal-momentum channel and is not the ion charge state's bulk poloidal flow velocity. The convective contribution to the momentum-flux closure is defined by: $$ \Pi_{s,\mathrm p}^{\mathrm{conv}} = V_{s,\mathrm p}\,g_{s,\mathrm p} $$ where $s$ identifies the ion species and charge state, $\mathrm p$ denotes the poloidal momentum component, $\Pi_{s,\mathrm p}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is its convective flux through an oriented surface, $g_{s,\mathrm p}$ is its local momentum density, and $V_{s,\mathrm p}$ is this effective convection coefficient. The poloidal direction is tangent to a magnetic flux surface within a plane containing the toroidal symmetry axis. The poloidal label identifies the transported momentum component; it does not independently specify the direction through which that momentum is transported. The positive flux direction must therefore be specified by the oriented transport surface. This coefficient applies to one charge state, without summation or averaging over charge states. It excludes the gradient-driven diffusive contribution described by [poloidal ion charge-state momentum diffusivity], as well as separately represented residual stress and external momentum sources. Sign convention: Positive when positive poloidal momentum is convected along the positive normal of the oriented transport surface.

rows.name: poloidal_ion_charge_state_particle_flux
rows.description: Poloidal ion charge-state particle flux is the signed net ion crossing rate per unit area normal to the local poloidal direction for one species and ionization state, including thermal and nonthermal ions.
rows.documentation: Poloidal ion charge-state particle flux is the signed net number flow of ions of one specified species and ionization charge state per unit area perpendicular to the local poloidal direction. It describes local poloidal particle transport in the edge plasma, including thermal and nonthermal ions. The flux is the poloidal projection of the state's particle-flux vector: $$ \Gamma_{s,q,\mathrm{p}} = \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{s,q}\cdot\hat{\mathbf e}_{\mathrm{p}} $$ where $\Gamma_{s,q,\mathrm{p}}$ is the poloidal particle flux, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{s,q}$ is the net particle-flux vector including thermal and nonthermal contributions, $s$ identifies the ion species, $q$ identifies its ionization charge number, and $\hat{\mathbf e}_{\mathrm{p}}$ is the local poloidal unit vector. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The poloidal unit vector lies in a plane of constant $\phi$ and follows increasing poloidal angle $\theta$; the geometric orientation of that angle must be specified. This is the [ion charge-state particle flux](name:ion_charge_state_particle_flux) evaluated through an oriented surface whose normal is the poloidal unit vector. It is local, not surface-integrated or flux-surface-averaged, and it is not summed over charge states. Summing the charge-state contributions for the same species gives the [poloidal ion particle flux](name:poloidal_ion_particle_flux). Unlike [parallel ion charge-state particle flux](name:parallel_ion_charge_state_particle_flux), this projection selects a geometric poloidal direction rather than the magnetic-field direction. Sign convention: Positive when the net ion number flow follows increasing poloidal angle $\theta$.

rows.name: poloidal_ion_charge_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift
rows.description: Signed poloidal projection of the E×B guiding-center drift for one ion charge state in the edge plasma, along a specified local poloidal direction.
rows.documentation: The poloidal component of the [ion charge-state E×B drift velocity](name:ion_charge_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift) is its signed projection along a specified local poloidal direction. This direction lies in the meridional plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; its positive orientation must be specified. For the ideal E×B guiding-center drift, the defining projection is $$ v_{E,\mathrm{p}} = \mathbf{v}_E \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{p}} = \frac{(\mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{B})\cdot\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{p}}}{|\mathbf{B}|^2}. $$ Here $v_{E,\mathrm{p}}$ is the poloidal drift component for the specified ion charge state, $\mathbf{v}_E$ is its ideal E×B drift velocity, $\mathbf{E}$ is the local electric field, $\mathbf{B}$ is the local magnetic field, and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{p}}$ is the unit vector along the specified positive local poloidal direction. The definition requires a nonzero magnetic field and magnetized ions. This quantity applies locally to one specified charge state of one ion species in the edge plasma; it is neither summed nor averaged over charge states or species. At fixed local fields, the ideal drift is independent of ion mass and charge. Other contributions to the ion fluid velocity are excluded. It is a linear velocity component, not a poloidal angle or angular velocity. Unlike the [parallel component](name:parallel_ion_charge_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift), which vanishes identically for the ideal E×B drift, the poloidal projection need not vanish: the local poloidal direction is not generally aligned with the magnetic field. Sign convention: Positive when the E×B drift has a component along the specified positive local poloidal unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{p}}$.

rows.name: poloidal_neutral_internal_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient
rows.description: Fick's-law poloidal neutral internal-state energy diffusion coefficient multiplying the poloidal temperature gradient of neutral particles in a specified internal state in diffusive thermal-energy transport. It is internal-state-resolved and represents only the Fickian poloidal contribution.
rows.documentation:
Fick's-law poloidal neutral internal-state energy diffusion coefficient is the scalar poloidal diffusivity for energy transport by neutral particles in a specified internal state, and is the poloidal component form of the [neutral internal-state energy diffusion coefficient](name:neutral_internal_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient). It is resolved for one internal state, not summed or averaged over internal states, and relates only the poloidal projection of the diffusive thermal-energy flux to the poloidal temperature gradient of those same particles. The poloidal projection is taken along the tangent obtained by increasing the poloidal angle $	heta$ at constant flux coordinate $ho$ and toroidal angle $\phi$ in a chosen flux-coordinate system $(ho, 	heta, \phi)$. The Fickian poloidal contribution is defined by $$ q^{\mathrm{diff}}_{E,n,s,	heta} = - n_{n,s} D^{	heta}_{E,n,s} \, \hat{\mathbf{e}}_{	heta}\cdot
abla T_{n,s} $$ where $q^{\mathrm{diff}}_{E,n,s,	heta}$ is the poloidal component of the diffusive thermal-energy flux carried by neutral particles in internal state $s$, positive in the direction of increasing $	heta$; $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{	heta}$ is the corresponding unit poloidal tangent; $n_{n,s}$ is the number density of those particles; $D^{	heta}_{E,n,s}$ is this coefficient; and $T_{n,s}$ is their temperature. The coefficient includes only the diagonal Fickian term driven by $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{	heta}\cdot
abla T_{n,s}$ and excludes convective energy transport, sources, sinks, cross-gradient tensor terms, and effective coefficients that absorb non-diffusive contributions. The factor $n_{n,s}\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{	heta}\cdot
abla T_{n,s}$ is the temperature-gradient contribution to the poloidal gradient of internal thermal-energy density; an energy-density-gradient form using $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{	heta}\cdot
abla(n_{n,s}T_{n,s})$ is equivalent only when the density-gradient contribution along the poloidal tangent is absent. It specializes the internal-state energy diffusion coefficient to neutral particles and the poloidal projection. It is distinct from the [radial neutral internal-state energy diffusion coefficient](name:radial_neutral_internal_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient), where radial denotes the $\hat{R}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and is the internal-state-resolved counterpart of the [poloidal neutral energy diffusivity](name:poloidal_neutral_energy_diffusivity).

rows.name: power_density_due_to_collisions
rows.description: Signed local rate of collisional energy exchange per unit volume for a specified plasma population, species, charge state, or internal state.
rows.documentation: This quantity is the net local volumetric energy exchange caused by Coulomb collisions for a designated target population. It is positive for energy deposited in the target and negative for energy transferred from it. $$ P_a^{\mathrm{coll}} = \sum_b Q_{a\leftarrow b}^{\mathrm{coll}} $$ where $P_a^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the target power density in W m$^{-3}$, $Q_{a\leftarrow b}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the collisional energy-transfer rate per unit volume from partner population $b$ to target $a$, and the sum includes the collision partners and subpopulations specified by the quantity's aggregation scope. The target may be a broad population, as in particle collisional power density, or a species, ion charge state, internal state, or electron population. Aggregated electron and ion quantities include the designated contributing species and states, whereas resolved quantities retain only their specified target, as in [ion charge-state collisional power density](name:ion_charge_state_power_density_due_to_collisions) and internal-state collisional power density. Sign convention: Positive when the designated target population gains energy from its collision partners.

rows.name: radial_conductivity
rows.description: Local electrical response coefficient relating a major-radius electric field to the conductive current density it drives along the cylindrical major-radius direction.
rows.documentation: Radial conductivity is the major-radius–major-radius projection of the local plasma electrical-conductivity tensor in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Here $R$ is major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; the radial direction points toward increasing $R$. The defining tensor projection is $$ \sigma_{RR} = \hat{R} \cdot \boldsymbol{\sigma} \cdot \hat{R} $$ where $\sigma_{RR}$ is radial conductivity, $\boldsymbol{\sigma}$ is the [plasma electrical-conductivity tensor](name:plasma_electrical_conductivity), and $\hat{R}$ is the unit vector in the major-radius direction. For an electric field directed solely along the major-radius direction, the conductive response satisfies $j_R^{\mathrm{cond}} = \sigma_{RR} E_R$, where $j_R^{\mathrm{cond}}$ is the major-radius component of conductive current density and $E_R$ is the major-radius electric-field component. For a general electric field, off-diagonal tensor components can also contribute to the major-radius current density. This is a local plasma transport coefficient, not a spatial average or integrated conductance. Its projection direction is geometric: it is not defined by a minor-radius flux label, a flux-surface normal, or the magnetic-field direction. In contrast, [parallel conductivity](name:parallel_conductivity) projects the same electrical response along the local magnetic field.

rows.name: radial_diamagnetic_current_density
rows.description: Radial diamagnetic current density is the signed major-radius projection of pressure-gradient-driven electric current in the edge plasma.
rows.documentation: Radial diamagnetic current density is the local major-radius projection of the pressure-gradient-driven contribution to [current density](name:current_density) in the edge plasma. It is a signed component of the vector [current density due to diamagnetic drift](name:current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift). The projection is defined by: $$ j_{\mathrm{dia},R} = \hat{R}\cdot\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{dia}} $$ where $j_{\mathrm{dia},R}$ is the radial diamagnetic current density, $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the diamagnetic current-density vector, and $\hat{R}$ is the unit vector toward increasing major radius. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. This quantity includes the algebraic sum of diamagnetic contributions from all included charge carriers, without species or charge-state resolution. It excludes current contributions attributed to other mechanisms. The radial direction is the cylindrical major-radius direction, not a flux-surface-normal direction or the magnetic-field-perpendicular projection. The [diamagnetic current density](name:diamagnetic_current_density) is the magnitude of the same vector, whereas this component retains its directional sign. The [parallel diamagnetic current density](name:parallel_diamagnetic_current_density) instead projects that vector onto the local magnetic-field direction. Sign convention: Positive when the diamagnetic conventional current flows toward increasing major radius $R$, away from the toroidal symmetry axis.

rows.name: radial_effective_electron_diffusivity
rows.description: Effective coefficient relating the radial diffusive flux of electron particles to the radial gradient of electron number density in edge-plasma transport.
rows.documentation: Effective coefficient relating the radial diffusive flux of electron particles to the radial gradient of electron number density is the scalar Fickian closure coefficient for radial electron particle diffusion in the edge plasma. It describes the diffusive, cross-field radial part of electron particle transport. The radial diffusive electron particle flux is related to the radial density gradient by $$ \Gamma_{e,r}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{e,r}^{\mathrm{eff}}\,\frac{\partial n_e}{\partial r} $$ where $\Gamma_{e,r}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the radial diffusive electron particle flux, $D_{e,r}^{\mathrm{eff}}$ is this effective radial electron diffusivity, $n_e$ is the [electron number density](name:electron_number_density), and $r$ is the radial transport coordinate. The scope is electron particles in the edge plasma and the radial component of the diffusive particle-flux closure. It excludes the convective or advective part of electron particle flux, particle sources and sinks, parallel transport along the magnetic field, and the total electron particle flux. It is the radial member of the direction-dependent [effective electron diffusivity](name:effective_electron_diffusivity). The broader [electron diffusion coefficient](name:electron_diffusion_coefficient) denotes electron particle diffusion without the radial effective-component restriction, while the radial electron diffusion coefficient denotes the corresponding radial coefficient when the effective-closure distinction is not made. With the minus sign in the defining relation, a positive $D_{e,r}^{\mathrm{eff}}$ produces diffusive electron particle flux down the gradient of $n_e$; an effective negative value represents an up-gradient flux contribution in the same closure.

rows.name: radial_effective_ion_diffusivity
rows.description: Effective Fickian coefficient relating the radial diffusive flux of the charge-state-summed ion population to its total particle-density gradient.
rows.documentation: The radial effective ion diffusivity is the Fickian transport coefficient for ion particle diffusion in the radial direction. It applies to the ion population summed over all ionic charge states and is the radial component of [effective ion diffusivity](name:effective_ion_diffusivity). The defining relation is $$ \Gamma_{i,r}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{i,r}^{\mathrm{eff}}\,\frac{\partial n_i}{\partial r} $$ where $\Gamma_{i,r}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the radial diffusive ion-particle flux, $D_{i,r}^{\mathrm{eff}}$ is this effective diffusivity, $n_i$ is the total ion particle number density, and $r$ is the radial coordinate. The radial flux is positive away from the magnetic axis; consequently, a positive diffusivity gives flux down the total-ion density gradient. This quantity excludes convective, conductive, and source terms.

rows.name: radial_ion_charge_state_diffusion_coefficient
rows.description: Effective Fickian coefficient relating major-radius-directed diffusive particle flux to the opposing number-density gradient for ions of one species and charge state.
rows.documentation: The radial ion charge-state diffusion coefficient characterizes particle diffusion of one specified ion species and charge state along the major-radius direction. It selects the radial-radial diagonal response in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. For the diffusive flux contribution driven by the major-radius density gradient, the defining relation is: $$ \Gamma_{s,q,R}^{\mathrm{diff},RR} = -D_{s,q,RR}\frac{\partial n_{s,q}}{\partial R} $$ where $s$ identifies the ion species, $q$ is its ionic charge number, $\Gamma_{s,q,R}^{\mathrm{diff},RR}$ is the radial diffusive particle flux density contributed by this diagonal response, $D_{s,q,RR}$ is the radial ion charge-state diffusion coefficient, and $n_{s,q}$ is that species' number density in the specified charge state. The derivative is taken at fixed toroidal angle and vertical height. The minus sign expresses down-gradient transport for positive diffusivity. The population includes thermal and nonthermal ions of the specified species and charge state, without summing over charge states. This is a particle transport coefficient, not an energy or momentum transport coefficient, and it excludes convective contributions. The major-radius direction is not generally normal to magnetic flux surfaces or perpendicular to the magnetic field. This is the radial-radial diagonal specialization of the [ion charge-state diffusion coefficient](name:ion_charge_state_diffusion_coefficient), not a sum of directional coefficients. Off-diagonal diffusion-tensor couplings, when present, provide additional radial flux contributions outside the defining relation above. In contrast, the [ion diffusion coefficient](name:ion_diffusion_coefficient) applies to a charge-state-summed ion population; its effective value is not obtained by simply summing charge-state diffusion coefficients.

rows.name: radial_ion_charge_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient
rows.description: Fick's-law proportionality coefficient relating the density-normalized radial diffusive thermal energy flux of a specified ion charge state to its local temperature gradient.
rows.documentation: The ion charge-state energy diffusion coefficient in the radial direction quantifies gradient-driven diffusive transport of thermal energy carried by ions in one specified charge state. It is the radial directional specialization of the [ion charge-state energy diffusion coefficient](name:ion_charge_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient), applying to the component along increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The defining relation for the density-normalized radial diffusive energy flux of charge state $z$ is: $$ \frac{Q_{i,z,\mathrm{diff},R}}{n_{i,z}} = -D_{i,z,E,R}\,\frac{\partial T_{i,z}}{\partial R} $$ where $Q_{i,z,\mathrm{diff},R}$ is the radial component of the diffusive thermal energy flux carried by ions in charge state $z$, $n_{i,z}$ is their number density, $T_{i,z}$ is their [temperature](name:ion_charge_state_temperature), and $D_{i,z,E,R}$ is this radial diffusion coefficient. The minus sign denotes radial transport down the local radial temperature gradient. This quantity applies to one specified ion charge state and is not an aggregation over charge states. It excludes convective, advective, and $E \times B$ contributions to the total ion heat flux; the charge-state-aggregated [ion energy diffusion coefficient](name:ion_energy_diffusion_coefficient) is a density-weighted mean over all ion species and charge states. Other directional specializations include the [parallel ion charge-state energy diffusion coefficient](name:parallel_ion_charge_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient) and the [poloidal ion charge-state energy diffusion coefficient](name:poloidal_ion_charge_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient).

rows.name: radial_ion_charge_state_velocity
rows.description: Major-radius projection of the mean flow of ions of one specified species and ionization charge state, directed toward or away from the toroidal symmetry axis.
rows.documentation: The radial ion charge-state velocity is the projection of the bulk [ion charge-state velocity](name:ion_charge_state_velocity) onto the direction of increasing major radius in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It describes mean translational motion within one specified ion species and ionization charge state. The component is defined by the projected first velocity moment: $$ u_{R,q}(\mathbf r)=\hat{\mathbf R}\cdot\mathbf u_q(\mathbf r)=\frac{\int (\mathbf v\cdot\hat{\mathbf R})f_q(\mathbf r,\mathbf v)\,d^3v}{\int f_q(\mathbf r,\mathbf v)\,d^3v} $$ where $u_{R,q}$ is the radial bulk velocity, $\mathbf u_q$ is the charge-state bulk velocity vector, $q$ is the ionic charge number, $\mathbf r$ is position, $\mathbf v$ is particle velocity, and $f_q$ is the velocity distribution of the selected species and charge state. The integration covers particle velocity space. Here $R$ is distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, $Z$ is vertical position, and $\hat{\mathbf R}$ is the unit vector toward increasing $R$. The component is evaluated at the position of maximum major radius on each magnetic flux surface; it is not a flux-surface average. It retains charge-state resolution rather than combining charge states. The corresponding [radial ion velocity](name:radial_ion_velocity) is the density-weighted mean over all ionic charge states of the species, not their sum. This signed component is distinct from flow speed, random thermal motion, and particle flux. The major-radius direction is not generally normal to a magnetic flux surface, so this quantity is not a flux-surface-normal velocity. Sign convention: Positive when the charge-state bulk flow projects toward increasing major radius, away from the toroidal symmetry axis.

rows.name: radial_ion_diffusion_coefficient
rows.description: Effective Fickian diffusivity for total-ion particle transport, relating the radial diffusive flux across magnetic surfaces to the opposing radial gradient of charge-state-summed ion density.
rows.documentation: Radial ion diffusion coefficient is the effective particle diffusivity for total ions moving radially across nested magnetic flux surfaces. It parameterizes Fickian radial mixing of charge-state-summed ion density. For radial transport, the defining relation is $$ \Gamma_{i,\mathrm{diff}}^{(r)} = -D_i^{\mathrm{eff},(r)}\nabla_r n_i $$ where $\Gamma_{i,\mathrm{diff}}^{(r)}$ is the radial diffusive particle-flux component, $D_i^{\mathrm{eff},(r)}$ is the radial effective diffusivity, $\nabla_r n_i$ is the radial gradient of total ion number density, and $n_i$ is the ion density summed over all ionic charge states. The minus sign specifies transport down the density gradient. This is the radial member of the general [ion diffusion coefficient](name:ion_diffusion_coefficient) family. Neutral particles and charge-state-resolved coefficients, such as the [radial ion charge-state diffusion coefficient](name:radial_ion_charge_state_diffusion_coefficient), are excluded.

rows.name: radial_ion_momentum_flux_over_edge_region
rows.description: Radial ion momentum flux in the edge region is the signed transfer of a specified ion species' major-radius-directed momentum per unit area and time across a magnetic flux surface.
rows.documentation: Radial ion momentum flux in the edge region describes transport of the major-radius component of [momentum](name:momentum) carried by a specified ion species across a magnetic flux surface. It includes the total momentum transport, rather than an isolated diffusive or convective contribution. The defining projection is: $$ \Gamma_{i,R} = \hat{R} \cdot \boldsymbol{\Pi}_i \cdot \hat{n}_{\mathrm{out}} $$ where $\Gamma_{i,R}$ is this momentum flux, $i$ identifies the ion species, $\boldsymbol{\Pi}_i$ is its total linear-momentum-flux tensor, $\hat{R}$ is the unit vector toward increasing major radius, and $\hat{n}_{\mathrm{out}}$ is the outward unit normal to the magnetic flux surface. The major-radius direction belongs to the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The transported momentum projection and the surface-normal transport direction are distinct; the surface normal need not coincide with $\hat{R}$. The flux is summed over all ionic charge states of the specified species, excluding neutral atoms, electrons, and other ion species. Its individual charge-state contributions are [radial ion charge-state momentum fluxes](name:radial_ion_charge_state_momentum_flux). The total tensor includes convective momentum transport, pressure, and viscous or turbulent stresses. This quantity is a flux per unit surface area, not momentum density, a local momentum source, or an area-integrated momentum transfer rate. Sign convention: Positive when the net transport carries momentum directed toward increasing major radius outward across the magnetic flux surface, or equivalently carries momentum directed toward decreasing major radius inward.

rows.name: radial_neutral_internal_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient
rows.description: Fick's-law radial neutral internal-state energy diffusion coefficient multiplying the R-direction temperature gradient, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, of neutral particles in a specified internal state in diffusive thermal-energy transport. It is internal-state-resolved and represents only the Fickian radial contribution.
rows.documentation: Fick's-law radial neutral internal-state energy diffusion coefficient is the scalar radial diffusivity for energy transport by neutral particles in a specified internal state, and is the radial component form of the [neutral internal-state energy diffusion coefficient](name:neutral_internal_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient). Here radial denotes projection along $\hat{R}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is resolved for one internal state, not summed or averaged over internal states. The radial Fickian contribution is defined by $$ q^{\mathrm{diff}}_{E,n,s,R} = - n_{n,s} D_{E,n,s,R} \frac{\partial T_{n,s}}{\partial R} $$ where $q^{\mathrm{diff}}_{E,n,s,R}$ is the radial component of the diffusive thermal-energy flux carried by neutral particles in internal state $s$, $n_{n,s}$ is their number density, $D_{E,n,s,R}$ is this coefficient, and $T_{n,s}$ is their temperature. The coefficient includes only the Fickian term driven by $\partial T_{n,s}/\partial R$ and excludes convective energy transport, sources, sinks, and effective coefficients that absorb non-diffusive contributions.
